docs.title: Install the tools: Windows
docs.text:
This series runs on macOS and Linux. On Windows, you work inside WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux: a real Linux system running alongside Windows. Later lessons give the agent a workspace that only works on macOS and Linux, so a native Windows setup would stop working partway through the series. With WSL, every lesson works the same as on Linux.

We have not run these steps on Windows: everything here comes from Microsoft's and VS Code's documentation, linked below. If a step does not do what it says, the lesson has a gap: please report it.

Installing WSL can take longer than the lesson itself, and is not counted in its 15 minutes. You do it once.

docs.title: How WSL works
docs.text:
In Microsoft's words, WSL "allows you to run a Linux environment on your Windows machine". WSL 2, the version installed by default, runs a real Linux kernel inside a lightweight virtual machine that Windows starts and stops for you. You do not manage the virtual machine: you open a Linux terminal, and it is there.

The two systems share files:

  • From Linux, your Windows drives appear under /mnt/: C:\Users is /mnt/c/Users.
  • From Windows, your Linux files appear in File Explorer: type \\wsl$ in the address bar.

Keep your projects in Linux, in your Linux home folder (~), not under /mnt/c. Microsoft: "For the fastest performance speed, store your files in the WSL file system if you are working in a Linux command line." Every command in this series runs in the Linux terminal, so the project belongs there.

Sources: What is WSL?, Working across file systems.

docs.title: Install WSL
docs.text:
You need Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or newer (build 19041 or newer).

  1. Open PowerShell as administrator: right-click it in the Start menu and choose Run as administrator.
  2. Run:
wsl --install

This turns on the features WSL needs, sets WSL 2 as the default, and installs the Ubuntu distribution of Linux. 3. Restart Windows when it asks. 4. Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. The first time, it finishes installing and asks you to create a Linux user name and password: - They are for Linux only, and have nothing to do with your Windows account. - Nothing appears on screen while you type the password. That is normal. - You will need the password whenever a command starts with sudo.

Source: Install WSL, Set up a WSL development environment.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
From PowerShell (it does not need to be administrator), check that Ubuntu runs on WSL 2:

wsl -l -v

You should see Ubuntu listed, with 2 in the VERSION column. If it says 1, switch it with wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2.

In the Ubuntu terminal, bring Ubuntu's packages up to date, entering your Linux password when asked:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

Then check where you are:

cd ~
pwd

You should see /home/ followed by your Linux user name. That is your Linux home folder: make the lesson's project here.

Microsoft recommends Windows Terminal for working with WSL: each Linux distribution you install gets its own entry in it. The Ubuntu app from the Start menu works too.

docs.title: Connect VS Code to WSL
docs.text:
If you use VS Code, it runs on Windows and works on your Linux files through an extension. Do not install VS Code inside Linux.

  1. Install VS Code on Windows. In the installer, keep Add to PATH checked, so you can open it from the Ubuntu terminal.
  2. In VS Code, open the Extensions view, search for WSL, and install the extension by Microsoft (identifier ms-vscode-remote.remote-wsl).
  3. In the Ubuntu terminal, go to a folder and open it in VS Code:
cd ~
code .

The first time, VS Code installs its server inside WSL, which takes a moment. Then a VS Code window opens on your Linux folder, with a WSL indicator in its bottom-left corner. A terminal opened in that window is an Ubuntu terminal. 4. Extensions that work on your code, such as the Python extension, must be installed again for WSL: with the WSL window open, install them from its Extensions view. Themes need installing only once.

If code . is not found, VS Code was installed without Add to PATH: reinstall it with that box checked, then open a new Ubuntu terminal.

If you use PyCharm instead, it works with WSL too, through a WSL interpreter. JetBrains' guide, Configure an interpreter using WSL, shows how. Like the rest of this page, that route comes from the documentation and has not been run.

Sources: Get started using VS Code with WSL, Developing in WSL.

docs.title: Then follow the Linux guide
docs.text:
From here on, everything happens inside Ubuntu: follow Install the tools: Linux, then go back to Setting up the environment and run every command there in the Ubuntu terminal, starting in your Linux home folder (cd ~).

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: The example you'll work with
docs.text: A short reading page, before the setup lesson. Nothing to install or run yet.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Before you build, a quick look at the two pieces of code this series hands you. You don't need to learn either one — they're given, not taught — but it helps to know what they're for.

The project you're building is a coding assistant: an agent that answers questions about code. That makes the cast simple:

  • tinyjobs is the sample codebase it practises on — a small job-queue program. What it does barely matters, and you'll never need to run it. It's just some code to answer questions about.
  • The codebase API is a small ready-made module your agent's tools call to read a codebase — listing its modules, reading what each says about itself. It's ours, not part of Pydantic AI, and you'll see it again on this page.

That's the whole cast.

This is a reading page; no commands to run.

docs.title: What tinyjobs is, at a glance
docs.text:
As a program, tinyjobs is a job queue: you submit jobs, it runs them, it remembers them. That's all you need to know about what it does — what matters is what it is: about 250 lines of plain Python in five modules, with a test suite.

One of its tests fails, and that's on purpose: tinyjobs has a known bug. You don't need to find it. Later in the series, your agent does.

docs.title: What your agent will be asked
docs.text:
Over the series, your agent gets more ways to reach into tinyjobs, and each one lets it answer a harder question. Roughly in order:

Your agent can… So you can ask it… From List its modules and read what each says about itself "What does the jobs module do?" Chapter 1 Read its files, but never its secrets "Explain the command's flags." Chapter 3 Run its tests "The test suite has a failure. Why?" Chapter 3 Remember what you decided "What did we decide about logging?" Chapter 4 Change it, once you approve "Add a --verbose flag, and a test for it." Later

You don't need to remember this table. Each lesson says what your agent can do by the end of it.

docs.title: How it works, at a high level
docs.text:
tinyjobs is about 250 lines of plain Python, with no dependencies. Its code is in five modules, under src/tinyjobs/:

Module What it holds tinyjobs The package itself: what it offers to other code tinyjobs.jobs A job, and the queue that holds jobs tinyjobs.storage Saving the queue to its JSON file, and loading it back tinyjobs.cli The tinyjobs command line tinyjobs.log Where log messages go

Its tests are in tests/, beside src/. A real project also keeps secrets out of its code, in a .env file. Later lessons give tinyjobs one, with a fake secret in it, to check that your agent never shows it.

docs.title: Your code, and the example's
docs.text:
Your project holds three kinds of code, and it helps to keep them apart:

Kind Where What you do with it Your code src/pydantic_tutor/ (all but codebase.py), scripts/ You write it, lesson by lesson. This is what the series teaches The codebase API src/pydantic_tutor/codebase.py Given to you. Your tools call it; you don't need to read it tinyjobs sample_code/tinyjobs/ Given to you. Your agent reads it, and later changes it once you approve; you never change it yourself

The codebase API is a small module that reads a codebase for your agent's tools. It's ours, not part of Pydantic AI. You call two functions:

  • codebase.list_modules(root=...) gives a codebase's modules by name, such as tinyjobs.jobs.
  • codebase.read_docstring(root=..., module=...) gives what one module says about itself, in its docstring, without running it.

It refuses a name the codebase doesn't have, so a name that sneaks outside the codebase, such as "../../.env", reads nothing. Later, when your agent gets a workspace, the API reads through that instead, and the lesson that does it says how.

Why hand you this code rather than have you write it? Because finding a codebase's modules is ordinary Python. It isn't what this series teaches. The tools that call it are, and you write those.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
You can say what tinyjobs does, and what your agent will be asked about it. It's a small job queue with a command line, a test suite with one known failure, and a plan to have your agent read it, run its tests and, in the end, change it.

You can tell your code from the example's. You write the agent and its tools. You're given the codebase API and tinyjobs. Your agent reads tinyjobs; you never change it yourself.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Next, you set up the project for real: you install Pydantic AI with uv, run your first agent with no API key, and check and commit your code. tinyjobs joins the project when your agent gets its first tools, in the function tools lesson.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Let's create the project you'll build in for the rest of the series. You start from an empty folder, run a handful of commands, and write one small file: check your tools, create a Python project with uv, install Pydantic AI and its harness at pinned versions, run a five-line agent — no API key, no cost — protect a secrets file you haven't made yet, add the code checks, and commit the lot to git.

That commit is on your own machine; nothing needs a GitHub account. From the next lesson on you can keep building on this project, or clone the lesson starting points we publish — handy if you skip a lesson or yours breaks. A starting point isn't always identical to what you built: some lessons add files on it, such as their own tests. Both routes work, and each lesson says which files it expects.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Check your tools: git, and uv 0.13.1 or newer.
  2. Create a uv project pinned to pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0 on Python 3.14, say why those two pins must move together, and check its code with Ruff and mypy.
  3. Run an agent with no API key, and make sure your .env file can't be committed by accident.

About 15 minutes, not counting installing tools. The series is tested with Python 3.14, uv 0.13.1, Ruff 0.16.10 and mypy 2.4.0.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
You start from an empty folder and end with a Python project, in its own git repository, with a first agent in it. Almost every file is made by a command you run. You write one file yourself, add an empty one, and add a few lines to two others:

pydantic-tutor/
├── .gitignore              made by uv; you add one line for .env
├── .python-version         made by uv: 3.14
├── README.md               made by uv, empty
├── hello_agent.py          you write it: a five-line agent that needs no API key
├── pyproject.toml          made by uv: the project, its dependencies and their pins;
│                           you add the code checks' settings
├── uv.lock                 made by uv: the exact version of every package installed
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── __init__.py     made by uv: the package, with a hello-world command
        └── py.typed        you add it, empty: the package's types can be trusted

There's nothing to fetch first: this lesson starts from an empty folder. The steps, in order:

  1. Check your tools: git and uv, and that git knows your name.
  2. Create the project with uv init, and run its command.
  3. Install Pydantic AI and the harness, at pinned versions.
  4. Run your first agent: five lines of Python on TestModel.
  5. Keep secrets out of git: make sure .env can't be committed by accident.
  6. Check your code: add Ruff and mypy, and run them until they report nothing.
  7. Commit.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Step 1: Check your tools
docs.text:
Goal: confirm you have git, and uv 0.13.1 or newer, and that git knows your name and email.

Everything in this lesson runs in a terminal, on macOS or Linux, with two tools: git and uv. You don't need to install Python: uv downloads the version the project asks for, the first time it needs it.

Check that both tools are there:

git --version
uv --version

If either command isn't found, or uv is older than 0.13.1, follow the guide for your system, then come back:

  • macOS
  • Linux
  • Windows: you work inside WSL, a Linux system on Windows

Then check that git knows who you are:

git config user.name
git config user.email

If either prints nothing, set it:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Tip

Check: the first two commands print versions, such as:

git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155)
uv 0.13.1 (62faed335 2026-10-13 aarch64-apple-darwin)

uv is 0.13.1 or newer, and the two git config commands each print a value.

What it means

Your versions may be newer than these; that's fine. Your name and email matter because two things use them. uv copies them into the project's pyproject.toml in the next step, and every commit records who made it. On some systems a commit fails without them. On others git guesses, and the guess ends up in your history.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the project
docs.text:
Goal: create a uv project for Python 3.14, and run the command it comes with.

This makes the project every later lesson adds to. It comes first because every other command runs inside it.

Make an empty folder for the project, outside any other git repository, and go into it. Every command from here on runs inside this folder.

mkdir pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv init --package --python 3.14

You should see:

Initialized project `pydantic-tutor`

List what's there now:

ls -A

.git
.gitignore
.python-version
README.md
pyproject.toml
src

The order can differ on your system, which sorts names its own way; the six names must all be there.

Tip

Check: run the command the project comes with:

uv run pydantic-tutor

You should see this. Your paths and timings will differ, and so may Python's patch version (3.14.8 here). If uv already has a Python 3.14, the two download lines are missing:

Downloading cpython-3.14.8-macos-aarch64-none (download) (25.4MiB)
Downloaded cpython-3.14.8-macos-aarch64-none (download)
Using CPython 3.14.8
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Building pydantic-tutor @ file:///Users/you/pydantic-tutor
Built pydantic-tutor @ file:///Users/you/pydantic-tutor
Installed 1 package in 1ms
Hello from pydantic-tutor!

What it means

The last line is a small hello-world that uv init wrote for you: a main() function in src/pydantic_tutor/__init__.py, which pyproject.toml turns into the pydantic-tutor command you ran.

Everything above it is uv's one habit: sync, then run. Every uv run first makes the environment match the project, then runs your command. Before running yours, uv downloaded Python 3.14 (only the first time), created .venv — the project's private virtual environment, where its packages live — and installed your project into it. ls -A showed no .venv a moment ago. It exists now because you ran uv run.

The two flags shaped what you got. --package makes the project installable, with its code under src/; that's already uv's default at 0.13.1, so passing it makes the layout explicit in the command itself. --python 3.14 wrote 3.14 to .python-version, which uv reads to choose this project's Python. It also added requires-python = ">=3.14" to pyproject.toml: the project runs on 3.14 here, and declares that it needs 3.14 or newer wherever it runs next. uv also filled in your name and email there, from your git settings.

The folder wasn't a git repository yet, so uv init made it one (.git) and wrote a .gitignore along with it. That's why the folder had to be outside any other repository: inside one, uv init skips both, and steps 5 and 7 won't work as written.

docs.title: Step 3: Install Pydantic AI and the harness
docs.text:
Goal: add the two packages the series is built on, at pinned versions, and see the third one they bring in.

The project runs, but it has no Pydantic AI in it yet. One command adds it, at the versions this lesson was tested with:

uv add "pydantic-ai==2.56.0" "pydantic-ai-harness==0.56.0"

uv prints a few lines of progress (the first time, it names the larger packages as it downloads them). Then it prints one line for every package it installed: about a hundred, each starting with +, in alphabetical order. Your two, + pydantic-ai==2.56.0 and + pydantic-ai-harness==0.56.0, are somewhere in the middle. You don't need to read the list. The check below shows what matters.

Why two pins? pydantic-ai installs the framework through pydantic-ai-slim, along with optional integrations. pydantic-ai-harness adds capabilities such as access to files and a shell. For these releases, both depend on the same exact version of pydantic-ai-slim: 2.56.0. That's why we pin them together. You don't need to remember the packaging details; the check below lets you see the shared dependency for yourself.

Open pyproject.toml. Yours should look like this, with your own name and email:

pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "pydantic-tutor"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Ada Student", email = "ada@example.com" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pydantic-ai==2.56.0",
    "pydantic-ai-harness==0.56.0",
]

[project.scripts]
pydantic-tutor = "pydantic_tutor:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.1,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

Before you run the check, predict: you asked for two packages. Which package do you think both of them depend on?

Tip

Check: ask uv what depends on pydantic-ai-slim:

uv tree --invert --package pydantic-ai-slim --depth 1

You should see this. Check that pydantic-ai-slim says v2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness says v0.56.0. The number of packages resolved can differ: uv picks the newest releases of the packages your pins don't fix, and those change over time:

Resolved 107 packages in 2ms
pydantic-ai-slim v2.56.0
├── pydantic-ai[anthropic, cli, evals, google, logfire, mcp, openai, web] v2.56.0
├── pydantic-ai-harness v0.56.0
└── pydantic-evals v2.56.0

What it means

There's the shared dependency: pydantic-ai-slim at 2.56.0. The square brackets on the pydantic-ai line list optional integrations; pydantic-evals is another dependency in the tree. You don't need to study those packages now. The important point is that your two pins resolve to a compatible framework version. When you upgrade later, check that the versions still agree.

Notice that you didn't edit pyproject.toml at all: uv init and uv add wrote all of it between them. Keep adding and removing dependencies through uv, never by hand, so the file always matches what's installed.

docs.title: Step 4: Run your first agent
docs.text:
Goal: run an agent with no API key, and read what Pydantic AI's banner tells you.

This first agent is deliberately small: it creates an Agent with TestModel, runs it on a greeting, and prints the result. Notice TestModel(): that's why this first run needs neither an API key nor a paid model. You don't need to understand the rest of the agent yet; the next lesson will unpack it.

Create a file called hello_agent.py in the project folder, next to pyproject.toml, with this content:

hello_agent.py:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

agent = Agent(model=TestModel())
result = agent.run_sync(user_prompt="Hello!")
print(result.output)

Tip

Check: run it:

uv run hello_agent.py

You should see this. The banner's layout depends on how wide your terminal is: in a narrower one, its lines wrap differently, and below about 60 columns the drawing is left out. Check the first line's versions and the last line:

pydantic-ai v2.56.0 • pydantic-ai-harness v0.56.0 • Python 3.14.8
/ \
/   \       agent: agent • model: test:test • tools: 0 • capabilities: 0
/___.___\
/    |    \    observability: off — see every model and tool call live, with cost
/      |      \    set it up free with Logfire and a GitHub login: https://pydantic.dev/ai-setup.md
`---.._|_..---'    or use any OpenTelemetry backend: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/logfire/#otel

goes away once observability is on — or PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1
success (no tool calls)

What it means

The last line is your first agent answering. run_sync ran the agent and waited for the result, and result.output is the answer. It came from TestModel, a stand-in model that ships with Pydantic AI: it answers at once, inside your own program, calling no provider, so it needs no API key and costs nothing. Unless you tell it what to say, it replies success (no tool calls) whenever no tool was called.

Everything above that line is the banner. Pydantic AI prints it once per process, the first time an agent runs. It confirms the versions you installed, the agent's name (taken from the variable you assigned it to, agent) and the model it used. It also points you toward observability, a way to watch every model and tool call, which a later lesson covers.

The banner is only there to confirm what you already know. Guess what the output looks like with it turned off, then set PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER and check your guess:

PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1 uv run hello_agent.py

success (no tool calls)

Notice the code itself: Agent(model=...), run_sync(user_prompt=...). Every argument has its name. Python would accept them without the names, but this series passes arguments by keyword everywhere, so every call says plainly what it's doing.

Keep hello_agent.py after this lesson. Whenever your environment looks wrong later on, running it again tells you in a second whether Pydantic AI still works.

docs.title: Step 5: Keep secrets out of git
docs.text:
Goal: make sure a .env file can't be committed by accident, before it exists.

You don't create .env yet. You make sure git will never pick it up by accident, because the only reliable time is before the file exists: from the chat lesson on, .env will hold your API key, and a key that reaches git history can be used by anyone with a copy of the repository — it stays there even if you delete the file in a later commit.

Ask git whether it would ignore a .env file now:

git check-ignore -v .env

It prints nothing: nothing in .gitignore covers .env yet.

Open .gitignore and add these lines at the end, starting with the blank line:

.gitignore (add at the end):

# Secrets: holds your API key from the chat lesson on. Never commit it.
.env
.env.*

The whole file should now read:

# Python-generated files
__pycache__/
*.py[oc]
build/
dist/
wheels/
*.egg-info

# Virtual environments
.venv

# Secrets: holds your API key from the chat lesson on. Never commit it.
.env
.env.*

Tip

Check: ask git again:

git check-ignore -v .env

You should see:

.gitignore:13:.env  .env

What it means

Git named the rule that matched: line 13 of .gitignore, the line you added. And there's still no .env in the folder. Git checks a name against .gitignore, not a file, so git add will skip .env from the day you create it. That stops accidents, not decisions: git add -f .env adds it anyway, so never use -f on a file that holds a secret.

The rest of the file is what uv init wrote. It already ignored Python's caches, build files and .venv, but it said nothing about secrets until you added that line.

docs.title: Step 6: Check your code
docs.text:
Goal: add Ruff and mypy to the project, and run them until they report nothing.

The code runs. Now you add the two checkers from the tools lesson — Ruff, which formats and lints, and mypy, which checks every use of a value against its type — so the code is also written to a standard before the first commit.

Add them to the project as development tools, with a third beside them, pytest, the test runner, at the versions this lesson was tested with:

uv add --dev "ruff==0.16.10" "mypy==2.4.0" "pytest==9.1.1"

uv lists what it installed, in lines starting with +: ruff, mypy, pytest, and six small packages they need. One line starts with ~: uv rebuilt your own project, pydantic-tutor.

The commands still need a little configuration. Add the following settings to pyproject.toml so the checks run consistently in later lessons. You don't need to study the individual settings now.

Add these lines at the end of the file, starting with the blank line:

pyproject.toml (add at the end):

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "E", "W",  # style: pycodestyle
    "F",       # unused imports and names, undefined names
    "I",       # import order
    "N",       # PEP 8 names
    "UP",      # modern syntax for this Python
    "B",       # likely bugs
    "ANN",     # every parameter and return annotated; ANN401 flags Any
    "FBT",     # no booleans by position, in a call or a def
    "SIM",     # simpler equivalents
    "RUF",     # Ruff's own rules
]
ignore = ["E501"]  # line length is the formatter's job

[tool.mypy]
strict = true
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]
exclude = ["^tests/"]  # the series' lesson tests refer to code you have not written yet

The whole file should now read, with your own name and email:

[project]
name = "pydantic-tutor"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Ada Student", email = "ada@example.com" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pydantic-ai==2.56.0",
    "pydantic-ai-harness==0.56.0",
]

[project.scripts]
pydantic-tutor = "pydantic_tutor:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.1,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "mypy==2.4.0",
    "pytest==9.1.1",
    "ruff==0.16.10",
]

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "E", "W",  # style: pycodestyle
    "F",       # unused imports and names, undefined names
    "I",       # import order
    "N",       # PEP 8 names
    "UP",      # modern syntax for this Python
    "B",       # likely bugs
    "ANN",     # every parameter and return annotated; ANN401 flags Any
    "FBT",     # no booleans by position, in a call or a def
    "SIM",     # simpler equivalents
    "RUF",     # Ruff's own rules
]
ignore = ["E501"]  # line length is the formatter's job

[tool.mypy]
strict = true
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]
exclude = ["^tests/"]  # the series' lesson tests refer to code you have not written yet

One more file, and it stays empty. Create src/pydantic_tutor/py.typed beside __init__.py, with nothing in it.

It's a marker, defined by PEP 561: it tells type checkers that your package's annotations can be trusted. mypy . doesn't need it, because it reads the package as part of the project. But check one script on its own, uv run mypy some_script.py, and mypy finds pydantic_tutor as an installed package. Without the marker, it refuses to read its types and reports module is installed, but missing library stubs or py.typed marker.

Last, let Ruff lay out your code in its style. Run this whenever you've written or pasted code:

uv run ruff format

It says how many files it reformatted and how many it left unchanged; the numbers depend on your files. This is the first uv command since you edited pyproject.toml, so uv first rebuilds the project and prints a few lines of its own (Building pydantic-tutor, Built pydantic-tutor, Uninstalled 1 package, Installed 1 package).

Tip

Check: run the two checks:

uv run ruff check
uv run mypy .

You should see:

All checks passed!
Success: no issues found in 2 source files

What it means

Clean, which is the normal state from here on, and the habit that keeps it that way: format, then check, before every commit. When a check finds something, fix it; a comment such as # noqa or # type: ignore hides a finding instead, so save it for the rare case where there's truly no better way. The three commands ran in a deliberate order. ruff format went first, so ruff check has nothing left to say about layout. Ruff looked at your two Python files and README.md, since it also formats any Python code blocks it finds inside Markdown. mypy . checked the project's two Python files.

You don't see a finding today, so here's one. Before you look, guess: a file has def greet(name): with no types at all, and calls it as greet("hello"). What would mypy say about it? Here's what it says:

bad.py:3: error: Function is missing a type annotation  [no-untyped-def]
bad.py:6: error: Call to untyped function "greet" in typed context  [no-untyped-call]
Found 2 errors in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Every finding names the file, the line and the rule, which makes it easy to find and fix. Both of these come from strict = true, which makes mypy treat a missing annotation, and a call to a function that has none, as an error rather than a pass.

The rest of the settings you added work the same way. Ruff's select list turns on rule sets by their code. A few hold you to the most: ANN means every parameter and return value is annotated, with ANN401 flagging Any; FBT means no True or False passed by position, and no bool parameter that could be; N is Python's naming conventions. The pydantic.mypy plugin teaches mypy how Pydantic models are built.

The --dev flag made these three a development dependency: a package you need to work on the project, but not to run it. uv records them under [dependency-groups] rather than dependencies, and uv run installs both. This lesson writes no tests, but pytest is there for the tests the project ends up holding, run with uv run pytest.

This is the one time in the lesson you edited pyproject.toml by hand. The dependencies are still uv's to write. The [tool.…] tables are settings uv never touches, so they're yours.

docs.title: Step 7: Commit
docs.text:
Goal: commit the project, and say why .venv isn't in it.

The project is complete and clean. Save it in git, so every later lesson starts from here.

See what you're about to commit:

git status --short --untracked-files=all

?? .gitignore
?? .python-version
?? README.md
?? hello_agent.py
?? pyproject.toml
?? src/pydantic_tutor/__init__.py
?? src/pydantic_tutor/py.typed
?? uv.lock

Commit them:

git add -A
git commit -m "Set up the project"

Tip

Check: you should see:

[main (root-commit) 84c723c] Set up the project
8 files changed, 2294 insertions(+)
create mode 100644 .gitignore
create mode 100644 .python-version
create mode 100644 README.md
create mode 100644 hello_agent.py
create mode 100644 pyproject.toml
create mode 100644 src/pydantic_tutor/__init__.py
create mode 100644 src/pydantic_tutor/py.typed
create mode 100644 uv.lock

Your commit id will differ, and your branch may be called master rather than main, depending on your git settings. The number of insertions can differ too, with the size of uv.lock. None of these matters here.

What it means

Eight files, and the biggest folder in the project, .venv, isn't among them: .gitignore leaves it out, and uv.lock goes in, so a copy of the project can rebuild .venv with the same versions you have. uv wrote uv.lock at your first uv run and updated it each time you added packages.

There's no .ruff_cache or .mypy_cache in the list either. Both tools keep a folder like that to run faster next time, and each one holds a .gitignore of its own that ignores everything inside it.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
That's the project, set up. You know what it asked for, what that resolved to and what's installed; why the framework's two pins move together; that an agent can run with no key; and that your code and your secrets are checked before anything is committed. Here's what you hold now:

File or command What it's for pyproject.toml What you asked for: the project, its pinned dependencies, and the checks' settings uv.lock What that resolved to: one exact version of every package, for every system .venv What's installed. Every uv run makes it match the lockfile first, so it's never committed pydantic-ai-slim The framework you import. pydantic-ai and the harness both require it at one exact version, so they move together uv run ruff format, ruff check, mypy . Your code checks, run before every commit hello_agent.py A one-second check that Pydantic AI works, with no API key .env in .gitignore Your key stays out of git, from the day you create it

docs.title: Docs vs reality
docs.text: The Pydantic AI installation page covers pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim, and says they need Python 3.11 or newer, which matches the 2.56.0 release. It doesn't mention pydantic-ai-harness, that the harness pins the library to one exact version, or the banner. When you upgrade this project later, upgrade the two packages together.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Nothing here is needed for the next lesson. Each item is for when you're curious.

  • The commands, as a checklist. For when you set up the project again, or on another machine. It's a checklist, not the whole recipe: the steps above have the file contents and what each command should print. Run it from the folder that will hold pydantic-tutor, with uv 0.13.1 or newer:
mkdir pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv init --package --python 3.14
uv run pydantic-tutor
uv add "pydantic-ai==2.56.0" "pydantic-ai-harness==0.56.0"
uv tree --invert --package pydantic-ai-slim --depth 1
# write hello_agent.py (step 4)
uv run hello_agent.py
# add .env to .gitignore (step 5)
git check-ignore -v .env
uv add --dev "ruff==0.16.10" "mypy==2.4.0" "pytest==9.1.1"
# add the checks' settings to pyproject.toml, and an empty
# src/pydantic_tutor/py.typed (step 6)
uv run ruff format
uv run ruff check
uv run mypy .
git add -A
git commit -m "Set up the project"
  • Put your project on GitHub (optional). No lesson needs it, and you don't need a GitHub account to follow the series: each lesson's starting point can be cloned without one. But a copy on GitHub is a backup, a way to share your work, and an everyday habit worth having. It takes three things, each covered by GitHub's own pages (theirs, so they may change): create an account, create a new repository with nothing in it (no README, license or .gitignore, since your project already has them), and push this project to it.
  • Why pin exactly. The == pins are a choice for a tutorial: the text you're reading was tested with exactly these versions, and your code must match it. An application would usually allow a range (>=2.56.0) and let uv.lock fix the exact versions.
  • One lockfile, every system. uv.lock covers macOS, Linux and Windows at once. A few packages are installed only on some systems: Windows gets two that macOS and Linux don't. Everyone gets the same version of every package they do install.
  • uv run adds, uv sync also removes. uv run installs whatever the lockfile lists and the environment lacks, but leaves anything extra you installed by hand. uv sync makes .venv match the lockfile exactly, removing extras.
  • What the src/ layout protects you from. With your code under src/, Python can't pick it up from the project folder by accident: the tests and commands you run use the installed package, so they fail if the install is wrong. (Setting PYTHONPATH by hand would get around this.)
  • When the banner appears. It's written to stderr, and only when stderr is a terminal or a coding agent is running the command: redirecting the output (> out.txt) still shows it; redirecting stderr (2> err.txt) leaves it out. It's also left out under pytest and in CI, and goes away once observability is set up.
  • Installing less. If you need only one provider, pydantic-ai-slim with extras such as openai installs a fraction of the packages. The installation page lists the extras.
  • Fixing findings for you. A finding Ruff can fix itself is marked [*], and uv run ruff check --fix fixes those, such as an unused import. Read the finding first: in code you copied, an unused import usually means a line is missing, and --fix would delete the clue. With the Ruff extension, most editors can format and fix on save, once you switch that on in the editor's settings.
  • Checking without changing. uv run ruff format --check reports which files it would reformat and changes nothing, for places where nothing should change, such as a check run on every push.
  • Your editor and .venv. Editors such as VS Code, PyCharm and Spyder ask which Python interpreter a project uses. Choose the one in the project, .venv/bin/python: then the editor finds pydantic_ai for its hints, and uses the versions of Ruff, mypy and pytest this project pins. In PyCharm that's enough to run the tests from the editor; other editors may also need their Python or testing extension set up, which their own docs cover.
  • Your editor's files. Editors write settings folders into your project: PyCharm makes .idea/, VS Code .vscode/. They belong to you, not to the project, so keep them out of its .gitignore and ignore them for every repository at once, in a personal ignore file:
printf '.idea/\n.vscode/\n' >> ~/.gitignore_global
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global

Once your editor has made its folder, git check-ignore -v .idea names ~/.gitignore_global as the rule that matched. (Unlike step 5's check, it prints nothing before the folder exists: a pattern ending in / matches only folders.) - uv itself. The uv docs cover projects, lockfiles and Python versions in depth.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You have a project and an agent that answers, but you haven't yet seen what an agent does. In the next lesson you build your first real Agent, look at the messages it sent and received (the same history you met in the orientation, now for real), and script its model yourself, still with no API key.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: An agent, and a model you can script
Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In setup you installed Pydantic AI and ran a five-line agent to prove it worked. This lesson slows down and looks at what that agent actually did.

It's about three things: the model, the agent, and the messages they send each other. You build the project's agent, print every message of a run, and then write a model of your own, a Python function, so you decide what it says.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Say what the model is and what the agent is, and why this project gives the agent its model on each run.
  2. Print the messages of a run, and find your prompt, the instructions and the reply in them.
  3. Stand in for the model with FunctionModel, and say when TestModel is enough.

About 15 minutes.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The model is the part that answers. You send it text, and it sends text back. Usually it's a large language model at a provider, such as Anthropic or OpenAI, and every request goes over the network and is billed.

It doesn't have to be. Pydantic AI also ships two models that run inside your own program. They need no API key and cost nothing:

  • TestModel, which you used in setup. It always gives the same kind of reply. With no tools, that's success (no tool calls).
  • FunctionModel, which calls a Python function you write. Whatever your function returns is the model's answer.

TestModel tells you the agent runs. FunctionModel lets you choose the exact reply, so you can test what your code does with it. This lesson uses both.

docs.title: The agent
docs.text:
The agent is the part of your program that talks to the model. You configure it. Today it gets a name and instructions: text the agent sends with every request, to tell the model what its job is. (Lesson 01-05 compares instructions with a system prompt.) Later lessons give it tools.

Creating an agent sends nothing. Nothing happens until you run it. A run is one use of the agent: you give it a prompt, it asks the model, and it hands you the answer.

The agent and the model are separate objects. In this project the agent has no model of its own; each run says which model to use. So the same agent runs on TestModel today and on a real model later, without a change to the agent.

docs.title: They talk in messages
docs.text:
The agent and the model communicate by passing messages. The agent sends a request, and the model sends back a response. A run keeps every message, in order, and result.all_messages() gives them to you.

Each message is made of parts. In a request, your prompt is a user-prompt part. In a response, the model's reply is a text part. Later lessons add other kinds, such as a tool call.

The answer your code gets back, result.output, is taken from the last response.

The smallest run is one request and one response, and that's the run in this lesson:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Y as your code
    participant A as agent
    participant M as model
    Y->>A: run_sync("What does this codebase do?", model=...)
    A->>M: request: instructions + your prompt
    M->>A: response: the model's text
    A->>Y: result: the output, and the messages

One thing to guess before step 2: the agent sends its instructions with every request. Are they one of the request's parts?

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
You add the agent to the project's package, and two scripts that run it. One prints every message of a run on TestModel. The other runs the agent on a model you write.

pydantic-tutor/
├── hello_agent.py          from setup, unchanged
├── scripts/
│   ├── inspect_run.py      new: runs the agent on TestModel and prints its messages
│   └── scripted_run.py     new: runs the agent on a function you write
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── __init__.py     from setup, unchanged
        └── agent.py        new: the project's agent

And the steps, in order:

  1. Create the agent, with a name and instructions, and no model.
  2. Read a run: run it on TestModel and print every message.
  3. Write the model: a function that answers from what it's sent.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from setup.

Tip

Check: from the project folder, run:

uv run hello_agent.py

You should see the banner, then the agent's answer on the last line. The banner's layout depends on how wide your terminal is; check the first line's versions and the last line:

pydantic-ai v2.56.0 • pydantic-ai-harness v0.56.0 • Python 3.14.8
/ \
/   \       agent: agent • model: test:test • tools: 0 • capabilities: 0
/___.___\
/    |    \    observability: off — see every model and tool call live, with cost
/      |      \    set it up free with Logfire and a GitHub login: https://pydantic.dev/ai-setup.md
`---.._|_..---'    or use any OpenTelemetry backend: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/logfire/#otel

goes away once observability is on — or PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1
success (no tool calls)

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

git clone --branch 01-01-setup/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the agent
docs.text:
Goal: build the project's agent, with a name and instructions, and no model.

You put the agent in the project's package, where the scripts can import it.

We'll give the agent a name and instructions, but won't ask it anything yet. Notice there's no model= argument: each run will say which model to use.

Create agent.py in src/pydantic_tutor/, next to __init__.py:

src/pydantic_tutor/agent.py:

from pydantic_ai import Agent

# No model here: each run says which model to use, so the same agent runs on
# a test model now and a real one later.
agent = Agent(
    name="assistant",
    instructions="You answer questions about a Python codebase. Answer briefly.",
)

Tip

Check: import it, and print its name and its model:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.agent import agent; print(agent.name, agent.model)"

You should see:

assistant None

What it means

None means the agent has no model. That's the choice from Concepts: the model comes with each run.

The name shows in the banner when the agent runs. In setup's hello_agent.py you didn't set one, so Pydantic AI used the variable's name, agent.

What if neither the agent nor the run names a model? Guess the error before you read on. The run stops before it sends anything, and the error ends:

pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError: `model` must either be set on the agent or included when calling it.

docs.title: Step 2: Read a run
docs.text:
Goal: run the agent on TestModel, and read the messages it sent and received: their kind, their parts, and where the instructions are.

You run the agent once and print every message, to see the request and the response for yourself.

Instead of looking only at result.output, let's inspect the messages that produced it. Watch the distinction between a request and a response: the script prints what the agent sent to the model and what the model sent back.

Create a folder, scripts/, in the project folder, and inspect_run.py in it:

scripts/inspect_run.py:

"""Run the agent once on TestModel and print every message it sent and received."""

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelRequest
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

from pydantic_tutor.agent import agent

# TestModel answers at once, inside this program: no key, no cost.
result = agent.run_sync(user_prompt="What does this codebase do?", model=TestModel())

# Every message of the run, in order: requests to the model, responses back.
for message in result.all_messages():
    # The message's kind, and the kind of each of its parts.
    print(message.kind, [part.part_kind for part in message.parts])
    if isinstance(message, ModelRequest):
        # The instructions travel on the request itself, not as a part.
        print("  instructions:", message.instructions)

print("output:", result.output)

Run it:

uv run scripts/inspect_run.py

Tip

Check: you should see the banner, with the agent's name and the model, then four lines. The banner's layout depends on how wide your terminal is:

pydantic-ai v2.56.0 • pydantic-ai-harness v0.56.0 • Python 3.14.8
/ \
/   \       agent: assistant • model: test:test • tools: 0 • capabilities: 0
/___.___\
/    |    \    observability: off — see every model and tool call live, with cost
/      |      \    set it up free with Logfire and a GitHub login: https://pydantic.dev/ai-setup.md
`---.._|_..---'    or use any OpenTelemetry backend: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/logfire/#otel

goes away once observability is on — or PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1
request ['user-prompt']
instructions: You answer questions about a Python codebase. Answer briefly.
response ['text']
output: success (no tool calls)

From here on, the outputs are shown without the banner.

What it means

The run made one request and got one response:

  • The request has one part, user-prompt: your question.
  • The response has one part, text: the model's reply.
  • output is that same text, taken from the response.

Now your guess from Concepts. The instructions are not one of the request's parts. They travel on the request itself, as message.instructions, next to the parts.

The reply is what TestModel always says. It shows the agent works, but not what your code does with a real answer. For that you need to choose the answer, which is the next step.

docs.title: Step 3: Write the model
docs.text:
Goal: replace the model with a function you write, which answers from what it's sent.

You write the model yourself. FunctionModel calls your function once for each request, passes it the messages so far and the instructions, and uses what it returns as the model's reply.

This time you'll provide the model's reply yourself. The reply function receives a model request and returns a model response. Watch where the reply is made: the FunctionModel calls your Python function instead of a remote LLM. The agent still handles the run.

Create scripted_run.py in scripts/:

scripts/scripted_run.py:

"""Run the agent on a model you write: a function that answers from the request."""

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage, ModelResponse, TextPart, UserPromptPart
from pydantic_ai.models.function import AgentInfo, FunctionModel

from pydantic_tutor.agent import agent


def reply(messages: list[ModelMessage], info: AgentInfo) -> ModelResponse:
    """Stand in for the model: answer from what the model is sent.

    FunctionModel calls this once for each request the agent makes, with
    every message of the run so far, and `info`, which carries what is sent
    beside the messages, such as the agent's instructions. What it returns
    is what the model said.
    """
    request = messages[-1]  # the latest message: the request to answer
    # A request is made of parts; the user's prompt is one of them.
    for part in request.parts:
        if isinstance(part, UserPromptPart):
            text = f"You asked {part.content!r}, and my instructions say: {info.instructions}"
            # One text part: the model's whole answer, which becomes result.output.
            return ModelResponse(parts=[TextPart(content=text)])
    # This agent has no tools, so every request carries the prompt. With
    # tools, a request can carry only a tool's return, and this function
    # would have to answer that too.
    raise ValueError("the request has no user prompt")


# The model is given for this run only; the agent itself has none (agent.py).
result = agent.run_sync(
    user_prompt="What does this codebase do?", model=FunctionModel(function=reply)
)
print(result.output)

Run it:

uv run scripts/scripted_run.py

Tip

Check: after the banner (its model line now names your function), you should see exactly the sentence your function built, with your prompt in it:

You asked 'What does this codebase do?', and my instructions say: You answer questions about a Python codebase. Answer briefly.

What it means

Your prompt and your instructions are both in the answer, so your function wrote it, not a canned reply.

Your function got the same things step 2 printed:

  • messages is every message so far. Here that's one request. messages[-1] is the request to answer, and its UserPromptPart holds your prompt.
  • info.instructions is the agent's instructions. They arrive beside the messages, not inside them, as step 2 showed.

It returns a ModelResponse with one TextPart, and that becomes result.output. If the request had no prompt, the function raises an error instead of inventing an answer.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
You know the three pieces every Pydantic AI program is built from:

  • The model answers. It can be a real LLM or a stand-in: TestModel to check the agent runs, FunctionModel to choose the reply.
  • The agent is your program's side: a name, instructions, and later tools. In this project it gets its model on each run.
  • Messages carry everything between them: requests and responses, each made of parts. The instructions travel on each request, beside the parts.

Writing the model yourself is what lets every later lesson be checked without an API key.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Right now the agent can only answer from its instructions. In the next lesson you give it tools, and see the model ask to call one, and the tool's return going back.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Tools, and the loop that calls them
Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson you built an agent and read the messages of a run: one request, one response, and the model's text.

This lesson follows one question: what actually happens when a model asks to use a tool? You'll see what the model is told about your functions, how the agent runs one on the model's behalf, and what happens when the model supplies an argument that needs correcting.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Say what a tool is, and what the model is told about it.
  2. Trace the loop a tool call makes, and count its requests.
  3. Check the arguments the model wrote, and tell it what to fix with ModelRetry.

About 15 minutes.

docs.title: What a tool is
docs.text:
A tool is a Python function you give the agent. The model can't run it. The model only reads messages and writes messages. When it needs a tool, it writes a tool call in its response: the tool's name, and the arguments to call it with. The agent runs your function and sends back what it returned, the tool return.

So the model needs to know which tools exist and how to call them. With every request, the agent sends a tool definition for each tool, built from your function:

From your function What the model receives The function's name The tool's name The docstring's description The tool's description Parameter names and types A JSON schema of the arguments Parameter descriptions, under Args: Each argument's description The function's body Nothing

The tool definition doesn't include your function's Python body. The docstring is the tool's manual: the clearer it is, the better the model can tell when to use the tool and what to pass.

docs.title: A tool call makes a loop
docs.text:
A run with a tool call takes more than one request:

  1. The agent sends your prompt and the tool definitions.
  2. The model's response is a tool call.
  3. The agent runs the tool, and sends the tool return in a new request.
  4. The model's response is the answer.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as agent
    participant M as model
    participant T as your tool
    A->>M: request: your prompt, the tool definitions
    M->>A: response: a tool call
    A->>T: runs it
    T->>A: what it returned
    A->>M: request: the tool return
    M->>A: response: the answer

That's two requests instead of one. Each response that holds a tool call adds a request, and with a real model every request is billed.

docs.title: The model writes the arguments
docs.text:
The model decides when to call a tool and what arguments to send. Your program decides which tools exist and what they do with those arguments. So a tool treats its arguments like anything a stranger types into a form: it checks them before using them.

Pydantic AI checks the types for you. A number where the schema says string never reaches your function. But a string of the right type can still be wrong, such as the name of a product that doesn't exist. That check is your tool's.

When the value is wrong, the tool raises ModelRetry with a message saying what was wrong and what to do instead. The run doesn't stop: the agent sends the message back to the model, which can try again. Each tool gets one retry by default. If the model gets it wrong a second time, the run fails.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
A small agent with two tools over a price list, and two scripts that run it on stand-in models we give you, in given/. The prices sit in the same file as the tools, because this lesson is about the tools, not where data comes from.

pydantic-tutor/
├── scripts/
│   ├── show_tools.py       new: prints what the model is told about each tool
│   └── tool_loop.py        new: a model that calls a tool, gets it wrong, then answers
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── given/
        │   └── tool_models.py  given: the stand-in models
        └── prices.py       new: the price agent and its two tools

And the steps, in order:

  1. Write two tools, and call them yourself.
  2. Print what the model is told about them.
  3. Watch the loop, with a model that gets the name wrong first.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. This lesson hands you some code you run but don't write: stand-in models, in src/pydantic_tutor/given/. From the project folder, fetch them:

Tip

uv run hello_agent.py

After the banner, the last line should be:

success (no tool calls)

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

docs.title: Step 1: Write two tools
docs.text:
Goal: two plain functions the model will be able to ask for.

You write the tools and call them yourself, before any model is involved. The first function provides a list of products; the second looks up one price. Pay attention to their docstrings: those are part of what the model will later see when the functions become tools.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/prices.py:

"""A small agent with two tools: a price list it can read for the model.

The prices live in this file, to keep the example about its tools rather
than where data comes from.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRetry

# Whole cents, so no price is ever rounded.
PRICES_IN_CENTS = {"apple": 50, "bread": 225, "coffee": 700}


def list_products() -> list[str]:
    """List the products that have a price."""
    return sorted(PRICES_IN_CENTS)


def price_of(*, product: str) -> int:
    """Look up the price of one product, in cents.

    Args:
        product: The product's name, as `list_products` gives it.
    """
    # The model wrote `product`: check it before using it.
    if product not in PRICES_IN_CENTS:
        raise ModelRetry(
            message=f"There is no product {product!r}. Call list_products to see them."
        )
    return PRICES_IN_CENTS[product]


# No model here: each run says which model to use.
price_agent = Agent(
    name="prices",
    instructions="You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.",
    tools=[list_products, price_of],
)

Tip

Check: call both tools yourself:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.prices import list_products, price_of; print(list_products()); print(price_of(product='coffee'))"

You should see:

['apple', 'bread', 'coffee']
700

Now ask for a product that doesn't exist:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.prices import price_of; price_of(product='apples')"

The last line of the error is your tool's message:

pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelRetry: There is no product 'apples'. Call list_products to see them.

What it means

The tools are ordinary functions. tools=[list_products, price_of] is all it takes to give them to the agent.

ModelRetry is the only Pydantic AI name the tools use. Called directly, as here, it's an ordinary exception. Inside a run, the agent catches it and sends its message to the model, as step 3 shows.

The message says what was wrong and what to do: call list_products. That's the model's only help, so make it specific.

docs.title: Step 2: Print what the model is told
docs.text:
Goal: see the tool definitions the model receives.

The model for this step is given: prints_tool_definitions() is a FunctionModel, like the one you wrote in the last lesson. It prints the tool definitions it is sent, then answers "Done." so the run can finish.

Here we aren't asking the model to call a tool yet. We're using the given FunctionModel to inspect the definitions the agent sends: the names, descriptions and arguments—not the Python function bodies.

Create scripts/show_tools.py:

"""Print what the model is told about the price agent's tools."""

from pydantic_tutor.given.tool_models import prints_tool_definitions
from pydantic_tutor.prices import price_agent

price_agent.run_sync(
    user_prompt="How much is an apple?", model=prints_tool_definitions()
)

uv run scripts/show_tools.py

Tip

Check: the banner now says tools: 2. After it:

list_products
description: List the products that have a price.
parameters: {
"additionalProperties": false,
"properties": {},
"type": "object"
}
price_of
description: Look up the price of one product, in cents.
parameters: {
"additionalProperties": false,
"properties": {
"product": {
"description": "The product's name, as `list_products` gives it.",
"type": "string"
}
},
"required": [
"product"
],
"type": "object"
}

What it means

This is the whole of what the model knows about your tools. Match it to prices.py:

  • The name is the function's name.
  • The description is the docstring's first line.
  • The Args: line for product became that argument's description in the schema. product is "required" because it has no default.

PRICES_IN_CENTS and the if that checks the name aren't there. The model knows how to ask for price_of, not how it works.

docs.title: Step 3: Watch the loop
docs.text:
Goal: run a model that calls a tool, gets the name wrong, tries again, and answers.

The model in this step is given too, asks_with_a_wrong_name(). It follows a fixed script:

  1. On the first request: call price_of with product="apples", a name that doesn't exist.
  2. If the latest request holds a retry: call it again, with "apple".
  3. If it holds the tool return: answer with the price.

A real model decides for itself. The script lets you see each message.

Before you run it, guess: how many requests will the run make? Write your guess down.

Now we'll watch a whole tool-call loop. The given model requests a tool, the agent runs it, and the model responds again. Follow the message order in the printed output: it makes the extra model request visible.

Create scripts/tool_loop.py:

"""Run the price agent on a model that calls a tool, gets it wrong, then answers."""

from pydantic_ai.messages import RetryPromptPart

from pydantic_tutor.given.tool_models import asks_with_a_wrong_name
from pydantic_tutor.prices import price_agent

result = price_agent.run_sync(
    user_prompt="How much is an apple?", model=asks_with_a_wrong_name()
)

for message in result.all_messages():
    print(message.kind, [part.part_kind for part in message.parts])
    for part in message.parts:
        if isinstance(part, RetryPromptPart):
            print("  told the model:", part.content)
print("output:", result.output)
print("requests:", result.usage.requests)

uv run scripts/tool_loop.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, six messages, your tool's message, the answer, and the count:

request ['user-prompt']
response ['tool-call']
request ['retry-prompt']
told the model: There is no product 'apples'. Call list_products to see them.
response ['tool-call']
request ['tool-return']
response ['text']
output: An apple costs 50 cents.
requests: 3

What it means

Three requests. Was that your guess?

  • Request 1 carries your question. The model asks for price_of with "apples".
  • Request 2 carries your tool's ModelRetry message, as a retry-prompt part. The model asks again, with "apple".
  • Request 3 carries the tool return, 50. The model answers.

Your tool ran twice, in your program, between the requests. The model never ran it.

Without the wrong name, the run would have made two requests, as in Concepts. The retry cost one more. With a real model that's one more billed request, so a clear tool message is worth writing.

The model gets your ModelRetry message with one line from Pydantic AI after it, asking it to fix the error and try again.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• A tool is a Python function the agent runs for the model. The model sees only its definition: the name, the docstring and a schema of the arguments.
  • A tool call makes a loop. The model asks, the agent runs the tool, and the tool return goes back in the next request. Each response that holds a tool call adds a request.
  • The model writes the arguments, so your tool checks them. When one is wrong, ModelRetry tells the model what to fix, and the run goes on.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
So far every value a tool uses is fixed in its file. In the next lesson each run hands the agent values of its own, its dependencies, which your tools and instructions can read and the model never sees.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson you gave an agent tools over a price list that sat in the tools' own file.

This lesson is about dependencies, or deps: the information a question needs right now, such as which shop it's about, passed to the agent as an object with each run.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Pass the information a run needs as deps, and read it in a tool and in the instructions.
  2. Say why an agent needs deps, rather than a value fixed in its code.

About 15 minutes.

docs.title: What deps are
docs.text:
Deps are the information a run needs right now: which shop the question is about, which user is asking, a connection to a database. You put it in one object, usually a small dataclass, and pass it with the run. The next run can pass a different one.

The name is Pydantic AI's: the run's dependencies. It has nothing to do with the package dependencies in pyproject.toml.

There are three pieces:

  • The agent says what type they are: deps_type=Shop. Shop is a small class of our own.
  • Each run passes a value: run_sync(..., deps=Shop(...)).
  • Your code reads it as ctx.deps. ctx is the run's context, a RunContext. The agent passes it to your code; the model never does.

Two kinds of code read the deps in this lesson:

  • A tool takes ctx: RunContext[Shop] as its first parameter. ctx isn't in the tool definition, so the model can't see the shop or pick one.
  • An instructions function, decorated with @agent.instructions, takes ctx and returns text. Before each request, the agent calls it and adds the text to the agent's fixed instructions. That's how the model learns which shop this run is for: from a sentence your code wrote, not from the deps.

The model sees what your code makes of the deps (the instructions text, and whatever a tool returns), never the deps themselves.

docs.title: Why not put it in the code?
docs.text:
You build an agent once, when your program starts, and run it many times. In a real program those runs are for different users, accounts or shops, often at the same moment.

A value fixed in the agent's code, like last lesson's price list, is the same for every run. Deps let the code that starts a run decide what the run is about. The same agent, with the same tools, answers for whichever shop it's handed.

The model isn't given the deps object to choose a different shop. Your program selects the shop before the run begins, and the tool reads it from ctx.deps. That helps keep responsibilities clear, but it isn't a security boundary by itself. In a real application, your tools must still check that the caller is authorized to access that shop's data.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
A shop agent whose shop is the run's dependency, and a script that runs it for two shops, on a stand-in model we give you.

pydantic-tutor/
├── scripts/
│   └── two_shops.py        new: one agent, two shops
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── given/
        │   └── shop_model.py   given: the stand-in model
        └── shop.py         new: Shop, the agent, its tool and its instructions

And the steps, in order:

  1. Write the shop agent, with a tool and instructions that read the deps.
  2. Run it for two shops.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. This lesson hands you one more stand-in model. From the project folder, fetch it:

uv run https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student/main/starter/get_starter.py shop-model

Tip

Check: from the project folder, run:

uv run hello_agent.py

After the banner, the last line should be:

success (no tool calls)

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

git clone --branch 01-03-function-tools/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
