The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the shop agent
docs.text:
Goal: a tool and instructions that read the shop from the run's deps.

We'll move the shop's prices out of the agent's fixed code and into run-specific dependencies. Look at RunContext[Shop] in the tool: ctx.deps is how the tool receives the particular shop selected for this run. The model doesn't select that object.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/shop.py:

"""An agent that answers for whichever shop a run is about.

The shop is the run's dependency:
each run passes one, and the tool and the instructions read it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRetry, RunContext


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Shop:
    """What one run needs: the shop it answers for."""

    name: str
    prices_in_cents: Mapping[str, int]


def price_of(ctx: RunContext[Shop], *, product: str) -> int:
    """Look up the price of one product, in cents.

    Args:
        product: The product's name.
    """
    # ctx.deps is the Shop this run was given; the model never sees it.
    prices = ctx.deps.prices_in_cents
    if product not in prices:
        raise ModelRetry(message=f"{ctx.deps.name} doesn't sell {product!r}.")
    return prices[product]


# No model and no shop here: each run says which model to use, and which
# shop it's about.
shop_agent = Agent(
    name="shop",
    deps_type=Shop,
    instructions="You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.",
    tools=[price_of],
)


@shop_agent.instructions
def name_the_shop(ctx: RunContext[Shop]) -> str:
    """Tell the model which shop this run is for."""
    return f"You answer for {ctx.deps.name}."

ctx comes first in price_of, before the *, because the agent passes it by position. The model's argument, product, stays keyword-only.

Now run the agent without passing a shop. Guess what happens before you run it:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel; from pydantic_tutor.shop import shop_agent; shop_agent.run_sync(user_prompt='How much is a coffee?', model=TestModel())"

Tip

Check: it fails. The last lines of the error are:

return f"You answer for {ctx.deps.name}."
^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'name'

What it means

The run started, and ctx.deps was None: no run passed a shop. The first code to read it was name_the_shop, before the first request, so the model was never asked anything.

deps_type=Shop tells mypy what ctx.deps is, so mypy checks a deps= you pass. Nothing checks that you pass one at all.

docs.title: Step 2: Run it for two shops
docs.text:
Goal: run the same agent for two shops, and see that only the deps change.

The script runs the agent twice, once for each shop, with a given model, asks_for_coffee(). On the first request it prints what it was sent: the instructions, and the arguments of each tool. Then it asks for the price of coffee, and answers with it.

Before you run it, guess: will the model see the shop's prices?

This script runs the same agent twice, each time with a different Shop passed as deps. Watch the deps=shop argument in run_sync: that's what changes between the runs, not the agent definition.

Create scripts/two_shops.py:

"""Run one agent for two shops: only the run's dependencies change."""

from pydantic_tutor.given.shop_model import asks_for_coffee
from pydantic_tutor.shop import Shop, shop_agent

shops = [
    Shop(name="Corner Cafe", prices_in_cents={"coffee": 350, "tea": 300}),
    Shop(name="Station Kiosk", prices_in_cents={"coffee": 500}),
]
for shop in shops:
    print(shop.name)
    result = shop_agent.run_sync(
        user_prompt="How much is a coffee?", model=asks_for_coffee(), deps=shop
    )
    print("  output:", result.output)

uv run scripts/two_shops.py

Tip

Check: after the banner:

Corner Cafe
instructions: 'You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.\n\nYou answer for Corner Cafe.'
price_of's arguments: ['product']
output: Coffee is 350 cents.
Station Kiosk
instructions: 'You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.\n\nYou answer for Station Kiosk.'
price_of's arguments: ['product']
output: Coffee is 500 cents.

What it means

Same agent, same tool, same model, same question. Only deps= changed, and each run got its own shop's price.

The model didn't see the prices. It saw two things:

  • The instructions: the fixed sentence, a blank line (the \n\n), then the sentence name_the_shop wrote for this run.
  • The tool's arguments: only product. ctx isn't there.

It learned a price only when the tool returned one: 350 in the first run, 500 in the second.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Deps are the information a run needs right now, in one object you pass with the run, and it can be different on every run. The agent declares its type with deps_type, each run passes one with deps=, and your tools and instructions read it as ctx.deps. The model sees what your code passes on, never the object itself.
  • One agent serves many runs, so a value fixed in its code is the same for all of them. Deps let each run carry its own, and because the model isn't given the deps object, it doesn't select the shop for that run. Tools still enforce access permissions.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Your agent's instructions now come from two places: fixed text, and a function that reads the deps. In the Pydantic AI docs you'll also meet a system prompt, which looks like a third way to say the same thing. The next lesson is a short note on how the two compare.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: A word on system prompts and instructions
Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson the shop agent's instructions came from two places: fixed text, and a function that names the shop.

This lesson is a short note, with nothing to build. It's about system prompts and instructions: two ways to tell the model what its job is. Your agents use instructions=. In the Pydantic AI docs, and in other people's code, you'll also meet system_prompt=. They're nearly the same thing, and there's one place they differ.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Say how a system prompt and instructions differ, and why this project uses instructions.

About 5 minutes.

docs.title: Two ways to describe the model's job
docs.text:
Both system_prompt= and instructions= tell the model how to behave. For example, either can tell an agent to answer questions about prices:

Agent(system_prompt="You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.")
Agent(instructions="You answer questions about prices. Answer briefly.")

In either case, Pydantic AI supplies guidance to the model along with the conversation. Providers may package that guidance differently, but the important distinction here isn't the provider's request format. It's what happens to the guidance when you continue a conversation.

docs.title: What the history keeps
docs.text:
The difference is in Pydantic AI's own record of a run, its list of messages: the history. The two are kept in different places:

Where Pydantic AI keeps it What a later request is sent system prompt Inside the first request, so it's one of the messages The copy in the history instructions Beside the messages, not in them The running agent's own, fresh every request

For the single-run examples you've built so far, this distinction has little practical effect. It matters when a run continues an earlier conversation by being handed that conversation's messages, which Chapter 2 does. Then a system prompt is the one saved at the start: change it in your code, and the conversation keeps the old one. Instructions are always what the agent says now. That's also why name_the_shop, from the last lesson, works: it's called before every request, so its sentence can't go stale.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text: The Pydantic AI docs recommend instructions "for most use cases", and this project uses only instructions. If you ever give an agent both, the system prompt is sent first and the instructions after it. Don't let them disagree: which one the model then follows is up to the model, not Pydantic AI.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text: You can say how a system prompt and instructions differ, and why this project uses instructions. Both forms guide the model. Pydantic AI handles their history differently: a system prompt is kept with the messages; instructions come from the running agent on each request.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Your agent still answers in plain text. In the next lesson you ask an agent for a typed answer instead, a value your code can use, and give it a rule that sends the model back when that value is wrong.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson each run handed the agent a shop. The answer was still a text sentence.

This lesson is about structured output: asking a model to return data in a known shape, so your program receives an object it can use. We'll extract an Invoice from a document, then catch an incorrect total.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Explain the division of work between the model, Pydantic AI and Pydantic when an agent returns a typed answer.
  2. Get an Invoice from an agent without expecting the model to make a Python object.
  3. Add a validation rule and understand what it can—and cannot—check.

About 15 minutes.

docs.title: What changes when you ask for a type?
docs.text:
So far, your agents have answered in words: result.output was a string. But imagine you're writing a program that needs an invoice number, a date, and a total. You don't want to search a paragraph for those values. You want an Invoice object with named fields.

You can tell Pydantic AI what kind of answer your program needs:

extractor = Agent(output_type=Invoice)

When the run succeeds, result.output is an instance of Invoice. If the model cannot supply a valid answer within the allowed attempts, the run fails instead.

But the model doesn't create that Python object. So who does?

docs.title: Who does what?
docs.text:
There are four parts to the exchange:

  1. You define the answer. You write a Pydantic Invoice class with fields such as number: str and total: Decimal, then pass it as output_type.
  2. Pydantic AI tells the model what to return. From your class it prepares a schema describing the fields. With the default tool-based structured-output mode used here, it offers the model a special output tool whose arguments must follow that schema. This isn't a Python function you'll write or run.
  3. The model proposes the field values. It reads the document and responds with a structured output-tool call: data containing an invoice number, dates, line items and a total. These are not Python Invoice or Decimal instances.
  4. Pydantic AI and Pydantic process the response. Pydantic AI receives the model's proposed data and passes it to Pydantic for validation and construction. If it passes, your program receives result.output as an Invoice. If not, Pydantic AI can send the validation error back to the model and request another attempt.

Here's the important part of step 3. The model's response contains structured values conceptually like these output-tool arguments:

{
  "number": "INV-0042",
  "issued": "2026-09-30",
  "supplier": "Acme Paper Co.",
  "currency": "GBP",
  "lines": [
    {"description": "A4 paper, box of 5", "quantity": 3, "unit_price": "24.50"},
    {"description": "Stapler", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": "12.00"}
  ],
  "total": "73.50"
}

The model supplies these values; it doesn't execute Python or call Invoice(...). Pydantic interprets them according to your class, including converting the date and decimal strings into Python values.

Other Pydantic AI output modes can ask for JSON text instead of an output-tool call. The format of the model response changes; the division of work does not.

docs.title: What validation can—and cannot—tell you
docs.text:
Pydantic first checks that the supplied data fits your model: required fields exist and the values can be interpreted as the declared types. But a well-formed Invoice isn't necessarily an accurate extraction.

The document below says the total is 85.50. The model might send 73.50 instead. That's still a perfectly valid Decimal, so the type check alone won't catch the mistake.

We can add another rule to the Invoice class: the total must equal the sum of each line's quantity times its unit price. Pydantic then checks that rule too. If it fails, Pydantic AI sends the error to the model and asks for another attempt, once by default.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as your Python code
    participant A as Pydantic AI agent
    participant M as model
    participant P as Pydantic
    C->>A: run_sync(invoice document)
    A->>M: document + Invoice output schema
    M-->>A: structured values (total 73.50)
    A->>P: validate and build Invoice
    P-->>A: validation error (sum is 85.50)
    A->>M: validation error - try again
    M-->>A: corrected values (total 85.50)
    A->>P: validate and build Invoice
    P-->>A: Invoice instance
    A-->>C: result.output (Invoice)

A rule checks only what it knows how to check. If the model copies the wrong quantity and returns a matching total, the arithmetic rule can pass even though the extraction is wrong. Validation enforces types and rules you define; it doesn't prove every value matches the source.

docs.text:
An agent called extractor whose answer is an Invoice, and a script that runs it on one document with a stand-in model we give you. That model gets the total wrong the first time, on purpose.

├── pyproject.toml               changed: pydantic, pinned
├── scripts/
│   └── extract_invoice.py       new: the extractor on one invoice
└── src/

And the steps, in order:

  1. Describe the answer: write Invoice and the extractor, and run it.
  2. Check the answer: give Invoice a rule, and see a wrong answer sent back.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Step 1: Describe the answer
docs.text:
Goal: write the answer as a type, Invoice, and an agent whose answer is one.

Here's the invoice the agent reads:

ACME PAPER CO.
12 Mill Lane, Leeds LS1 4AB

INVOICE                                  No. INV-0042
Date: 30 September 2026
Bill to: Harbour Books Ltd, 4 Harbour Street, Hull HU1 2AA

Description                     Qty    Unit price      Amount
A4 paper, box of 5                3         24.50       73.50
Stapler                           1         12.00       12.00

Total due (GBP)                                         85.50

Payment within 30 days. Thank you for your business.

Add up the total yourself: three boxes of paper at 24.50, plus one stapler at 12.00. Keep that number in mind.

We're going to describe the answer before asking a model to extract anything. LineItem describes one product on the invoice; Invoice brings those lines together with the invoice number, date, supplier and total. Look at the agent declaration at the bottom: output_type=Invoice is the line that tells Pydantic AI what kind of answer our program expects.

We're about to import pydantic directly, so add it to our project's dependencies, pinned to the version this lesson was tested with. pydantic-ai already installed a version of it; if that one is newer, uv moves it to the pin:

uv add "pydantic==2.14.1"

Create src/pydantic_tutor/invoices.py:

"""An invoice, as a type, and an agent that reads one out of a document."""

from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic_ai import Agent


class LineItem(BaseModel):
    """One line of an invoice."""

    description: str
    quantity: int
    unit_price: Decimal = Field(description="The price of one, as printed.")


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    """An invoice, as printed on the document."""

    number: str = Field(description="The invoice number, as printed.")
    issued: date = Field(description="The date the invoice was issued.")
    supplier: str = Field(description="Who sent the invoice.")
    currency: str = Field(description="The three-letter currency code, such as GBP.")
    lines: list[LineItem]
    total: Decimal = Field(description="The total due, as printed.")


# No model here: each run says which model to use.
extractor = Agent(
    name="invoice_extractor",
    output_type=Invoice,
    instructions="Extract the invoice from the document you are given. Copy every value as printed.",
)

The money fields are Decimal, not float, because money needs exact decimals. We've defined the structure of an invoice, but we haven't written any code to read values out of the document. That is the model's job; Pydantic AI and Pydantic handle the structured result.

Next, we'll run the extractor on the invoice above. The given DOCUMENT contains its text, and misreads_the_total() is a stand-in model that intentionally copies the first line's amount instead of the invoice total. Notice result.output: the script treats it as an Invoice and reads its fields directly. It also prints the number of model requests.

Create scripts/extract_invoice.py:

"""Extract an invoice from a text document, on a model that misreads it once."""

from pydantic_tutor.given.invoice_model import DOCUMENT, misreads_the_total
from pydantic_tutor.invoices import extractor

result = extractor.run_sync(user_prompt=DOCUMENT, model=misreads_the_total())
invoice = result.output  # an Invoice, not text
print("number:", invoice.number)
print("issued:", invoice.issued)
print("total:", invoice.total, invoice.currency)
print("requests:", result.usage.requests)

uv run scripts/extract_invoice.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, you should see:

number: INV-0042
issued: 2026-09-30
total: 73.50 GBP
requests: 1

What it means

The model returned structured field values, not a Python object. Pydantic AI handed those values to Pydantic, which built an Invoice. So invoice.total is a Decimal, and invoice.issued is a date: the document says "30 September 2026", and your code gets 2026-09-30.

Now compare the total with yours. The invoice says 85.50, but this printed 73.50, the first line's amount. Every field passed the type checks, so Pydantic accepted the values. The object is valid according to the rules we've written so far, but its total is wrong.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the answer
docs.text:
Goal: give Invoice a rule, that its total is the sum of its lines, and see the agent send a wrong answer back to the model.

The rule is a Pydantic model validator: a method marked @model_validator(mode="after"). It runs after Pydantic has interpreted the fields and raises ValueError if the line totals don't add up.

We're keeping the same Invoice and the same extractor. The new part is check_total, a method on Invoice marked with @model_validator. Watch what it compares: it computes a total from the quantities and unit prices, then raises ValueError if that sum disagrees with the model's proposed total. We aren't teaching the model arithmetic here; we're adding a check that runs in Python.

In src/pydantic_tutor/invoices.py, import Self and model_validator, and add the method to Invoice. The whole file is now:

"""An invoice, as a type, and an agent that reads one out of a document."""

from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Self

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator
from pydantic_ai import Agent


class LineItem(BaseModel):
    """One line of an invoice."""

    description: str
    quantity: int
    unit_price: Decimal = Field(description="The price of one, as printed.")


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    """An invoice, as printed on the document."""

    number: str = Field(description="The invoice number, as printed.")
    issued: date = Field(description="The date the invoice was issued.")
    supplier: str = Field(description="Who sent the invoice.")
    currency: str = Field(description="The three-letter currency code, such as GBP.")
    lines: list[LineItem]
    total: Decimal = Field(description="The total due, as printed.")

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_total(self) -> Self:
        """Refuse a total that is not the sum of the lines."""
        expected = sum(
            (line.quantity * line.unit_price for line in self.lines),
            start=Decimal(value=0),
        )
        if self.total != expected:
            raise ValueError(
                f"The total {self.total} is not the sum of the lines, {expected}."
            )
        return self


# No model here: each run says which model to use.
extractor = Agent(
    name="invoice_extractor",
    output_type=Invoice,
    instructions="Extract the invoice from the document you are given. Copy every value as printed.",
)

The script from Step 1 hasn't changed. What changes is what happens to its first proposed result: the validation error sends the model back for another attempt. Before you run it, guess: how many requests will the run make this time?

uv run scripts/extract_invoice.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, you should see what the model was sent back, then the corrected invoice:

sent back to the model:
1 validation error:
```json
[
{
"type": "value_error",
"loc": [],
"msg": "Value error, The total 73.50 is not the sum of the lines, 85.50.",
"input": {
"number": "INV-0042",
"issued": "2026-09-30",
"supplier": "Acme Paper Co.",
"currency": "GBP",
"lines": [
{
"description": "A4 paper, box of 5",
"quantity": 3,
"unit_price": "24.50"
},
{
"description": "Stapler",
"quantity": 1,
"unit_price": "12.00"
}
],
"total": "73.50"
}
}
]
```

Fix the errors and try again.
number: INV-0042
issued: 2026-09-30
total: 85.50 GBP
requests: 2

What it means

Two requests, where step 1 took one. Pydantic ran check_total and rejected the model's first values. Pydantic AI then sent that error back to the model instead of ending the run. The retry prompt holds:

  • the error your ValueError raised, in msg;
  • the model's own answer, in input;
  • then "Fix the errors and try again."

The second answer passed Pydantic's checks, so the run ended with an Invoice instance.

The rule belongs to Invoice, not to the agent. Other Python code that constructs the same model gets the same validation rule. And notice what we haven't established: a matching total doesn't prove the model copied the correct quantities, prices or supplier from the document. This rule catches an arithmetic inconsistency, not every extraction error.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• A typed answer has several participants: you define Invoice; Pydantic AI tells the model the expected structure; the model returns structured values; Pydantic validates them and constructs the Python object available in result.output.
  • Validation isn't fact-checking: types and your own validators enforce specific rules. They can catch errors such as a mismatched total, but they cannot guarantee that every value was copied from the document correctly. Pydantic AI can send a validation error back to the model for another attempt.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The extractor answers with an Invoice, always. What if someone says "Hello"? In the next lesson you find out, and meet the trap waiting for an agent that should sometimes answer in words.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson the extractor learned to answer with an Invoice, and to catch its own errors.

This lesson is about a trap in structured output: what happens when an agent that can only answer with an Invoice is asked a question that the agent can't answer with an Invoice?

For example, what if we just say something like "Hello"?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

  1. Explain why an Invoice-only extractor fails on a greeting, even when the model tries to answer.
  2. Allow text or an Invoice when an agent's job requires both.

About 10 minutes.

docs.title: The output type must fit the job
docs.text:
The extractor has output_type=Invoice, so a run can end one way only: with an Invoice. Words are not an answer.

That's right for the extractor. Your code calls it with a document, and wants nothing back but the record.

It isn't right for every job. An assistant that greets people and also extracts invoices must be able to return words when there's no invoice. If its only permitted output is Invoice, a greeting isn't an acceptable answer: the agent asks the model to try again, then the run fails. A model forced to return an Invoice might instead invent one.

The lesson isn't that structured output and conversation can't mix. It's that the permitted output types must match the agent's job.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
One script, scripts/output_trap.py, that first says "Hello" to the extractor, then tries an agent that permits either words or an Invoice. Both use a stand-in model we give you.

pydantic-tutor/
├── scripts/
│   └── output_trap.py          new: greet the extractor, then allow both output types
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        └── given/
            └── greeting_model.py  given: the stand-in model

There are two steps: see why the extractor fails on a greeting, then allow an assistant to return words or an invoice.

docs.title: Step 1: Say hello to the extractor
docs.text:
Goal: greet the agent whose answer must be an Invoice, and read how the run fails.

The model in this lesson is given, greets_on_hello(). Told "Hello", it answers in words, as a real model would. It prints whether the agent offered it a way to answer in words, and anything it's sent back.

First we'll deliberately give the extractor a job it cannot finish: answering a greeting when its only permitted output is an Invoice. Watch the try/except: it lets us inspect the failure instead of ending the script at the exception.

Create scripts/output_trap.py:

"""Say "Hello" to an agent whose answer must be an Invoice, then to one that may answer in words."""

from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UnexpectedModelBehavior

from pydantic_tutor.given.greeting_model import greets_on_hello
from pydantic_tutor.invoices import extractor

print('The extractor, told "Hello":')
try:
    extractor.run_sync(user_prompt="Hello", model=greets_on_hello())
except UnexpectedModelBehavior as error:
    print("  the run failed:", error)

Before you run it, guess: the agent will send the model back once. What will the message say?

uv run scripts/output_trap.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, you should see:

The extractor, told "Hello":
a text answer offered: False
a text answer offered: False
sent back to the model:
1 validation error:
```json
[
{
"type": "json_invalid",
"loc": [],
"msg": "Invalid JSON: expected value at line 1 column 1"
}
]
```

Fix the errors and try again.
the run failed: Exceeded maximum output retries (1)

What it means

a text answer offered: False, on both requests: the agent gave the model no way to answer in words. The model greeted anyway.

The agent could only read the greeting as an Invoice, written as JSON. "Hello! Send me an invoice…" isn't JSON, so it sent back Invalid JSON. The model greeted again, the one retry was spent, and the run ended in your except block.

That message is the trap's disguise. It says nothing about a greeting or an output type. Find it in a log, and you'd suspect a broken request. The real cause is that the agent's output type has no room for words.

docs.title: Step 2: Allow words or an Invoice
docs.text:
Now imagine an assistant with two responsibilities: greeting people and extracting invoices when they paste one. Its permitted outputs should reflect both jobs. Set output_type=[str, Invoice]. A run can then return a str or an Invoice, and your code checks which it received with isinstance.

This second agent keeps the invoice option but also permits an ordinary string. Notice both changes: output_type=[str, Invoice] accepts one of two result types, and isinstance(answer, Invoice) lets your Python code handle each kind appropriately.

In scripts/output_trap.py, replace the imports at the top with these. Agent, DOCUMENT and Invoice are new:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UnexpectedModelBehavior

from pydantic_tutor.given.greeting_model import greets_on_hello
from pydantic_tutor.given.invoice_model import DOCUMENT
from pydantic_tutor.invoices import Invoice, extractor

Then add this code to the end of the file:

# Words or an Invoice: either ends a run. With a list, the type parameters
# say so to the type checker: the deps type (none), then the output type.
desk = Agent[None, str | Invoice](
    name="invoice_desk",
    output_type=[str, Invoice],
    instructions="Greet people briefly. When you are given an invoice, extract it.",
)
for prompt in ["Hello", DOCUMENT]:
    answer = desk.run_sync(user_prompt=prompt, model=greets_on_hello()).output
    if isinstance(answer, Invoice):
        print("an Invoice:", answer.number, answer.total)
    else:
        print("words:", answer)

Run it again, on the same given model. After the extractor's lines, it prints:

  a text answer offered: True
words: Hello! Send me an invoice and I will read it.
  a text answer offered: True
an Invoice: INV-0042 85.50

What it means

The agent can now accept a greeting as text while still returning an Invoice for a document. Structured output hasn't disappeared. We've chosen permitted outputs that fit both responsibilities.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text: • The output type must fit the job. An Invoice-only extractor cannot accept a greeting as its final answer. An assistant that needs words and invoice records can use output_type=[str, Invoice], and the calling code checks which kind of result it received.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The extractor gives up after one retry, and only a default of 50 requests stops an agent that keeps calling tools. The last lesson of this chapter sets limits of your own: on requests, on retries, and on time.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson you saw an agent fail on a plain "Hello", because its answer had no room for words.

This lesson asks one practical question: what should your program do when a run can't proceed normally? A tool problem may be something the model can recover from. A run that keeps calling tools needs a stopping point. A slow tool needs a deadline. These are different kinds of trouble, and each calls for a different safeguard.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Tell the model whether a failed tool call can be fixed, with ModelRetry or ToolFailed.
  2. Stop a runaway run with a request limit.
  3. Give up on a slow tool with a tool timeout.

About 15 minutes.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: There are three different decisions here: can the model recover from this tool failure?, how many requests should the run be allowed to make?, and how long should the agent wait for a tool? A retry, a request limit, and a timeout answer different questions. None replaces the others.

docs.title: Two ways a tool can fail
docs.text:
You met ModelRetry in the tools lesson: the tool tells the model "fix your call", and the model gets one more try. That fits a mistake the model can fix, like a misspelt name.

Some failures can't be fixed by asking again. If a supplier's stock feed is down, it's down on the tenth ask too. For that, the tool raises ToolFailed: "this won't work". The model gets a tool return marked failed, with your message, and the run goes on, so the model can tell the user.

The tool raises The model gets The run ModelRetry Your message, and "try again". One retry per tool, by default Goes on; a second miss ends it ToolFailed A tool return marked failed, with your message Goes on Any other exception Nothing Ends, with the exception in your code

docs.title: A limit on requests
docs.text:
Nothing in the tool loop makes a model decide it's done. A model that keeps calling tools keeps the run going, and with a real model every request costs.

So you give the run a limit: usage_limits=UsageLimits(request_limit=5). Before each request the agent checks the count, and a request that would go over is never sent. The run raises UsageLimitExceeded in your code instead. A run with no limit of your own stops at 50 requests.

That matters most for ToolFailed. A tool that fails the same way every time uses no retries, so nothing but the request limit stops a model that keeps asking.

docs.title: A limit on time
docs.text:
A tool can wait on something that never answers. tool_timeout=, on the agent, gives up on a tool call after that many seconds, and the model gets a retry prompt saying it timed out.

A similar setting, ModelSettings(timeout=...), bounds a request to a real model. The stand-in models here send no request anywhere, so you'll meet it with a real one.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
A stock agent with a tool that can fail in two ways, plus three scripts that show recovery, a stopping limit, and a timeout. We'll use stand-in models so each failure happens predictably.

pydantic-tutor/
├── scripts/
│   ├── stock_check.py        new: a misspelt product, then one whose feed is down
│   ├── runaway.py            new: a model that never stops, and a limit
│   └── slow_tool.py          new: a tool that takes too long
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── given/
        │   └── limit_models.py  given: the stand-in models
        └── stock.py          new: the stock agent and its tool

And the steps, in order:

  1. Tell the model a tool can't work, and compare it with a retry.
  2. Stop a runaway, with a request limit.
  3. Give up on a slow tool, with a timeout.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Step 1: Tell the model a tool can't work
docs.text:
Goal: a tool that raises ModelRetry for a mistake the model can fix, and ToolFailed for one it can't.

We'll give one tool two different ways to report trouble. A misspelled product raises ModelRetry, asking the model to correct its call. A supplier feed that's down raises ToolFailed, because another attempt won't repair the feed. Look at those two branches inside stock_of as you read the code.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/stock.py:

"""An agent with one tool that can fail in two ways."""

from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRetry, ToolFailed

IN_STOCK = {"apple": 12, "bread": 8, "coffee": 40}
# Products whose stock feed is down, so their stock can't be read.
FEED_DOWN = frozenset({"bread"})


def stock_of(*, product: str) -> int:
    """Look up how many of one product are in stock.

    Args:
        product: The product's name: apple, bread or coffee.
    """
    if product not in IN_STOCK:
        # The model wrote `product`: tell it what to fix.
        raise ModelRetry(message=f"There is no product {product!r}.")
    if product in FEED_DOWN:
        # Asking again won't help: the feed is down. Say so, and the model
        # can tell the user instead of retrying.
        raise ToolFailed(message=f"The stock feed for {product} is down.")
    return IN_STOCK[product]


# No model here: each run says which model to use.
stock_agent = Agent(
    name="stock",
    instructions="You answer questions about stock. Answer briefly.",
    tools=[stock_of],
)

Next we'll trigger both branches with a stand-in model, misspells_then_asks_for_bread(). It first asks for the misspelled "bred", then for "bread". Notice that the script itself doesn't handle the two tool failures: the agent carries their messages back to the model, which then answers.

Create scripts/stock_check.py.

"""Ask about two products the tool can't answer for: one misspelt, one whose feed is down."""

from pydantic_tutor.given.limit_models import misspells_then_asks_for_bread
from pydantic_tutor.stock import stock_agent

result = stock_agent.run_sync(
    user_prompt="How much bread is there?", model=misspells_then_asks_for_bread()
)
print("output:", result.output)

uv run scripts/stock_check.py

Tip

Check: after the banner:

asked to retry: There is no product 'bred'.

Fix the errors and try again.
tool return (failed): {"error":"The stock feed for bread is down."}
output: I can't check bread right now.

What it means

Two failures, two rows of the table in Concepts:

  • bred got a retry prompt: your ModelRetry message, then "Fix the errors and try again."
  • bread got a tool return marked failed, with your ToolFailed message.

The run went on after both, and the model told the user what it could. The difference is what you tell the model: "fix it" for a misspelling, "this won't work" for a feed that's down.

docs.title: Step 2: Stop a runaway
docs.text:
Goal: run the stock agent on a model that never stops calling the tool, and stop it with a request limit.

The model is given, keeps_asking_for_bread(): on every request it asks for bread, and prints a line. Every call gets ToolFailed, which uses no retries.

The given model keeps requesting the same unavailable stock, so a normal tool retry won't stop it. Look at UsageLimits(request_limit=5) in the call: this puts a cap on the number of model requests in this run, and the except block shows how your code learns the limit was hit.

Create scripts/runaway.py:

"""Stop a run whose model never stops calling a tool, with a request limit."""

from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UsageLimitExceeded
from pydantic_ai.usage import UsageLimits

from pydantic_tutor.given.limit_models import keeps_asking_for_bread
from pydantic_tutor.stock import stock_agent

try:
    stock_agent.run_sync(
        user_prompt="How much bread is there?",
        model=keeps_asking_for_bread(),
        # This job needs two or three requests; five is room to spare.
        usage_limits=UsageLimits(request_limit=5),
    )
except UsageLimitExceeded as error:
    print("stopped:", error)

Before you run it, guess: with request_limit=5, how many request lines will you see?

uv run scripts/runaway.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, five requests, then the stop:

request 1: the model asks for bread
request 2: the model asks for bread
request 3: the model asks for bread
request 4: the model asks for bread
request 5: the model asks for bread
stopped: The next request would exceed the request_limit of 5. Consider raising the limit, or see the docs on usage limits for budget-aware patterns: https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/agent/#usage-limits

What it means

Five, not six. The agent checked before each request, and the sixth would have gone over, so it was never sent. Your except caught UsageLimitExceeded.

Five failed calls, and no retry was used, because ToolFailed doesn't use one. Without the limit, this model would have made 50 requests before the run stopped. With a real model, that's 50 paid requests for nothing.

docs.title: Step 3: Give up on a slow tool
docs.text:
Goal: give an agent a tool timeout, and see a slow tool time out.

The script builds a small agent of its own, whose one tool takes two seconds. The agent gives up after half a second. The model is given, calls_once_then_answers(): it calls the tool, and answers with what comes back.

Now we'll limit how long the agent waits for a tool, rather than how many requests it makes. The wait_for_delivery tool sleeps for two seconds; tool_timeout=0.5 tells the agent to stop waiting sooner. Notice that the tool is async def, so the waiting operation can be cancelled.

Create scripts/slow_tool.py:

"""Give up on a tool that takes too long, with a tool timeout."""

import asyncio

from pydantic_ai import Agent

from pydantic_tutor.given.limit_models import calls_once_then_answers


async def wait_for_delivery() -> str:
    """Wait for the supplier to confirm a delivery."""
    await asyncio.sleep(delay=2)  # the supplier is slow to answer
    return "Delivery confirmed."


# Half a second, so the timeout shows quickly. A real tool gets seconds,
# set from what it waits on.
slow = Agent(name="deliveries", tools=[wait_for_delivery], tool_timeout=0.5)
result = slow.run_sync(
    user_prompt="Is the delivery confirmed?", model=calls_once_then_answers()
)
print("output:", result.output)

uv run scripts/slow_tool.py

Tip

Check: after the banner, about half a second later:

asked to retry: Timed out after 0.5 seconds.

Fix the errors and try again.
output: The supplier didn't answer.

What it means

The tool never returned "Delivery confirmed." After half a second the agent gave up on the call, and the model got a retry prompt saying so. The timeout uses the tool's one retry, like any ModelRetry.

wait_for_delivery is async def, so it was cancelled, and the script ends about half a second in. A plain def tool can't be cancelled: the agent stops waiting, but the function runs on to its end. If a tool might hang, make it async.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Recover when recovery is possible. Use ModelRetry when the model can fix its call; use ToolFailed to report a problem another attempt won't fix. The run can continue so the model can explain it.
  • A request limit stops a runaway. usage_limits=UsageLimits(request_limit=N) on the run; without one, a run stops at 50 requests.
  • A tool timeout stops a slow tool. tool_timeout= on the agent gives up on a call and tells the model.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
That's Chapter 1: an agent, a model, the messages between them, tools, deps, typed answers and limits. Chapter 2 builds a chat.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. Chapter 1 ran every agent on a stand-in model, inside your own program. That's how you learned what each piece does.

Chapter 2 begins a different kind of project. Instead of making a separate little example in each lesson, you'll build one terminal chat and keep improving it through the rest of the tutorial. First it needs a real model — and this lesson is about that: setting up access to one, and seeing what changes when a model makes its own decisions.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Get an OpenAI key and keep it out of your code and out of git.
  2. Run an agent from Chapter 1 on a real model, unchanged.
  3. Read what a real run cost, and keep it under a limit you set.

Tested on gpt-4o-mini. About 15 minutes.

docs.title: An API key is your account's password
docs.text:
A model is a service you pay for. Different providers — Anthropic, OpenAI and others — offer their own models. You sign up with one and get an API key: a secret string that works like a password for your account. Anyone who has it can spend your money.

Never put the key in source code or commit it to git. In these lessons, you'll supply OPENAI_API_KEY through your shell environment. Pydantic AI reads it when the program uses the OpenAI provider. An environment variable helps keep the key out of the repository; it does not make the secret impossible for other programs on your computer to read.

docs.title: The model is one setting
docs.text:
In Chapter 1 every agent ran on a stand-in model that Pydantic AI provides: model=TestModel(), or a FunctionModel. A real model is passed the same way, as a name: model="openai:gpt-4o-mini". The part before the colon is the provider; the part after is the model.

The agent doesn't change. Its instructions, tools and code are the same; only what answers is different. To keep it that way, the model's name lives in one place in your project, and every script reads it from there. Changing the model is then one line.

The next few lessons use gpt-4o-mini, a relatively inexpensive OpenAI model, so you'll need an OpenAI API key. Later on, you'll plug in any provider you choose.

docs.title: A real run costs money
docs.text:
In Chapter 1 the usage was made up: TestModel invented its token counts, and nothing was billed. A real model consumes billable tokens. Pydantic AI reports usage in result.usage, including a cost estimate when pricing data is available.

The exact charge depends on the model, the tokens used, and current provider pricing. Even small charges add up if a loop keeps making requests. Set a modest budget before you start, and check whether your provider treats that budget as an alert or a hard limit.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
Your key in an environment variable, the model's name in one setting, and a script that runs the price agent from the tools lesson on the real model.

pydantic-tutor/
├── scripts/
│   └── first_real_run.py    new: the price agent on a real model
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        └── model.py         new: the model's name, in one place

And the steps, in order:

  1. Get a key, set a spending limit, and set the key in your shell.
  2. Name the model in one setting.
  3. Run the agent on the real model.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson.

Tip

Check: from the project folder, run:

uv run hello_agent.py

The last line should be:

success (no tool calls)

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

git clone --branch 01-08-limits/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Get a key
docs.text:
Goal: an OpenAI key, a spending limit on your account, and the key in an environment variable.

OpenAI's site changes its pages from time to time, so the names below may differ a little from what you see. At the time of writing:

  1. Sign in, or sign up, at platform.openai.com.
  2. Under Billing, add a small amount of credit. A key doesn't work on an account with none.
  3. Under Limits, set a monthly budget you're comfortable with. A few dollars is far more than this Chapter needs.
  4. On the API keys page, create a key, and copy it. You'll only see it once.

One key works for every OpenAI model: you choose the model in code, not when you create the key.

Now supply the key as an environment variable in the terminal where you'll run the project. Replace the placeholder with your real key. Don't paste the real value into a commit, screenshot, or chat message. For a longer-lived setup, you can use a secret manager or your shell's startup configuration; remember that a plaintext startup file also stores the secret on disk.

One more variable while you're here: Chapter 2's checks read each script's own output, so Pydantic AI's startup banner is only noise — hide it:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here
export PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1

Keep using this terminal for the following commands.

Tip

Check: confirm the key is set without printing any part of it:

test -n "$OPENAI_API_KEY" && echo 'Key is set' || echo 'Key is missing'

You should see:

Key is set

If you see Key is missing, set the variable in this terminal before continuing.

What it means

The Python program can access the key without keeping it in a tracked file. This reduces the risk of an accidental commit; you must still protect the key and your account.

Only programs started from a shell see it. Your editor's terminal does; an app started from the Dock or a desktop menu may not. Run the lessons' commands from a terminal.

docs.title: Step 2: Name the model
docs.text:
Goal: the real model's name, in one place.

The chat will need its model name from somewhere, so you'll put it in a small module the chat can import later. That keeps the choice separate from the code that asks questions: when you change providers or models, you change one line instead of hunting through the program. The file holds a single setting, CHAT_MODEL.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/model.py:

"""The real model the chat runs on, in one place.

Every script that uses a real model
reads it from here, so changing the model is one line.
"""

# The model used by the chat throughout this chapter.
CHAT_MODEL = "openai:gpt-4o-mini"

Tip

Check: print it:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL; print(CHAT_MODEL)"

You should see:

openai:gpt-4o-mini

What it means

The check confirms the setting can be imported by another Python file. That's the whole setting: a provider, openai, and a model, gpt-4o-mini. Every script in this Chapter reads CHAT_MODEL, so if you ever want another model, you change this one line.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the agent on the real model
docs.text:
Goal: run the price agent on the real model, and read what it cost.

This is a bridge from Chapter 1 into the chat you'll soon build. The price_agent and its tools are familiar; the new piece is model=CHAT_MODEL. Look at the final four lines too: they let you inspect what happened instead of taking the answer on trust.

Create scripts/first_real_run.py:

"""Run the price agent on a real model, unchanged.

Run it with `OPENAI_API_KEY` set:
`uv run scripts/first_real_run.py`.
"""

from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL
from pydantic_tutor.prices import price_agent

result = price_agent.run_sync(user_prompt="How much is a coffee?", model=CHAT_MODEL)

for message in result.all_messages():
    print(message.kind, [part.part_kind for part in message.parts])
print("output:", result.output)
print("requests:", result.usage.requests)
print("cost in dollars:", result.usage.cost)

Run it. This is the first time the script contacts the provider, so it uses your key:

uv run scripts/first_real_run.py

Before you look at the output, write down a guess: how many requests will the run make? A real model chooses its own route through the tools, so compare the kind of messages and the final answer, not every word or number.

And here's what each message line is, when it prints:

  • request ['user-prompt'] — your question went to the model: "How much is a coffee?"
  • response ['tool-call'] — the model asked the agent to run the price_of tool.
  • request ['tool-return'] — the agent sent the tool's answer back to the model.
  • response ['text'] — the model answered in words: a coffee costs 700 cents.

Tip

Check: you should see something like this:

request ['user-prompt']
response ['tool-call']
request ['tool-return']
response ['text']
output: A coffee costs 700 cents, or $7.00.
requests: 2
cost in dollars: 0.00004845

Your output will differ, and that's expected. What must match: at least one tool-call and its tool-return, a text answer that says coffee is 700 cents, and a cost of a small fraction of a cent.

What it means

A real model read your question and the tool definitions, decided to call price_of, and answered from what it returned. That's the loop from the tools lesson, with a model that decides for itself instead of following a script.

Deciding for itself means it doesn't always decide the same way. In another of our runs, it called a tool twice before answering, and made three requests instead of two:

request ['user-prompt']
response ['tool-call']
request ['tool-return']
response ['tool-call']
request ['tool-return']
response ['text']
output: A coffee costs 700 cents, or $7.00.
requests: 3
cost in dollars: 0.00007560

Same agent, same question, a different path to the same answer. That's why a real model's output can't be checked line for line, and why Chapter 1 used stand-ins to show each piece exactly.

The reported cost helps you understand the run. Use your provider's billing dashboard to confirm actual charges.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• The key stays out of the source: you supplied it through the environment rather than hard-coding it. That reduces risk, but is not a guarantee of security.
  • The model is one setting, CHAT_MODEL. The agent from Chapter 1 ran on a real model without a single change.
  • A real run costs money, and result.usage.cost tells you how much. Check billing too; a budget is not always an enforced hard cap.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
You now have the real model connection that the growing chat program will use. Next you'll build its first version: a terminal loop that accepts questions and prints replies.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson you ran an agent on a real model, once, and the script ended.

Now you'll create the first version of the chat program that you'll keep extending in later lessons and Chapters. It will be simple at first: type a line, receive an answer, and repeat. Building the loop yourself makes it clear where the application ends and an agent run begins.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Write a chat in the terminal, as a loop around the agent's runs.
  2. Say why it forgets what you told it a moment ago.

Tested on gpt-4o-mini. About 10 minutes.

docs.title: A chat is a loop around runs
docs.text:
You've run an agent many times now: one prompt in, one answer out. A chat is that, again and again. Read what the person types, run the agent on it, print the answer, and go back for the next line. The loop is yours, in plain Python; the agent does what it always did.

A run is one question and its answer: one call to run_sync. Everything the agent does before it answers, every tool call and every request to the model, is part of the same run. In this chat, each line you type starts a run, and its answer ends it.

docs.title: Each run starts fresh
docs.text:
In this particular chat, a run includes the agent's instructions and the current prompt, but no earlier chat messages. Other agents can supply tools or additional context; we're deliberately leaving out conversation history for now.

So when the loop starts a new run for each line you type, the model doesn't receive the earlier lines. It never sees the questions before it. Tell the chat your name, then ask it what your name is, and it can't say: the second run didn't carry the first.

That's not the model being forgetful. It remembers nothing between requests anyway. It's the chat not sending what came before. The next lesson does.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
The first version of your continuing application: a chat agent and a terminal program that calls it repeatedly. They live in a chat/ package, which you'll keep as the lessons add memory, streaming and web search.

pydantic-tutor/
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── __main__.py      new: runs the chat with `python -m pydantic_tutor`
        └── chat/
            ├── __init__.py  new: makes `chat/` a package
            ├── agent.py     new: the agent the chat talks to
            ├── console.py   new: blue and dim, only on a terminal
            └── loop.py      new: the chat, a loop around the agent

And the steps, in order:

  1. Create the chat's agent.
  2. Write the loop, and chat.
  3. Watch it forget.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. If you're in a new terminal, set OPENAI_API_KEY and PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER again: an environment variable lasts only as long as the terminal you set it in.

Tip

Check: the key is set in this terminal. Print its first three characters, and no more:

echo $OPENAI_API_KEY | cut -c1-3

You should see:

sk-

If you see nothing, set the key again (Step 1 of the last lesson): an environment variable lasts only as long as the terminal you set it in.

Then run the last lesson's script and wait for the response:

uv run scripts/first_real_run.py

It should end with an answer saying coffee is 700 cents, and a cost.

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

git clone --branch 02-01-real-model/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the chat's agent
docs.text:
Goal: an agent for the chat, with instructions and no model.

The chat will need an agent to answer each message. We'll keep its definition separate from the terminal loop, so later lessons can add capabilities without changing how we read and print messages. For now, the agent only needs a name and brief instructions; the loop will select the model when it runs.

First, make chat/ a package. Create src/pydantic_tutor/chat/__init__.py:

"""The chat application: its agent, console and loop."""

Then create src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in
this project: the chat passes `CHAT_MODEL` on each run.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent

chat_agent = Agent(
    name="chat",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
)

Tip

Check: print its name and its model:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import chat_agent; print(chat_agent.name, chat_agent.model)"

You should see:

chat None

What it means

An agent like the first one you built: a name, instructions, and no model. The chat gives it CHAT_MODEL on each run.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the loop
docs.text:
Goal: a chat in your terminal: you type, the agent answers.

Now we can build the part that makes this feel like a chat. The program will wait for a line of text, hand it to our agent, show the reply, and wait again until you enter an empty line. That's the job of the Python loop, not the model. The first version won't pass earlier messages to a new run; we'll see the consequence shortly.

First, a small helper so the chat can color its lines. Colors are cosmetic and aren't what this lesson teaches. The helper colors text only when the output is a terminal and NO_COLOR is not set, so piped output and files stay plain. Create src/pydantic_tutor/chat/console.py:

"""Terminal colors for the chat, used only where someone will see them.

Text is colored only when the output
is a terminal and `NO_COLOR` is not set, so piped output, files and tests
get the plain text.
"""

import os
import sys

_BLUE = "\033[38;5;75m"
_DIM = "\033[2m"
_RESET = "\033[0m"


def _wanted() -> bool:
    """Whether to color: output goes to a terminal, and `NO_COLOR` is unset."""
    return sys.stdout.isatty() and not os.environ.get("NO_COLOR")


def blue(*, text: str) -> str:
    """The text in blue, or as it is when colors are not wanted."""
    return f"{_BLUE}{text}{_RESET}" if _wanted() else text


def dim(*, text: str) -> str:
    """The text dimmed, or as it is when colors are not wanted."""
    return f"{_DIM}{text}{_RESET}" if _wanted() else text

Now create src/pydantic_tutor/chat/loop.py. As you read it, find the line that calls the agent, and the condition that ends the loop:

"""A chat in the terminal: type a message, read the answer.

Run it with `OPENAI_API_KEY` set:
`uv run python -m pydantic_tutor`. An empty line, or Ctrl-D, ends
it. Each line you type starts a run of its own, so the agent remembers
nothing from one run to the next.
"""

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.chat.console import blue
from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL


def main() -> None:
    """Read a line, run the agent on it, print the answer; until an empty line."""
    print("Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.")
    while True:
        try:
            line = input("you> ").strip()
        except EOFError:  # Ctrl-D, or the end of piped input
            break
        if not line:
            break
        result = chat_agent.run_sync(user_prompt=line, model=CHAT_MODEL)
        print(blue(text=f"agent> {result.output}"))

loop.py only defines main. To run the package, create src/pydantic_tutor/__main__.py, which Python runs for python -m pydantic_tutor:

"""Run the chat: `uv run python -m pydantic_tutor`."""

from pydantic_tutor.chat.loop import main

main()

Now chat:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Type a message after you>, press Enter, and read the answer. Press Enter on an empty line to stop.

Tip

Check: you should see something like this, with your own messages:

Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.
you> Hello!
agent> Hello! How can I assist you today?
you>

The agent's words will differ; what matters is that it answers each line you type. In a terminal the agent> line is blue; the colors are not part of the check.

What it means

You can now stay in one terminal program and exchange several messages with the agent. Each reply still comes from a separate agent run. The Python loop gives the application its repeated interaction; it doesn't yet give those runs a shared conversation.

docs.title: Step 3: Watch it forget
docs.text:
Goal: see that each line you type is a run of its own.

Now test whether a chat interface is the same thing as conversation memory. You'll tell it a name, then ask for that name in the very next message. If the program hasn't passed earlier messages along, the second run has no reliable way to know the answer.

Start the chat again, and type these two lines, one at a time:

My name is Sam.

What is my name?

Before you send the second, guess: will it know?

Tip

Check: something like this:

you> My name is Sam.
agent> Hi, Sam! How can I assist you today?
you> What is my name?
agent> I’m not sure what your name is. Can you tell me?

In another of our runs it said "I don’t know your name. You can tell me if you’d like!" The wording varies; it doesn't know.

What it means

It greeted you by name, then couldn't reliably recall it. This isn't a failure of the loop: you wrote the loop to pass only the current prompt. The next improvement to this same program will be to preserve and resend previous messages.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• A chat is a loop around runs: read a line, run the agent on it, print the answer. A run is one question and its answer, tool calls included. The loop is plain Python.
  • Each run starts fresh, so a chat that runs the agent once per line forgets everything before the current question.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The chat now works, but its conversations don't continue across runs. Next you'll change chat/loop.py to carry earlier messages into each new run. The loop stays; the application gets memory of the current chat.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson your chat forgot your name one line after you told it.

This lesson is about history: handing each run the messages of the chat so far, so the model can see what was said.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Make the chat remember, by passing each run the messages before it.
  2. Say what the model is sent each time, and why it grows.

Tested on gpt-4o-mini. About 10 minutes.

docs.title: The chat sends what came before
docs.text:
Your terminal loop already works. What's missing is the conversation. The model doesn't retain the earlier requests on its own, so your program must keep the messages and supply them on later runs.

A run's result has them all, result.all_messages(): every request and response of this run, and of any history it was given. You pass them to the next run as message_history=, and that run sends them to the model before your new question.

docs.title: Every request carries the whole chat
docs.text:
So the model is sent more each time: the first question, its answer, the second question, its answer, and so on, then the new one. A long chat means long requests, and on a real model you pay for every token sent.

This is the central idea behind conversation history: continuity comes from context the application supplies, not from a model quietly remembering a previous request. Production applications can manage, summarize or retrieve history in other ways; this chat starts by resending the messages.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
You'll revise the same chat/loop.py from the previous lesson. It will keep messages between runs and pass them to the agent. You'll also print input-token usage to see a consequence of including history.

pydantic-tutor/
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        └── chat/
            └── loop.py  changed: history between runs, and the tokens sent

There's one step: give the chat a history, and watch it remember.

Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. If you're in a new terminal, set OPENAI_API_KEY and PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER again: an environment variable lasts only as long as the terminal you set it in.

Tip

Check: from the project folder, start the chat, send one line, and end it with an empty line:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

The agent should answer your line. It still forgets: that is this lesson.

Warning

The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Give the chat a history
docs.text:
Goal: a chat that remembers what you told it, and shows what the model is sent.

As it stands, your loop works fine: you can chat with the model as long as you like. But the model forgets each line the moment it answers it, because every run is sent only the one new line. To answer a follow-up, the model needs the conversation that came before — and it can't get that on its own. Your program has to keep a record of the chat and pass that history along with every question.

Here's the part that makes this easy: pydantic-ai already keeps the record. Each run's result carries the log of every message that run saw — the history it was handed, plus its own request and answer — and result.all_messages() gives you that whole log. Feeding it forward takes one new argument: message_history=.

So the terminal loop stays as it is, and only a few lines around the run change. Open src/pydantic_tutor/chat/loop.py and make these edits.

Add the import for ModelMessage — the type of the history list — at the top of the file, and extend the color import with dim:

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage
from pydantic_tutor.chat.console import blue, dim

Before the while loop, start an empty history:

history: list[ModelMessage] = []  # every message of the chat so far

Then, inside the loop, hand that history to the run, print what the model was sent, and save the log the run returns for next time:

result = chat_agent.run_sync(
    user_prompt=line, model=CHAT_MODEL, message_history=history
)
print(blue(text=f"agent> {result.output}"))
print(dim(text=f"  (the model was sent {result.usage.input_tokens} tokens)"))
history = result.all_messages()

With those edits in, src/pydantic_tutor/chat/loop.py should look like this (the docstrings are updated to match):

"""A chat in the terminal that remembers: type a message, read the answer.

Run it with `OPENAI_API_KEY` set:
`uv run python -m pydantic_tutor`. An empty line, or Ctrl-D, ends
it. Each run is handed the messages of the runs before it, so the model is
sent the whole chat so far.
"""

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.chat.console import blue, dim
from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL


def main() -> None:
    """Read a line, run the agent on it with the chat so far, print the answer."""
    print("Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.")
    history: list[ModelMessage] = []  # every message of the chat so far
    while True:
        try:
            line = input("you> ").strip()
        except EOFError:  # Ctrl-D, or the end of piped input
            break
        if not line:
            break
        result = chat_agent.run_sync(
            user_prompt=line, model=CHAT_MODEL, message_history=history
        )
        print(blue(text=f"agent> {result.output}"))
        print(dim(text=f"  (the model was sent {result.usage.input_tokens} tokens)"))
        history = result.all_messages()

Start the chat, and send these three lines, one at a time:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

My name is Sam.

What is my name?

Thanks!

Before starting, notice the order: the program first sends history, then replaces it with the messages returned by this run. Watch whether the input-token count grows as you add turns.

Tip

Check: something like this:

Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.
you> My name is Sam.
agent> Nice to meet you, Sam! How can I help you today?
(the model was sent 25 tokens)
you> What is my name?
agent> Your name is Sam.
(the model was sent 52 tokens)
you> Thanks!
agent> You’re welcome, Sam! If you need anything else, just let me know!
(the model was sent 67 tokens)

The words and numbers will differ. The important observations are that the second answer can use your name and that sending longer history generally increases input-token usage.

What it means

The second answer could use the name from the first exchange because your program carried that exchange forward. The model didn't gain persistent memory; the next run received earlier messages as input. The next model request included "My name is Sam." along with "What is my name?".

In this sample, input usage grew from 25 to 52 to 67 tokens as the conversation accumulated. Exact counts vary and aren't guaranteed to rise on every individual turn, but carrying more history generally requires more input tokens. Nothing about the model changed; your program supplied more context.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• The chat remembers because it sends what came before: each run gets message_history= the messages of the runs before it, from result.all_messages().
  • This version passes the accumulated chat on every run. Longer context generally uses more tokens and can increase cost.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The application now remembers within a session. Next you'll keep that history behavior while changing how replies reach the terminal: instead of waiting for a whole answer, you'll stream it as it arrives.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson your chat learned to remember, by sending the chat so far with each run.

You'll keep improving the chat program, this time changing the user's experience rather than its memory. Streaming lets the terminal show pieces of a reply as they arrive instead of displaying the entire reply at the end.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Stream the chat's answers as they're written.
  2. Say what streaming changes, and what it doesn't.

Tested on gpt-4o-mini. About 10 minutes.

docs.title: The answer arrives in pieces
docs.text:
The model generates its output incrementally. Your existing run_sync call waits until the run finishes, then gives you the answer. For a long answer, that means staring at nothing, then a wall of text.

Streaming hands you the pieces as they arrive. You start the run with run_stream_sync instead of run_sync, and read the text from result.stream_text(delta=True): each piece is the new text since the last one. Print each as it comes, and the answer appears as it's written.

docs.title: The run is the same
docs.text: Streaming changes how the final text reaches your program. You still supply message_history, and after consuming the stream, you still save the messages for the next turn. The underlying run may involve other events, including tool calls; this example focuses on streaming the final answer.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
You'll revise chat/loop.py again. The chat still accepts a line and keeps its history; the difference is that it prints response text incrementally.

pydantic-tutor/
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        └── chat/
            └── loop.py  changed: answers are streamed

There's one step: stream the answers.

docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. If you're in a new terminal, set OPENAI_API_KEY and PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER again: an environment variable lasts only as long as the terminal you set it in.

Tip

Check: from the project folder, start the chat, send one line, and end it with an empty line:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

The agent should answer your line. The answer appears all at once: that is this lesson.

Warning

cd pydantic-tutor
