docs.title: Step 1: Stream the answers
docs.text:
Goal: a chat whose answers appear as they're written.

So far the program waits until a reply is complete before showing any of it. Feel that once before we change it: start the chat as it is, and ask for something with a little length:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tell me a short story about a lighthouse keeper, in four sentences.

A pause, then the whole story lands in one block. For four sentences that's a moment; a long answer is a wait spent staring at nothing. End the chat with an empty line, and open src/pydantic_tutor/chat/loop.py.

Let's make the chat stream its answers!

You'll edit loop.py. Three small edits, all inside the loop; the question-collecting and history-keeping don't move. Try the edits yourself, and compare with the full file at the end.

1. Use run_stream_sync. run_sync becomes run_stream_sync, with the same arguments:

        result = chat_agent.run_stream_sync(
            user_prompt=line, model=CHAT_MODEL, message_history=history
        )

The result can now hand over the answer in pieces as they arrive, not only as one string at the end.

2. Print each piece as it arrives. result.stream_text(delta=True) yields just the new text since the last piece — a few words at a time:

        for piece in result.stream_text(delta=True):
            print(piece, end="", flush=True)

flush=True makes each piece show at once; without it, Python may hold the text back until the line ends.

3. Split the agent> print around the stream. The single print becomes an opening print with no newline — so the first piece lands on the same line — and a closing print() that ends the line when the stream ends. The answer stays blue (blue is the helper from the console-chat lesson), so each piece is colored on its own:

        print(blue(text="agent> "), end="")
        for piece in result.stream_text(delta=True):
            print(blue(text=piece), end="", flush=True)
        print()

Because every piece carries its own color and reset, stopping the chat with Ctrl-C in the middle of an answer can't leave your terminal blue.

With all three edits, the middle of the loop reads like this — and here is the whole file, with history updated after the answer as before:

"""A chat in the terminal that remembers: type a message, read the answer.

Run it with `OPENAI_API_KEY` set:
`uv run python -m pydantic_tutor`. An empty line, or Ctrl-D, ends
it. Each run is handed the messages of the runs before it, so the model is
sent the whole chat so far, and its answer is printed as it is written.
"""

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.chat.console import blue, dim
from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL


def main() -> None:
    """Read a line, run the agent on it with the chat so far, print the answer."""
    print("Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.")
    history: list[ModelMessage] = []  # every message of the chat so far
    while True:
        try:
            line = input("you> ").strip()
        except EOFError:  # Ctrl-D, or the end of piped input
            break
        if not line:
            break
        result = chat_agent.run_stream_sync(
            user_prompt=line, model=CHAT_MODEL, message_history=history
        )
        print(blue(text="agent> "), end="")
        # Each piece of the answer as it arrives; flush, so it shows at once.
        for piece in result.stream_text(delta=True):
            print(blue(text=piece), end="", flush=True)
        print()
        print(dim(text=f"  (the model was sent {result.usage.input_tokens} tokens)"))
        history = result.all_messages()

Run the chat again, and ask it the same question:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tip

Check: the story appears a few words at a time, not all at once. When it's done, you see the tokens line, as before. Ours:

you> Tell me a short story about a lighthouse keeper, in four sentences.
agent> In a stormy coastal village, an old lighthouse keeper named Elias tended to his beacon with unwavering dedication. One fateful night, a fierce tempest threatened to engulf a passing ship, casting it into turmoil among the waves. As the light flickered, Elias steadfastly kept the flame alive, guiding the vessel to safety with his unwavering resolve. When dawn broke, the villagers gathered to thank the keeper, who simply smiled, saying, "The light shines brightest in the darkest of times."
(the model was sent 34 tokens)

Your story will differ. Then ask it something about the story, such as "What was his name?": it still remembers.

What it means

The reply appeared gradually, but the follow-up still worked. That combination is the point: a change to how the terminal displays an answer didn't require changing how the application remembers the conversation. The same history is supplied before the run and saved once the response is complete.

One thing to know if you stream in a script of your own: keep the streamed run inside a function, as main() does here. At this version, a streamed result left at the top level of a script can keep the program from exiting when it's done.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Streaming shows the answer as it's written: run_stream_sync, then print each piece from stream_text(delta=True).
  • The application retains history. Streaming changes how this example receives the final text, not how it supplies previous messages.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The chat now remembers and streams. Next you'll give that same agent a new source of information: the ability to request a web search.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In the last lesson your chat learned to stream its answers.

The chat can now carry on a conversation and stream its replies. But what if the user asks for something that changed yesterday? In this lesson you'll extend the same chat agent with web search, allowing it to look up information that isn't reliably available from its training alone.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Give an agent web search with one prebuilt capability.
  2. Say when the model searches, and what a search costs.

Tested on gpt-4o-mini. About 10 minutes.

docs.title: A capability adds a feature
docs.text:
Without an external source, a model may not know recent events or the latest version of a library. It can still sound confident, which is why current facts should be checked against sources.

Giving a model a way to check usually means plumbing it yourself: pick a search service, write the calls, parse what comes back, feed the result to the model. Pydantic AI ships ready-made features that do that plumbing for you, called capabilities. You add one in a line, capabilities=[...], and the agent gains what it does. WebSearch() gives the model a way to search the web.

Later Chapters build capabilities of your own; this one you just use.

docs.title: The model decides when to search
docs.text:
Making web search available lets the model choose to request it. It may search for the latest release of a library and may skip search for a simple arithmetic question. Availability doesn't guarantee that it will always make the best choice.

Here the searching itself is provided by OpenAI: when the model asks to search, the provider's own search runs and its results come back in the model's context — no search function of yours is involved. It's the zero-plumbing option, and less flexible than one you'd write yourself; WebSearch offers controls such as allowed_domains and max_uses, but the searching happens on the provider's side. For a demo like this one, that trade is worth it.

Provider support, pricing and billing rules can change; consult the current provider pricing before relying on any per-search estimate. Searching can add to the cost of your chat.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
One change to chat/agent.py gives your existing application another capability. You don't need to rewrite its input loop, history handling or streaming code.

pydantic-tutor/
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        └── chat/
            └── agent.py     changed: the agent can search the web

And the steps, in order:

  1. Ask the chat something it can't know.
  2. Give it web search, and ask again.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson. If you're in a new terminal, set OPENAI_API_KEY and PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER again: an environment variable lasts only as long as the terminal you set it in.

Tip

Check: from the project folder, start the chat, send one line, and end it with an empty line:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

The agent should answer your line.

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its pydantic-tutor folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including local credentials. Then, from the folder that should hold the project:

git clone --branch 02-04-streaming/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor

The copy also has a tests/ folder, our own checks for each lesson. You don't need it. Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Ask something it can't know
docs.text:
Goal: see what the chat says about something newer than the model.

Start the chat, and ask:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

What is the very latest release of pydantic-ai on PyPI, and when was it released?  Don't guess!

Tip

Check: without search, the model may say it cannot confirm the latest version, or it may offer an unverified guess. Ours said:

agent> You can check the latest release of `pydantic-ai` on PyPI directly at [pypi.org](https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-ai/) for up-to-date information. My knowledge is not current beyond October 2021, so I can't provide the most recent release details.
(the model was sent 40 tokens)

The wording can differ. What matters is that an answer without a current source isn't reliable evidence of the latest release.

What it means

The chat had no retrieval capability. It could provide background knowledge, but it couldn't verify the current PyPI release. Even a confident version number would need an up-to-date source.

docs.title: Step 2: Give it web search
docs.text:
Goal: a chat that searches the web when it needs to.

Our chat already knows how to receive messages, preserve context, and show replies as they arrive. The missing piece is a way to check information that changes after a model was trained. Instead of writing our own search function, we'll give the existing agent access to a provider-backed search capability. The model can then request a search as part of answering a question; making it available does not guarantee that it will search every time.

This time the change isn't in the chat loop at all — chat/loop.py stays exactly as it is. Open src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py and make two additions.

Add the import at the top of the file:

from pydantic_ai.capabilities import WebSearch

Add the capability to the agent — one new parameter that we pass to the Agent() call:

capabilities=[WebSearch()]

With those edits in, chat/agent.py should look like this (the docstring is updated to match):

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes
`CHAT_MODEL` on each run.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import WebSearch

chat_agent = Agent(
    name="chat",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
    # The model may search the web when it needs to. Each search is billed
    # by the provider, on top of the tokens.
    capabilities=[WebSearch()],
)

Now compare two kinds of question in the same application. One asks for a changing fact and benefits from a current source; the other can be answered without retrieval. The contrast may help you observe when the model chooses the new capability, though its decisions and token usage can vary.

Start the chat again, and send the same question, then a simple one:

What is the very latest release of pydantic-ai on PyPI, and when was it released?  Don't guess!

What is 2 + 2?

Notice the contrast between these prompts: one requires current information, while the other can be answered without looking anything up. See how the model behaves, but don't assume it must search on one and skip the other.

Tip

Check: something like this:

you> What is the very latest release of pydantic-ai on PyPI, and when was it released?  Don't guess!
agent> The latest release of pydantic-ai on PyPI is version 2.62.0, published on October 27, 2026. ([pypi.org](https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-ai/2.62.0/?utm_source=openai))
(the model was sent 8174 tokens)
you> What is 2 + 2?
agent> 2 + 2 equals 4.
(the model was sent 410 tokens)

The version, date, source formatting and token counts will vary. Check the cited PyPI release yourself. A source-backed answer is the goal; a particular token count or search decision is not guaranteed.

What it means

The chat didn't need a new input loop or a different history mechanism to look something up. Inside the run, the model decided it needed a current source and asked to search; the provider's search ran, and its results were added to what the model was sent — most of why the input-token count jumped. The model then answered from what the search brought back, and cited where it came from.

Here the fetched material was the answer: one fact, repeated back. The same mechanism matters more when the finding feeds a bigger question — a model that can reach for sources mid-run can weigh what it finds instead of just repeating a single result.

Worth noticing who set the terms of that reach. The model could only search because a capability said it may, on the provider's side. When you read that an agent "went rogue," look for the tool boundary: something executed the action, and someone set its scope. In a later Chapter you'll build the other half of that boundary: an agent that asks before it acts.

The follow-up arithmetic question used far fewer tokens, which is the cost contrast to notice; the search decisions themselves can vary from run to run.

That release is newer than the one this series is written against, 2.56.0. The series stays on 2.56; the chat illustrated how to check a newer release without changing the project dependencies.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• A capability adds a feature in one line: capabilities=[WebSearch()] gave the chat web search.
  • The model can choose to search when it has access to the capability. Verify important sources, and consult current provider pricing for search charges.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
That's Chapter 2: you now have one growing chat program, connected to a real model, with conversation history, streaming and optional web search. Chapter 3 continues building this application, adding settings and a workspace the agent can work in.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Chapter 3: The application and a workspace
docs.text:
In Chapter 2, you turned an agent into a chat. It can carry a conversation, stream its answers, and search the web. It works—but so far it has made most of its decisions in Python code, and its only way to help is to answer you.

In this chapter, we'll start treating that chat as an application. First, we'll decide how it gets its configuration: which model to use, which features are available, and where credentials come from. We'll assemble the pieces at startup instead of leaving important decisions until the first message.

Then we'll give the chat a place to work. A workspace identifies a folder; file tools let the model request reads and changes; a shell lets it request commands. Each addition gives the chat more reach. Each also raises a question: who decides what it may do?

This is a little different from learning another agent feature. We're beginning to make choices that matter in real applications: keeping configuration separate from code, constructing components in a predictable place, and distinguishing a convenient restriction from a real security boundary.

You'll keep working on the same chat application. Each lesson adds one piece and gives you a way to see what changed. You don't need to know application architecture before you start—we'll build the picture as we go.

Start with 03-01: Settings and a composition root.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. Your chat now remembers conversations, streams answers, and searches the web. We're beginning to turn it into an application you can configure without rewriting it.

Right now two decisions are made in Python code: the model's name lives in model.py, and web search is switched on inside chat/agent.py. That's a reasonable way to start. But suppose you want to switch off web search for one run, or choose a different model on another machine. Why should either choice require an edit?

Applications usually have a way to collect these choices, often called configuration. Some values have sensible defaults in code; others come from a file or from the environment where the program runs. We'll bring our two choices into a typed Settings class, try changing their values without editing Python, and then build the chat from those settings at startup.

There's a second payoff: a missing API key currently makes the chat fail after you type your first message. We'll move that failure to startup, before the chat invites you to type.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Separate values from objects: read every choice into one typed Settings, and build the agent and model from it in one place.
  2. Make a bad setting or a missing key stop the app at startup, by name, before the chat opens.

About 15 minutes. From Step 2 on, no API key is needed.

docs.title: Where the configuration lives
docs.text:
Our chat has two choices built into Python: which model it uses and whether web search is available. We'll collect them in a Settings class. Each setting has a name, a Python type, and a default value.

Pydantic Settings can read those choices from several places, including environment variables and files. It interprets incoming text according to the field's type: for example, false from the environment becomes the Python boolean False. That gives our application one consistent way to obtain its configuration, even when the values come from different places.

Later in the lesson, we'll use those settings to assemble the agent and model. For now, we'll concentrate on gathering the choices and seeing how overrides work.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
pydantic-tutor/
├── pyproject.toml                    changed: pydantic-settings, pinned
├── uv.lock                           changed: the same, resolved
└── src/
    └── pydantic_tutor/
        ├── chat/
        │   ├── agent.py              changed: build_chat_agent(web_search=...)
        │   └── loop.py               changed: reads the settings, runs on the built app
        ├── composition.py            new: App and build_app, the one place objects are built
        └── settings.py               new: Settings, every choice, typed

And the steps, in order:

  1. Create settings: collect the chat's two defaults in one class.
  2. Try overrides: read settings from the environment and a file.
  3. Assemble the application: build an agent and model from settings.
  4. Update the chat loop: use the assembled application.

Each step ends with a Check. If it doesn't show what it says, stop there: the next step builds on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Continue with the pydantic-tutor project you've been building. From its root folder, check that the Chapter 2 chat still works:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Check: send one short message, confirm that the agent replies, then end the chat with an empty line. Use the API key you set up in Chapter 2.

Warning

Only start fresh if you need to.

If you've been following the lessons, keep using your existing project. Do not run these commands.

If you're joining at this lesson or starting again without an existing project, run these commands from a parent directory where no folder named pydantic-tutor exists. Every lesson uses that same project folder name. If you already have pydantic-tutor, keep using it; do not run the clone commands or overwrite that folder. Starting again would lose the work and settings in your existing project.

git clone --branch 02-05-web-search/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

docs.title: Step 1: Create the chat's settings
docs.text: Goal: put the two existing choices in one typed class, with defaults that keep the chat behaving as before.

docs.title: Add pydantic-settings as a dependency
docs.text:
We're about to import pydantic-settings directly, so add it to our project's dependencies even if another package already installed it:

uv add pydantic-settings==2.16.0

Check: open pyproject.toml and confirm that pydantic-settings appears in its dependencies. If the command reported an error, stop before continuing.

docs.title: Create Settings with two defaults
docs.text:
Now create src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py. This is a new class with two fields: chat_model holds the model name, and web_search holds a true-or-false choice. Both start with the same values our chat already used in Python code. We're moving them into one place, not changing the behavior yet.

"""Every value the app is configured with, typed and checked at startup.

Values only: strings and flags read from the environment. The objects built
from them are in `composition.py`.
"""

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Read from variables named `PYDANTIC_TUTOR_<FIELD>`; frozen once created."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="PYDANTIC_TUTOR_", frozen=True)

    # A `<provider>:<model>` string, the name of the model: not the model.
    chat_model: str = CHAT_MODEL
    # Whether the chat may search the web. Each search is billed.
    web_search: bool = True

A Settings instance can read environment variables as well as those defaults. frozen=True prevents assigning a new value to a field after it has been created.

Let's first see the defaults:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings())"

Tip

Check: if you have no PYDANTIC_TUTOR_ overrides in your shell:

chat_model='openai:gpt-4o-mini' web_search=True

The chat's two choices now have one home. We haven't yet made the running chat use this class.

docs.title: Step 2: Change a setting without editing Python
docs.text: Goal: see how the same typed setting can get a value from an environment variable or a file without changing the class.

docs.title: Override a setting from the environment
docs.text:
Try changing web search for just this one command:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings().web_search)"

Tip

Check: it prints False.

The environment supplies text, but Pydantic Settings interprets false as a Python boolean. We didn't change the class or its default.

docs.title: Read a setting from a file
docs.text:
So far, the values came from Python defaults or variables on a command line. If you regularly run the chat with web search off, you might not want to type that override every time. A .env file is a plain text file of NAME=value lines. Create a practice file in the project root with an ordinary setting. We use a separate name so we don't overwrite your real .env file, which might contain an API key:

printf 'PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false\n' > lesson-settings.env

Check: open lesson-settings.env and confirm it contains the line PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false.

Now ask Settings to read it:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings(_env_file='lesson-settings.env').web_search)"

Tip

Check: it prints False. The file overrides the Python default.

Finally, override the file with an environment variable:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=true uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings(_env_file='lesson-settings.env').web_search)"

Tip

Check: this time it prints True.

What it means

The class hasn't changed. Its Python default is True; the file overrides it with false; and a variable supplied for that command takes precedence over the file. That's the useful idea: one setting, several possible sources, a predictable result. We're opting into the file for this experiment with _env_file. In the next lesson we'll configure Settings to read it routinely, including the credentials needed by model providers.

Your real .env is excluded by the project's .gitignore; keep it that way. You can delete lesson-settings.env after this experiment. Don't put real credentials in the practice file. A file on your machine is convenient configuration, not a secure secret store.

docs.title: Step 3: Assemble the agent and model from settings
docs.text:
Goal: build_app(settings=...) returns the agent and the model, built from the settings.

We've seen where configuration values can come from. Now it's time to make them change the running application. The agent needs the web-search flag, while the chat loop needs a model object rather than a name. We'll assemble those two pieces in build_app, so the loop doesn't need to know how either was chosen.

First we'll define a new build_chat_agent function. Instead of constructing the agent immediately with web search hard-coded, the function takes a web_search argument and builds the agent accordingly. This is a factory function—one straightforward way to configure an agent before using it. In the next file we'll call that function from build_app. We're separating those two actions deliberately. Replace src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability, WebSearch


def build_chat_agent(*, web_search: bool) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = []
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(web_search=True)

The header lists the pieces the agent is built from, and each is marked in the code by name. Each lesson that changes this file adds one.

We have now defined the factory, but our running chat doesn't use it yet. Next we'll call it from build_app, together with infer_model, which creates the model from its name. That gives us a single place to assemble the application's main pieces before the chat opens. This assembly point is often called the composition root.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py:

"""The composition root: the one place the app's objects are built.

`build_app` turns `Settings` (values) into the agent and the model (objects).
The model is built here, at startup, so an unknown provider or a missing API key
stops the app before the chat opens, not when the first message is sent.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class App:
    """What the chat needs to run, built once from the settings."""

    agent: Agent[None, str]
    model: Model


def build_app(*, settings: Settings) -> App:
    """Build the agent and the model from `settings`.

    Raises `pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError` if the model name's provider is
    unknown or its API key is not set.
    """
    return App(
        agent=build_chat_agent(web_search=settings.web_search),
        model=infer_model(model=settings.chat_model),
    )

App is a small frozen container for the agent and model. Notice the two different jobs in build_app: build_chat_agent uses the web-search choice to configure the agent; infer_model turns the model name into an object. The latter also builds the provider and checks for its key. That is why this is an application assembly step, rather than another way to read settings.

Try assembling an app with Pydantic AI's keyless test model. No model request will be sent:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.composition import build_app; from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; app = build_app(settings=Settings(chat_model='test')); print(type(app.model).__name__, app.agent.name)"

Tip

Check: the output is TestModel chat.

The string test was a configuration value; build_app constructed a TestModel and an agent. A real provider's missing key can now be noticed at assembly time, before the conversation starts.

docs.title: Step 4: Update the chat loop to use the configured application
docs.text:
Goal: run the same chat using the agent and model assembled from Settings.

Our chat already handles keyboard input, streams replies, and remembers message history. None of that needs to change. What does change is where the chat gets its agent and model.

Previously the loop imported a ready-made chat_agent and passed a hard-coded model name on each run. Now we'll build both at the beginning of main, before the first prompt. In the loop itself, app.agent and app.model replace those two old values.

We'll also handle startup configuration errors here. If settings are invalid or the model can't be built, the program should explain why before showing the you> prompt. We aren't going to trigger an error deliberately.

Replace src/pydantic_tutor/chat/loop.py with this complete version; compare the configuration block at the beginning of main:

"""The terminal chat, with streaming and conversation history.

The application is assembled from Settings before the chat opens.
"""

from pydantic import ValidationError
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UserError
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage

from pydantic_tutor.chat.console import blue, dim
from pydantic_tutor.composition import build_app
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings


def main() -> None:
    """Build the app, then run the chat with streaming and history."""
    try:
        app = build_app(settings=Settings())
    except (ValidationError, UserError) as error:
        # A bad setting or a missing key: say which, and do not open the chat.
        raise SystemExit(f"pydantic-tutor cannot start:\n{error}") from error
    print("Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.")
    history: list[ModelMessage] = []  # every message of the chat so far
    while True:
        try:
            line = input("you> ").strip()
        except EOFError:
            break
        if not line:
            break
        result = app.agent.run_stream_sync(
            user_prompt=line, model=app.model, message_history=history
        )
        print(blue(text="agent> "), end="")
        for piece in result.stream_text(delta=True):
            print(blue(text=piece), end="", flush=True)
        print()
        print(dim(text=f"  (the model was sent {result.usage.input_tokens} tokens)"))
        history = result.all_messages()

Notice the division of work: the beginning of main assembles the application once; the loop that follows only runs the conversation. The project's existing __main__.py can still call main() as before.

Run the chat with the keyless test model. Since that model doesn't support provider-hosted web search, disable web search for this run:

env -u OPENAI_API_KEY PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER=1 PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=test PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tip

Check: type hello, then an empty line. You should see:

Chat with the agent. An empty line ends it.
you> hello
agent> success (no tool calls)
(the model was sent 51 tokens)
you>

What it means

We've changed the agent's capabilities and the model with configuration, not by editing the conversation loop for each choice. The same chat still streams responses and carries its message history from one turn to the next.

Because assembly now happens before the chat opens, a missing key or an unknown provider is also reported earlier. (A misspelled model with a known provider, such as openai:gpt-4o-minii, isn't caught here: it builds, and the mistake shows only when the first message is sent.) That's a useful benefit of this design, although configuration—not failure handling—is the main idea of the lesson.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Separate values from objects: Settings holds the chat's choices as typed values read from the environment, and build_app is the one place that builds the agent and model from them.
  • Make a bad setting or a missing key stop the app at startup: a value that doesn't fit its type, an unknown provider and a missing key each end the app with a message before the chat opens.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The chat now reads configuration before it opens. In the next lesson you give that place more to decide: which provider the name resolves to, and how the provider gets its key.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. In 03-01, you moved the chat's choices into Settings and gave build_app the job of assembling the agent and model before the conversation opens. The chat itself still streams answers and remembers its messages.

You can now choose a model by changing a setting. But there's one part of model construction we haven't taken control of: how the model service gets its API key. Until now, Pydantic AI has been free to look for that key in the environment.

In this lesson, we'll prepare our chat to work with two model providers: OpenAI and Anthropic. We'll teach our application where to find each provider's API key and how to pass it along when creating a model, without changing the conversation loop.

We won't send a request to either provider yet. Instead, we'll use made-up API keys and run small checks to confirm that our application reads the right settings, selects the right provider, and passes the key where it belongs. That way, we can understand how the pieces fit together without needing real credentials or paying for model requests.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Read API keys through Settings without printing their values, and pass the selected key to a provider.
  2. Build either an OpenAI or an Anthropic model from configuration, leaving the chat loop alone.

docs.title: Where the key goes
docs.text:
The model is the object the agent uses to request an answer. A provider connects that model to a service that hosts it. For an OpenAI model, an OpenAIProvider supplies the connection details, including an API key. An AnthropicProvider plays the same role for Anthropic.

Think about the sequence before a chat message is sent:

  1. Settings reads the model choice and any configured keys.
  2. Our code creates the provider for that choice and hands it the right key.
  3. Pydantic AI constructs the model using that provider.
  4. build_app gives the model to the same chat you've already built.

Our code will choose a service and hand it the corresponding key. Pydantic AI still handles requests and responses. We are changing how the application starts, not how the chat converses.

We will make those changes in three files:

src/pydantic_tutor/
├── settings.py       edit: read keys and .env
├── providers.py      new: select a provider and pass its key
├── composition.py    edit: build models using our provider selection
└── chat/loop.py      unchanged

The last line matters: we're improving the existing application, not building a separate example.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Continue in your existing pydantic-tutor directory from 03-01. From the project root, open the keyless test chat:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=test PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tip

Check: enter hello, see the test model answer, and end with an empty line. If that doesn't work, resolve it before editing; this lesson builds on that application.

Warning

Already have the project? Do not run these clone commands.

Only if you're joining at 03-02 or starting again without an existing project, run these from a parent directory where no pydantic-tutor folder exists. Every lesson uses that same project folder name. If you already have pydantic-tutor, keep using it; do not delete or replace it. Starting over would lose the work and settings in your existing project:

git clone --branch 03-01-settings/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

docs.title: Step 1: Add provider keys to Settings
docs.text: In 03-01, Settings held two choices: chat_model and web_search. We're going to keep them, add one optional key for each provider, and teach Settings to read the same .env file you've been using. None of this contacts a model service.

docs.title: Import the two Pydantic helpers
docs.text:
An API key is sensitive text. Pydantic's SecretStr stores it as a string that is masked when displayed; it is not encryption, and your code can still retrieve the value deliberately. Field lets us configure how Settings reads a field.

Open src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py. Beneath the module docstring, add this import beside the existing pydantic_settings import:

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr

Check: the new import is at the top of the module, not inside Settings. Keep the existing imports.

docs.title: Add optional keys with their usual environment names
docs.text:
Normally, Settings looks for variables beginning with PYDANTIC_TUTOR_. Provider keys already have familiar names: OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. A validation_alias tells Pydantic Settings to read that exact name instead of deriving one from the field name.

The annotation SecretStr | None means a key can be missing. That matters for our no-key test model: it should still start without real credentials. default=None gives the field that starting value.

Inside class Settings, immediately after the existing web_search field, add:

    # One key per provider the composition root can build. SecretStr:
    # printing the settings shows `**********`, never the key.
    openai_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="OPENAI_API_KEY"
    )
    anthropic_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
    )

Check: both fields are indented inside Settings; chat_model and web_search are unchanged. At this point these fields read keys, but nothing passes a key to a provider yet.

docs.title: Tell Settings to read .env automatically
docs.text:
In 03-01, we passed _env_file explicitly when we wanted to read a practice file. Now we'll set a default. env_file=".env" means look for .env in the working directory when Settings() is created. A shell variable takes priority over the corresponding entry in that file.

There are two details that matter when reading an existing .env:

  • env_ignore_empty=True means an empty environment value is treated as absent instead of as an actual key.
  • extra="ignore" means unrelated names in the file won't cause a validation error. We shouldn't require every entry in your .env to belong to this app.

Locate the existing single-line model_config = SettingsConfigDict(...) inside Settings. Keep its existing env_prefix and frozen arguments, but expand it into this block:

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_prefix="PYDANTIC_TUTOR_",
        frozen=True,
        # Read here, into these fields only: a key in `.env` never enters
        # the process environment. A shell variable wins over `.env`.
        env_file=".env",
        # `OPENAI_API_KEY=` with nothing after it counts as unset.
        env_ignore_empty=True,
        # `.env` may hold variables for other tools; skip them.
        extra="ignore",
    )

Check: model_config remains inside Settings, and all five arguments are present. This changes where settings can come from, not their original defaults.

Important: don't delete, clear, or replace your real .env. It may hold credentials or settings you still need.

docs.title: Compare your finished Settings file
docs.text:
These were incremental changes to an existing file. Compare them with this optional finished-file reference. Do not paste it over your file; the small edits above are the exercise.

Show the finished src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py 
"""Every value the app is configured with, typed and checked at startup.

Values only: strings and flags read from the environment. The objects built
from them are in `composition.py`.
"""

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Read from variables named `PYDANTIC_TUTOR_<FIELD>`; frozen once created."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_prefix="PYDANTIC_TUTOR_",
        frozen=True,
        # Read here, into these fields only: a key in `.env` never enters
        # the process environment. A shell variable wins over `.env`.
        env_file=".env",
        # `OPENAI_API_KEY=` with nothing after it counts as unset.
        env_ignore_empty=True,
        # `.env` may hold variables for other tools; skip them.
        extra="ignore",
    )

    # A `<provider>:<model>` string, the name of the model: not the model.
    chat_model: str = CHAT_MODEL
    # Whether the chat may search the web. Each search is billed.
    web_search: bool = True
    # One key per provider the composition root can build. SecretStr:
    # printing the settings shows `**********`, never the key.
    openai_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="OPENAI_API_KEY"
    )
    anthropic_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
    )

docs.title: Verify that the key is read and masked
docs.text:
We'll test one field using a disposable file with a made-up key. This is deliberately separate from your real .env. From the project root, create it:

printf 'OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake-for-the-lesson\n' > lesson-provider.env

Check: open lesson-provider.env; it should contain exactly the single line above. Don't put a real key in it.

Now read it through Settings. The _env_file argument overrides the usual .env for this instance only. env -u OPENAI_API_KEY temporarily removes a shell-level OpenAI key for this command so it cannot override our placeholder:

env -u OPENAI_API_KEY uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings(_env_file='lesson-provider.env').openai_api_key)"

Tip

Check: it should print **********, not sk-fake-for-the-lesson. If it does not, stop here and inspect the field name, alias, and file path.

What it means: Pydantic Settings read a key from the practice file and SecretStr masked it when printed. This check does not authenticate a key, nor does masking prevent code from retrieving the real string with get_secret_value(). We'll pass that string to a provider in Step 2.

docs.title: Step 2: Give provider construction one home
docs.text:
We can read keys, but build_app still doesn't pass them to providers. We'll add a new file, src/pydantic_tutor/providers.py, for that responsibility.

A factory function is simply a function whose job is to create and return an object. Our build_provider factory will receive a provider name and the current Settings, and return the matching provider with its key.

Before writing the factory, there are two small pieces to recognize:

  • require_key will check for a missing key before we try to create a provider. If a key exists, it will retrieve its actual string value.
  • ProviderFactory will describe the shape of a function Pydantic AI can call: given a provider name, return a provider. This is a Python type alias, not a registration system. Provider[Any] accommodates the differing client types wrapped by OpenAI and Anthropic providers; it doesn't authorize every possible provider.

Because providers.py is new, we can show the full file. The two decisions to follow are whether the chosen key is present and which provider should receive it. The match statement selects one case according to the provider name.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/providers.py:

"""Build only the model providers this chat supports."""

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UserError
from pydantic_ai.providers import Provider
from pydantic_ai.providers.anthropic import AnthropicProvider
from pydantic_ai.providers.openai import OpenAIProvider

from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings

# The function shape expected by infer_model's provider_factory argument.
ProviderFactory = Callable[[str], Provider[Any]]


def require_key(*, key: SecretStr | None, variable: str) -> str:
    """Return a configured key or name the missing setting."""
    if key is None:
        raise UserError(f"Set {variable}, in .env or your shell, to use this model.")
    return key.get_secret_value()


def build_provider(*, name: str, settings: Settings) -> Provider[Any]:
    """Choose a supported provider and give it its configured key."""
    match name:
        case "openai" | "openai-chat" | "openai-responses":
            return OpenAIProvider(
                api_key=require_key(
                    key=settings.openai_api_key, variable="OPENAI_API_KEY"
                )
            )
        case "anthropic":
            return AnthropicProvider(
                api_key=require_key(
                    key=settings.anthropic_api_key, variable="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
                )
            )
        case _:
            raise UserError(
                f"Unknown provider {name!r} in {settings.chat_model!r}: "
                "pydantic-tutor builds openai and anthropic models only."
            )

Follow the OpenAI case. The match statement chooses a branch by name; three OpenAI-related names use the same OpenAI provider. require_key checks our setting and returns the underlying string; OpenAIProvider(api_key=...) receives it explicitly. The Anthropic case does the same with the Anthropic field.

The final case refuses unsupported providers rather than quietly letting some other provider obtain a key on its own. This function defines our policy about what the application can build. It does not, by itself, decide who is authorized to use a credential.

Check the new file: OpenAI cases read settings.openai_api_key; the Anthropic case reads settings.anthropic_api_key. Both pass the result of require_key as api_key. The fallback case rejects unsupported names.

What changed? We've written the provider factory, but no application code calls it yet. That is the next edit.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect the provider factory to model construction
docs.text: Recall composition.py from 03-01: build_app assembles the chat's agent and model before the user sees a prompt. We will keep that function and change only how it gets a model.

docs.title: Import the model type and provider factory
docs.text:
We need the model's type annotation and our new provider-building function before we can use them.

In src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py, keep the existing imports, including from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model, and add the import from our new module below it:

from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model
from pydantic_tutor.providers import ProviderFactory, build_provider

Model describes the type the new function returns; it doesn't construct an object.

Check: infer_model is still imported, along with Model, and build_provider comes from your new module.

docs.title: Add build_model
docs.text:
A model name such as openai:gpt-4o-mini identifies both the provider and the model. infer_model already understands that name; its provider_factory option lets us decide how its provider is created.

The lambda below is a small unnamed function. When Pydantic AI asks it for a provider name, it forwards that name and the current Settings to build_provider. The optional provider_factory argument allows a different function to be supplied later; we won't use that option here.

At the end of composition.py, after build_app, add:

def build_model(
    *, settings: Settings, provider_factory: ProviderFactory | None = None
) -> Model:
    """Build the model `settings.chat_model` names, its provider holding its key.

    `infer_model` picks the model class from the string, and asks
    `provider_factory` for the provider, by the part before the colon. The
    default is `build_provider`; pass another function to replace it.
    """
    return infer_model(
        model=settings.chat_model,
        # `infer_model` calls this with one argument, the provider's name.
        provider_factory=provider_factory
        or (lambda name: build_provider(name=name, settings=settings)),
    )

Check: build_model is at the same indentation level as build_app and returns the result of infer_model. At this point you've defined it, but build_app hasn't yet called it.

docs.title: Use build_model in build_app
docs.text:
Find the existing return App( inside build_app. Leave its agent line untouched. Replace only the expression that constructs its model:

        model=build_model(settings=settings),

Check: build_app still constructs the agent in the same way; only its model= expression changed. The model is still built before the chat opens. No edit to chat/loop.py is needed.

docs.title: Check your finished composition.py
docs.text:
You've made several focused edits to an existing file. To check their placement, compare your result with this complete reference version. This is not another editing instruction: keep the edits you've just made rather than copying over your file.

Show the finished src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py 
"""The composition root: the one place the app's objects are built.

`build_app` turns `Settings` (values) into the agent and the model (objects).
The model is built here, at startup, so an unknown provider or a missing API key
stops the app before the chat opens, not when the first message is sent.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.providers import ProviderFactory, build_provider
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class App:
    """What the chat needs to run, built once from the settings."""

    agent: Agent[None, str]
    model: Model


def build_app(*, settings: Settings) -> App:
    """Build the agent and the model from `settings`.

    Raises `pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError` if the model name's provider is
    unknown or its API key is not set.
    """
    return App(
        agent=build_chat_agent(web_search=settings.web_search),
        model=build_model(settings=settings),
    )


def build_model(
    *, settings: Settings, provider_factory: ProviderFactory | None = None
) -> Model:
    """Build the model `settings.chat_model` names, its provider holding its key.

    `infer_model` picks the model class from the string, and asks
    `provider_factory` for the provider, by the part before the colon. The
    default is `build_provider`; pass another function to replace it.
    """
    return infer_model(
        model=settings.chat_model,
        # `infer_model` calls this with one argument, the provider's name.
        provider_factory=provider_factory
        or (lambda name: build_provider(name=name, settings=settings)),
    )

Check: you should have the two imports, the updated model= line in build_app, and the new build_model function after it. The App class and the agent line should be unchanged.

docs.title: Check the OpenAI handoff without contacting OpenAI
docs.text:
We can check construction with the placeholder in lesson-provider.env. This one command also chooses the OpenAI model explicitly, rather than relying on the current default. It compares the key in the created model's client with the key in Settings, but prints only the result of the comparison, never the key.

env -u OPENAI_API_KEY PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=openai:gpt-4o-mini uv run python -c "
from pydantic_tutor.composition import build_model
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
settings = Settings(_env_file='lesson-provider.env')
model = build_model(settings=settings)
print(type(model).__name__, model.model_name)
print(model.client.api_key == settings.openai_api_key.get_secret_value())
"

Tip

Check: expect:

OpenAIResponsesModel gpt-4o-mini
True

True tells us the provider's client received the same value that Settings read. It does not mean the made-up key is valid. We built an object; we didn't send a request.

docs.title: Step 4: Use the same function for Anthropic
docs.text:
The OpenAI check established that our placeholder reached the client's configuration; it did not authenticate. Now change only the provider choice and the disposable credential to see the same construction path select Anthropic.

The second goal is to select a different provider without rewriting our chat. This time a one-command environment variable supplies a disposable Anthropic key. The chat_model argument chooses the model, and _env_file=None skips the local file for this check.

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-placeholder uv run python -c "
from pydantic_tutor.composition import build_model
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
settings = Settings(_env_file=None, chat_model='anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5')
model = build_model(settings=settings)
print(type(model).__name__, model.model_name)
"

Tip

Check: the output should name an Anthropic model and claude-sonnet-5-5. No model request is made.

The same build_model function routed the model name to the Anthropic provider and passed it the Anthropic setting. The chat still receives a model from build_app; it doesn't need to know which company serves it.

There's a boundary worth keeping: at startup we can tell whether a key was supplied. Only the remote service can confirm whether a real key is valid when we make a request.

docs.title: Remove the practice file
docs.text:
When you've finished checking, remove only the disposable file we created:

rm lesson-provider.env

Check: the disposable lesson-provider.env is gone. Your actual .env and any real credentials remain untouched.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
You wanted to make the model's credentials an explicit part of application configuration. Settings now reads and masks provider keys; build_provider chooses the supported service and hands it the matching key.

You also wanted one chat that can use more than one provider. build_model now builds either OpenAI or Anthropic models, while build_app and the existing conversation loop keep their roles. The checks demonstrated local construction and handoff—not remote authentication. A real request with a real credential remains outside this lesson.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
In the next lesson, we'll give this same chat a workspace: a folder its tools can read from and write to.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. We now have one place to choose the model, hand it its key, and build the chat before it opens. Next we'll give that chat somewhere to work.

Imagine asking it to inspect a small Python project. Before it can read a file or run tests, we need to answer a mundane question: which project? A workspace is the place its tools will start from. In this lesson we'll choose a folder through Settings and attach it while building the application.

We're deliberately not adding file or shell tools yet. The chat will still only talk. That separation helps us see an important distinction: a workspace tells tools where to begin, but doesn't itself grant the model permission to do anything—or keep tools from reaching beyond that folder.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Attach a workspace to the chat: name its folder in Settings, build it at the composition root, and have the app refuse to start without the folder.
  2. Say what a local workspace does not give you: it gives the agent no tools, and it does not keep anything inside its folder.

About 15 minutes. No API key is needed.

docs.title: A folder for our existing chat
docs.text:
In 03-02, Settings chose a model and build_app built it before the conversation opened. Now suppose you ask the chat to inspect a Python project. Which project should it inspect?

A workspace gives the tools of an agent a starting place for file operations. We'll use a disposable working copy of a small project called tinyjobs. This lesson attaches the workspace but does not add file tools to the chat. That distinction matters: naming a folder doesn't give a model the ability to read it.

We'll also see why a local workspace is not a sandbox. It starts paths at a folder, but it does not automatically keep them inside that folder. We'll demonstrate this using only a supplied sample project, never your private files.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
pydantic-tutor/
├── sample_code/tinyjobs/       given: original sample project
├── demos/
│   ├── fresh_copy.py          given: creates disposable work/tinyjobs
│   └── workspace_reach.py     new: explore what paths a tool can read
├── work/tinyjobs/             generated: disposable copy, not committed
└── src/pydantic_tutor/
    ├── settings.py            edit: add workspace_root
    ├── chat/agent.py          edit: attach LocalWorkspace
    └── composition.py         edit: check the folder and pass the setting

We'll name and create the folder, attach it when the app starts, then observe what it does and does not allow. Stop at any check that doesn't match before moving on.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Continue in your existing pydantic-tutor directory from 03-02. From the project root, check that the keyless chat still works:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=test PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tip

Check: type hello. You should see success (no tool calls); then finish with an empty line. No API key or paid model request is needed.

Warning

Already have pydantic-tutor? Do not run these clone commands.

Only if you're entering directly at this lesson, or starting again without an existing project, run them from a parent directory where no pydantic-tutor folder already exists. Do not delete or replace your existing project: starting again would lose the work and settings you have already added.

git clone --branch 03-02-models/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

docs.title: Fetch the starter files for this lesson
docs.text:
The next steps use a sample Python project and some helpers that weren't in 03-02. We can add them to your existing project, without starting another clone.

From the root of pydantic-tutor (where pyproject.toml lives), run:

uv run https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student/main/starter/get_starter.py workspace

This fetches sample_code/tinyjobs/, demos/fresh_copy.py, demos/show_chat_request.py, demos/show_capabilities.py, and src/tutor_given/. The supplied tutor_given code and the two show_ scripts also support later lessons; you won't need to recreate them.

Tip

Check: the utility lists the files it installed as wrote, or same if an identical file was already there. It then reminds you about the configuration edits below. If a file already exists with different content, the utility stops without replacing it. Review such a conflict before taking any further action; don't use --force without understanding what would be overwritten.

docs.title: Keep the disposable copy out of git
docs.text:
Later we'll make work/tinyjobs/, a disposable copy where tools can work. It isn't project source and shouldn't be committed.

Open the existing .gitignore. Keep the other entries, especially .env, and add at the bottom:

/work/

Check: the existing .env rule is unchanged; the new rule excludes the work/ folder at the project root.

docs.title: Keep the example project out of our routine checks
docs.text:
The fetched sample has its own code and tests. We want Ruff, mypy and pytest to check our tutorial project without treating the sample and its disposable copy as part of our application.

Open pyproject.toml. First, before the existing [tool.ruff.lint] section, add this new section:

[tool.ruff]
extend-exclude = ["sample_code", "work"]

Check: [tool.ruff.lint] and its existing rules are still there. The new section is separate from them.

Inside [tool.mypy], replace only the existing exclude = ... line with these entries:

exclude = [
    "^tests/",
    "^sample_code/",
    "^work/",
]

Check: strict = true and the Pydantic mypy plugin remain intact.

Finally, after the [tool.mypy] section, add a section for pytest, the test runner:

[tool.pytest]
addopts = ["--ignore=sample_code", "--ignore=work"]

Check: none of the project dependencies or build settings were changed. These exclusions protect the example project from our routine checks; they do not remove the files.

docs.title: Package the given code with yours
docs.text:
src/tutor_given/ is a second package beside pydantic_tutor. Unless told otherwise, uv's build backend packages only the one named after the project, so a wheel built from it would leave tutor_given out. Your own runs still work without this, because uv sync installs the project in place, but the project should build the same way it runs.

In pyproject.toml, after the [build-system] section, add:

[tool.uv.build-backend]
module-name = ["pydantic_tutor", "tutor_given"]

Check: the section matches the one in the finished file below.

Use the complete result below to compare placement. Do not paste it over your own file; the edits above are the exercise.

Show the finished pyproject.toml (reference only) 
[project]
name = "pydantic-tutor"

]

]

]

[tool.ruff.lint]
