The starter files and these three small configuration updates are now in place. You can continue to Step 1 without changing projects.

docs.title: Step 1: Name and create the workspace folder
docs.text: In 03-01 you gave the model choice a home in Settings. We'll do the same for the folder. We want the app to know the project location before it opens.

docs.title: Add a path to Settings
docs.text:
Python's Path represents a filesystem path. Unlike a plain string, it also has convenient operations, such as is_dir() to check whether a folder exists. A relative path such as Path("work/tinyjobs") begins at the directory where we launch the application.

Open src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py. Add this import with the other imports near the top:

from pathlib import Path

Check: the import is outside class Settings, above the existing third-party imports.

The app's paths shouldn't depend on where a program is started, or a run from your IDE would look for them in the wrong folder. project_root(), a given function in the tutor_given you just fetched, finds the folder holding pyproject.toml. Import it after the pydantic_tutor.model import:

from tutor_given.paths import project_root

In model_config, change env_file to use it:

        env_file=project_root() / ".env",

Inside Settings, add the new field just below web_search and above the API-key fields:

    # The folder the chat works in. `demos/fresh_copy.py` makes the default.
    workspace_root: Path = project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"

Check: chat_model, web_search, and the provider-key fields still appear as before. The new field sets a default; a shell variable named PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WORKSPACE_ROOT can override it.

For comparison, here is the resulting file. Don't replace your file; use this only if you want to confirm the placement of the two edits.

Show the finished src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py (reference only) 
"""Every value the app is configured with, typed and checked at startup.

Values only: strings and flags read from the environment. The objects built
from them are in `composition.py`.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL
from tutor_given.paths import project_root


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Read from variables named `PYDANTIC_TUTOR_<FIELD>`; frozen once created."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_prefix="PYDANTIC_TUTOR_",
        frozen=True,
        # Read here, into these fields only: a key in `.env` never enters
        # the process environment. A shell variable wins over `.env`.
        env_file=project_root() / ".env",
        # `OPENAI_API_KEY=` with nothing after it counts as unset.
        env_ignore_empty=True,
        # `.env` may hold variables for other tools; skip them.
        extra="ignore",
    )

    # A `<provider>:<model>` string, the name of the model: not the model.
    chat_model: str = CHAT_MODEL
    # Whether the chat may search the web. Each search is billed.
    web_search: bool = True
    # The folder the chat works in. `demos/fresh_copy.py` makes the default.
    workspace_root: Path = project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
    # One key per provider the composition root can build. SecretStr:
    # printing the settings shows `**********`, never the key.
    openai_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="OPENAI_API_KEY"
    )
    anthropic_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
    )

docs.title: Create a disposable working copy
docs.text:
The default names work/tinyjobs, but naming a folder doesn't create it. The given helper copies the small project from sample_code/tinyjobs into that working directory. Running it again replaces the disposable copy. Keep your own work elsewhere.

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py

Tip

Check: the script reports:

work/tinyjobs: a fresh copy of sample_code/tinyjobs, with a fake .env

That fake .env belongs to the sample project, not your own project credentials. Leave your actual .env untouched.

docs.title: Read the configured location
docs.text:
Now ask Settings what it will use:

uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings; print(Settings().workspace_root)"

Tip

Check: it prints the full path of work/tinyjobs inside your project, ending in pydantic-tutor/work/tinyjobs.

We have chosen a location and made it exist. Nothing has yet connected it to the agent.

docs.title: Step 2: Attach the workspace to the existing agent
docs.text:
In 03-02, build_app assembled the model from settings before the chat opened. We want the same startup process to attach our workspace.

Pydantic AI calls this sort of agent feature a capability. You've already seen WebSearch in the chat's capabilities. LocalWorkspace is a different capability: it tells tools where to work on this machine. It does not itself give the model a file tool.

docs.title: Add LocalWorkspace to the agent builder
docs.text:
This adds a workspace_root parameter to build_chat_agent, and LocalWorkspace as the first capability. Replace src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py with:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability, LocalWorkspace, WebSearch

from tutor_given.paths import project_root


def build_chat_agent(*, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

working_dir is the folder relative paths will start from. The web_search block is unchanged: we added a capability and removed none, so the workspace is present whether or not web search is on.

The ready-made chat_agent at the bottom needs a default workspace too, because earlier scripts still import it. This doesn't create the folder; Step 1 already did that.

docs.title: Check the folder when the app starts
docs.text:
We could attach LocalWorkspace without checking the folder. But then the chat might open and only report a missing folder when a future tool tries to read it. Let's instead give the learner a useful startup error.

Open src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py. Add the UserError import beside the existing Pydantic AI imports:

from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UserError

Check: the existing Agent and model imports remain unchanged.

Within build_app, before return App(...), insert the folder check:

    if not settings.workspace_root.is_dir():
        raise UserError(
            f"PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WORKSPACE_ROOT is {str(settings.workspace_root)!r}, "
            "which is not a folder. Make the default with "
            "`uv run demos/fresh_copy.py`, or set the variable to another folder."
        )

The is_dir() method checks that a folder exists. UserError is an error the existing chat loop already catches at startup; we don't need to modify the loop.

Check: the new if block is indented inside build_app, before its return.

One more focused change in the same return App(...): add workspace_root to the call that builds the agent, leaving model construction as it was:

        agent=build_chat_agent(
            web_search=settings.web_search, workspace_root=settings.workspace_root
        ),

Check: model=build_model(settings=settings) still appears underneath. The chat loop remains untouched.

Here is the finished module for comparison only:

Show the finished src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py (reference only) 
"""The composition root: the one place the app's objects are built.

`build_app` turns `Settings` (values) into the agent and the model (objects).
The model is built here, at startup, so an unknown provider or a missing API key
stops the app before the chat opens, not when the first message is sent.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UserError
from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.providers import ProviderFactory, build_provider
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class App:
    """What the chat needs to run, built once from the settings."""

    agent: Agent[None, str]
    model: Model


def build_app(*, settings: Settings) -> App:
    """Build the agent and the model from `settings`.

    Raises `pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError` if the model name's provider is
    unknown or its API key is not set.
    """
    if not settings.workspace_root.is_dir():
        # Checked here so the chat stops now, by the setting's name, instead
        # of at the first tool that uses the workspace.
        raise UserError(
            f"PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WORKSPACE_ROOT is {str(settings.workspace_root)!r}, "
            "which is not a folder. Make the default with "
            "`uv run demos/fresh_copy.py`, or set the variable to another folder."
        )
    return App(
        agent=build_chat_agent(
            web_search=settings.web_search, workspace_root=settings.workspace_root
        ),
        model=build_model(settings=settings),
    )


def build_model(
    *, settings: Settings, provider_factory: ProviderFactory | None = None
) -> Model:
    """Build the model `settings.chat_model` names, its provider holding its key.

    `infer_model` picks the model class from the string, and asks
    `provider_factory` for the provider, by the part before the colon. The
    default is `build_provider`; pass another function to replace it.
    """
    return infer_model(
        model=settings.chat_model,
        # `infer_model` calls this with one argument, the provider's name.
        provider_factory=provider_factory
        or (lambda name: build_provider(name=name, settings=settings)),
    )

docs.title: Confirm the chat still works
docs.text:
With the sample folder in place, run the same keyless chat command from Before you start:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=test PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Tip

Check: you can still send hello and see success (no tool calls). End with an empty line.

The agent now has a local workspace, but the conversation behaves just as before. We haven't given the model anything new to call.

The folder check also means a missing folder will stop the app before the first you> prompt, with a message naming PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WORKSPACE_ROOT. We don't need to break a working setup to demonstrate that in this lesson.

docs.title: Step 3: Observe what the workspace allows
docs.text:
We've attached a workspace without adding tools to our chat. There are two separate questions now: does the model have a file-reading tool? And if a tool is provided, does the workspace constrain its paths?

A tool that reads through the workspace uses ctx.workspace, the workspace available during a run. Its read_text method is asynchronous: the tool uses async def and await while it waits for a read. You'll see those details in this demonstration; the next lessons will work with file tools directly.

The demo uses TestModel to count the tools offered to the existing agent, then a given stand-in model to request a temporary file-reading tool. FunctionToolset supplies that tool for these runs, without permanently adding it to the chat. The path is chosen by the stand-in model, not by the workspace itself.

We're going to read just the first lines of known, non-secret files: one within the disposable copy and one in our tutorial project. No real credential files are involved.

Create the new file demos/workspace_reach.py:

"""Show what the chat's workspace is, and what it is not.

Needs no API key. Run `demos/fresh_copy.py`
first.
"""

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel
from pydantic_ai.toolsets import FunctionToolset

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.stand_ins import calls_tool_with_the_prompt

root = Settings().workspace_root
agent = build_chat_agent(web_search=False, workspace_root=root)

# Offer the tools without calling them: this run only counts them.
test_model = TestModel(call_tools=[])
agent.run_sync(user_prompt="hello", model=test_model)
parameters = test_model.last_model_request_parameters
assert parameters is not None  # the run made a request
print(f"tools the model is offered: {len(parameters.function_tools)}")


async def first_line(ctx: RunContext[None], *, path: str) -> str:
    """Read the first line of a file, by a path the model gives."""
    text = await ctx.workspace.read_text(path=path)
    return text.splitlines()[0]


# The folder is `work/tinyjobs`: `..` is `work/`, and `../..` is the project.
outside = "../../pyproject.toml"
paths = {
    "README.md": "README.md",
    outside: outside,
    "absolute path": str((root / outside).resolve()),
}
for label, path in paths.items():
    result = agent.run_sync(
        user_prompt=path,
        model=calls_tool_with_the_prompt(tool_name="first_line", argument="path"),
        # A tool for this run only: the chat has none of its own yet.
        toolsets=[FunctionToolset(tools=[first_line])],
    )
    print(f"{label}: {result.output}")

The path ../../pyproject.toml starts from work/tinyjobs, moves up twice, and reaches the tutorial's own project file. The absolute path points at that same file without using the workspace root as a starting point.

Run the demo:

uv run demos/workspace_reach.py

Tip

Check: the important four lines are:

tools the model is offered: 0
README.md: # tinyjobs
../../pyproject.toml: [project]
absolute path: [project]

If the disposable working copy is missing, rerun uv run demos/fresh_copy.py, then try again.

What happened? The configured chat offered the model zero function tools; its workspace alone adds none. In the demonstration runs, we temporarily supplied first_line. That tool could read a relative file inside the workspace, then ../../pyproject.toml outside it, and finally the same file by an absolute path.

That's the key limitation: a local workspace is a starting directory, not a permission boundary. A tool must validate paths and permissions independently. LocalWorkspace works with the permissions of your process on this machine; it isn't a sandbox. Never try the same experiment with a real .env file, because the demo prints what it reads.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
You can configure a workspace for the same chat: Settings names the folder, build_app checks it, and build_chat_agent attaches a LocalWorkspace before the conversation starts. The chat still streams and remembers messages, and no file tool has been added to it.

You can also explain what the workspace does not guarantee: tools can resolve paths outside its starting folder unless the tools enforce a boundary. This distinction matters in the next lesson, where we finally give the chat file tools.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The chat has a place to work. Next we'll give it file tools that can use the workspace—and must decide which paths they will accept.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Let the chat read your project
Welcome
docs.text:
Welcome back. Last lesson you gave our chat a workspace: a disposable copy of the small tinyjobs Python project. The agent knows where to work, but it still has no way to look at a file there.

In this lesson, you'll add Pydantic AI's FileSystem capability to the chat you've been building. We'll start the chat with a real model, and ask it to read tinyjobs files. We'll explore the project directories and ask the agent to read and explain a source file.

The goal is simple: turn our chat into an assistant that can answer questions about the project in front of it, rather than relying only on what the model already knows.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  1. Add file access to the existing chat agent.
  2. Explain what happens when the model requests a file tool and uses its result to answer you.

This lesson uses a real model and a valid API key, as in Chapter 2. It makes provider requests, which may incur charges. Follow the checks below in your own project; exact model replies may differ.

docs.title: A tool the model can actually use
docs.text:
Remember the distinction from Chapter 1: the model can request a tool, but it does not execute Python functions or open files itself. Our agent application receives that request, runs the tool, and passes the result back to the model. The model can then use the result to answer the student.

Previously, you wrote your own tools. FileSystem, from pydantic-ai-harness, supplies ready-made tools for reading, listing, finding and searching files. We attach it as a capability alongside LocalWorkspace. The workspace says where files live; FileSystem makes file operations available to the model.

FileSystem also offers tools that change files. This lesson only asks the model to read, and nothing yet asks you before it writes: a later chapter adds that. We'll also refuse access to common secret-file names, because a file tool that only reads is still not private.

docs.title: A useful boundary, not a sandbox
docs.text:
The file tools default to the workspace's working directory as their root. In our app that's work/tinyjobs. They check paths, including resolved links, and refuse attempts to read outside that root.

That's useful, but it is not the same as isolating an agent from your computer. LocalWorkspace runs with your account's access, and other capabilities—especially a shell—can have different rules. We'll explore that distinction later. For this lesson, work only with the disposable tinyjobs copy, only ask it to read, and do not ask the agent to inspect personal or sensitive files.

docs.title: What you'll change
docs.text:
Just one existing file:

src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py    add FileSystem to our chat

Then we'll run the existing chat, not a new demonstration agent. The plan is: add the capability, explore the workspace, and read real source files with the agent.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Continue in the pydantic-tutor project you've been building through Chapter 3. From its root (the folder containing pyproject.toml), make sure your dependencies are in place:

uv sync

You already have the workspace setup from 03-03, and this lesson needs no new starter files. Refresh the disposable tinyjobs copy:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py

Tip

Check: the command reports a fresh copy under work/tinyjobs. It includes a fake .env file used in earlier demonstrations. We'll exclude secret-like files from the new tools.

You'll also need the real API key you configured in Chapter 3, in the project's own .env or your shell, and a real model selected through PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL. Do not use the test model for this lesson: we want an actual model choosing file operations.

Warning

Already have pydantic-tutor? Do not run these clone commands.

Only if you're joining at this lesson or recovering without an existing project, run these commands from a parent directory where no folder named pydantic-tutor exists. Keep using your current project if you have one; do not delete, refresh, or replace it: doing so would lose the work and settings you have already added.

git clone --branch 03-03-workspace/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

This is a recovery option, not a step to repeat between lessons.

docs.title: Step 1: Give the chat file tools
docs.text:
Goal: attach ready-made file operations to our existing chat agent.

This adds FileSystem to the agent, and the names of the files its tools must not touch. Replace src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py with:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability, LocalWorkspace, WebSearch
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem

from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")


def build_chat_agent(*, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

FileSystem comes right after LocalWorkspace, which still supplies the folder. It makes the file tools available, the tools that change files included. The deny patterns add a separate restriction: they keep common secret files unreadable through these tools. They are a precaution, not a complete data-security policy.

Notice that we did not change chat/loop.py or the code that builds the model. The same chat now has an additional ability.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the project with your agent
docs.text:
Goal: see a real model use file tools to answer questions about the project, beginning with simple exploration.

Run the chat using your configured real model. Turn off web search so the answers come from the working copy:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

You now have a chat that can do something new: look around a real Python project. Start with simple questions, just as you might when getting to know a new teammate. Ask what the agent can do, then invite it to show you what's in the workspace.

The conversation below is taken from an actual session with the file-reading agent. Notice how the questions become more specific: first the available tools, then the project directory, and finally the src/ folder. Nothing about those files was included in the user's messages.

An actual conversation with the file-reading agent, recorded with its write tools turned off: yours has eight tools, not five. Your model's replies may differ; here, the agent lists the project and source files without the user supplying their contents.

That last directory listing is the important moment. The model didn't need a copy of the project in its prompt: it asked your application to list the directory and then explained the result. The answer is modest, but it's grounded in something the agent actually observed.

The small token counts beneath the replies are not the point of this exercise. Focus on what changed: the agent can now look inside the workspace and answer from what it finds.

Next, ask it to examine code instead of merely listing names:

Read src/tinyjobs/jobs.py. What does the JobQueue class do?
Explain the submit() and cancel() methods.

In our trial, asking it to read this file exposed the JobQueue class and its methods. The source shows that submit() creates a named job and adds it to the queue; cancel() changes the status of a job to CANCELLED (but refuses a running job). Ask the agent to show the methods if you want to compare its explanation with the code.

Tip

Check: your agent should be able to read src/tinyjobs/jobs.py and explain the methods using details from the file. If it says it cannot see the file, check your FileSystem setup and that work/tinyjobs exists. Exact model replies will vary.

There are other things you can try without needing to know anything about the file tools' arguments:

  • Read README.md. What is tinyjobs for?
  • List the files in src/tinyjobs. Which file looks most relevant to storing jobs?
  • Read src/tinyjobs/storage.py. What does this module do?
  • Read src/tinyjobs/jobs.py. What happens if run_next() encounters an error?

These are suggested explorations, not a set of scripted results. Feel free to follow your curiosity. We aren't relying on directory-wide text search in this first exercise: in our initial tests, searches sometimes missed code that a direct file read found.

What happened?

You asked about project-specific information without including any source files in your question. The model requested tools, your application executed them in the workspace, and the model used the returned information to answer. That's the tool loop from Chapter 1, now doing useful work in the chat you've built.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text: You added FileSystem to the chat you already had. With a real model, you can ask questions about files in the workspace and watch it use file tools to inspect them. Its root and deny rules restrict what its tools can reach. Neither turns LocalWorkspace into a sandbox, and nothing asks before a file tool writes: that comes in a later chapter.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Our chat can now inspect a project. In the next lesson we'll let it run a few simple commands through a shell. That is a bigger step: even commands that look harmless have different risks from reading files, so we'll be deliberate about what we allow.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Let the chat run a command
Welcome
docs.text:
Last lesson you gave our chat a way to look inside the tinyjobs project. It could list directories and read code, but it couldn't run the project's tests.

Now we'll give the same agent a shell. You'll add one capability to the chat, ask a real model to run pytest, and see it report what happened. We'll also try a command the shell isn't allowed to run, then discover why the agent can sometimes accomplish the same task using its existing file tools.

By the end, you'll have a chat that can both inspect code and run selected commands. More importantly, you'll know which part of your application actually executes those commands.

This lesson uses the real model and API key you configured earlier. Provider requests may incur charges. Model replies may differ from the recorded example.

docs.title: The shell is another capability
docs.text:
In 03-04, LocalWorkspace identified the folder and FileSystem gave the model ways to read files there. Shell, from pydantic-ai-harness, adds tools for running commands.

The distinction from Chapter 1 still holds. The model requests a command. The application executes it through the shell capability and returns the output. The model then interprets that output for you. The model is not itself a Python process running pytest.

We can supply allowed_commands to limit which commands the shell will start. For now we'll use pytest, pwd, ls, and cat.

docs.title: Two capabilities, two sets of rules
docs.text:
The shell's allowed-command list applies to shell commands, not to FileSystem operations. An agent may be unable to run the shell command grep but still search text through FileSystem's search tool.

Neither an allowlist nor the workspace folder creates a sandbox. Shell commands execute locally with your account's permissions; even an allowed program such as pytest can execute arbitrary project code. Use only this disposable sample project, and don't let the agent run commands against personal or sensitive files.

Warning

This chat can read your API key. The list checks only a command's first word, so ls && cat ../../.env runs. FileSystem's secret patterns don't apply to the shell, so cat can read your project's .env, and whatever a tool reads is sent to the model's provider. For this tutorial, on your own computer, that's an accepted risk. Don't use this setup as it stands anywhere that matters.

docs.title: What you'll change
docs.text:
Just the agent file you edited in 03-04:

src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py    add Shell alongside FileSystem

Then you'll run the existing chat. No new demo program or stand-in model is needed.

docs.text:
Continue in your existing pydantic-tutor project. From the project root, refresh the dependencies and disposable workspace:

uv sync
uv run demos/fresh_copy.py

Tip

Check: work/tinyjobs exists and your agent still has the FileSystem capability from 03-04. Keep your real API key and model configuration from the previous lessons.

Warning

Only if you're joining at this lesson or recovering without an existing project, run these commands from a parent directory where no folder named pydantic-tutor exists. Do not delete or overwrite your existing project: starting fresh would lose the work and settings you have added.

cd pydantic-tutor

docs.title: Step 1: Give the chat a shell
docs.text:
Goal: let the existing agent run a small selection of commands.

This adds Shell to the agent, and the commands it may start. Replace src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py with:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Shell tools: run a few commands there.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability, LocalWorkspace, WebSearch
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem, Shell

from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")

# The commands the shell may start. A precaution, not a boundary: it checks
# only a command's first word, so `ls && cat .env` still runs.
SHELL_COMMANDS = ("pytest", "pwd", "ls", "cat")


def build_chat_agent(*, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
        # Shell tools: run the allowed commands in that workspace.
        Shell(allowed_commands=SHELL_COMMANDS),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

Notice that we haven't replaced FileSystem. The agent now has both sets of tools available. We also haven't changed the chat loop or model-building code.

docs.title: Step 2: Run the project's tests
docs.text:
Goal: watch the agent execute a command and explain its result.

Run the same chat as before, with web search turned off:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Ask:

Can you run pytest?

Here is a real conversation from the tinyjobs project:

An actual agent session. The commands and responses shown are examples; your model's wording and token usage may vary.

In this session, pytest collected 151 tests: 150 passed and one failed. The agent reported the failing test_cancel test and described its assertion. A failing test is still a successful demonstration of the shell: the command ran, and the model interpreted its output. We aren't fixing that test in this lesson.

Tip

Check: your agent should be able to run pytest and tell you what happened. The exact test count and failure details can change as the sample project evolves. If it cannot run tests, check the Shell capability, its allowed commands, and that you're in the refreshed tinyjobs workspace.

You can experiment further:

  • Use the shell to run pwd. Where are you working?
  • Use the shell to run ls. What files are here?
  • Use the shell to run pytest and summarize the failing test.

Each request is useful on its own. You don't need to reproduce the transcript word for word.

docs.title: A boundary worth noticing
docs.text:
Now ask:

Can you run the shell command grep tinyjobs README.md?

Because grep isn't in our shell's allowed-command list, the agent should be unable to execute that shell command. But try a different request:

Can you find occurrences of "tinyjobs" in README.md using your file tools?

The agent may still succeed: FileSystem offers a separate way to search files. The shell hasn't secretly acquired permission to run grep; the model has another tool available for the task.

Tip

Check: the explicit shell command grep should be refused, while file searching may still work. If the model reports something surprising, remember that its explanation is not a tool log. We would inspect the actual tool calls to verify exactly what ran.

What happened?

Your agent now has two capabilities with different responsibilities. FileSystem lets the model request information about files. Shell lets it request execution of allowed commands. Your application, not the model, carries out both operations.

The shell's list helps avoid accidental commands, but it doesn't protect your computer from everything an allowed command can do. We'll return to stronger controls when we introduce human approval and isolation later in the tutorial.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text: You extended the same chat you started in Chapter 2: it can inspect project files, run selected commands, and explain real test results. You also saw why a restriction on one capability is not necessarily a restriction on the entire agent.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
We now have a chat that can read a project and run its tests. In Chapter 4, we'll build our own tools for the agent, giving it access to information and actions specific to our application.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Capabilities
docs.text:
In Chapter 3, you gave the chat a place to work: settings, a workspace, file tools and a shell. It can read a project and run its tests. Along the way, you've added entries to capabilities=[...]. This chapter explains what those entries do.

By the end, you'll know what a toolset and a hook contribute to the chat, and you'll have watched a run from the inside.

We'll start by giving the chat a toolset of its own. Then we'll look inside a run: a run is a loop, and you can attach code to named hooks in it. That code only watches, and your chat keeps a record of what it did on your machine.

That's as far as the chapter goes for now. Hooks that change a run, and capabilities of your own, may follow in later lessons.

You'll keep working on the same chat application, and each lesson gives you a way to see what changed. A few lessons are mostly new ideas, and one is mostly connecting work. Each says which it is at the start.

Start with 04-01: Toolsets.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson is about toolsets: groups of tools that carry their own instructions and time limits. Our chat can already inspect files and run selected commands. We'll take two tools supplied with the workspace starter, package them in a FunctionToolset, and attach it to the chat. Then we'll see how another agent can use different views of that toolset and ask the chat about the tinyjobs project.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Build a toolset for useful questions about the tinyjobs project.
  • Attach it to the chat, distinguishing the tools it exposes from the instructions it supplies.
  • Give an agent a prefixed or filtered view of a toolset, without changing the original.

About 15 minutes. Steps 1–3 need no API key; Step 4 uses a configured real model.

docs.title: A toolset keeps tool settings together
docs.text:
An agent can take a list of functions as tools, and that list can be reused. A toolset groups tools into one object that also carries instructions for the model and a per-tool-call time limit. Those settings travel with the tools rather than being configured separately for each agent.

We've used FileSystem and Shell, which already provide collections of tools. Now we'll assemble a FunctionToolset from two functions of our own. The chat will use their names, docstrings, and parameters to offer them to the model.

docs.title: Agents can use different toolset views
docs.text: An agent can use the complete toolset or take a view of it: prefixed renames its tools, and filtered hides some of them. This lets one agent see only the tools it should have, and the original toolset doesn't change.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
• src/pydantic_tutor/tools/workspace_toolset.py, new: the FunctionToolset that packages the two supplied tools
  • src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, changed: the chat takes the toolset
  • demos/toolset_views.py, new: shows two views of the toolset

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Keep working in your existing pydantic-tutor project. The workspace starter you fetched in 03-03 already supplied src/tutor_given/module_tools.py; you do not need to create or fetch the two tools again.

Tip

Check: from your project directory, run uv run demos/fresh_copy.py and then uv run demos/workspace_reach.py. Before adding your toolset, the output starts with tools the model is offered: 12.

You can also check that src/tutor_given/module_tools.py exists.

Warning

Starting at this lesson instead of continuing? Only use this recovery route if you do not already have a pydantic-tutor directory. Starting over in a fresh project will not carry over work, settings, or credentials from your existing project. Do not delete or overwrite that project to follow these commands.

From a parent directory with no pydantic-tutor folder:

git clone --branch 03-05-shell/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

If you take this route, make sure you also obtain the workspace starter files as described in lesson 03-03 before continuing.

docs.title: Step 1: Build a toolset
docs.text: Goal: create a FunctionToolset that offers two read-only tools, together with instructions and a ten-second tool-call limit.

docs.title: Look at the two workspace tools
docs.text:
Our chat will use list_modules() to discover modules in tinyjobs and read_docstring(module=...) to read a module's description without executing its code.

These tools are supplied code, not what we're learning to implement. You already have them: ModuleTools came with the starter files you fetched for the workspace lesson. You need to know what each tool takes and returns, not how the file discovery or AST parsing works.

ModuleTools(root=...) gives both tools the workspace path when the application starts. The model doesn't choose or receive that path.

Here are their signatures and docstrings, from src/tutor_given/module_tools.py. There's nothing to type here:

class ModuleTools:
    root: Path

    def list_modules(self) -> list[str]:
        """List the Python modules in the workspace, by dotted name."""

    def read_docstring(self, *, module: str) -> str:
        """Read a module's docstring, without running the module.

        Args:
            module: The module's dotted name, as `list_modules` gives it.
        """

docs.title: Create the FunctionToolset
docs.text:
Now create src/pydantic_tutor/tools/workspace_toolset.py. This is the file you write: it imports the supplied tools, then groups them into a FunctionToolset.

The tools= list selects what the model can call. The instructions= text tells the model which workspace it is inspecting, and timeout= sets a ten-second limit on each tool call. Unlike an ordinary list of functions, the toolset carries those settings along with its tools.

"""The workspace's tools, with their instructions and time limit, as one toolset.

Built once, where the app is built, with the
folder the tools read: they take no deps.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai.toolsets import FunctionToolset

from tutor_given.module_tools import ModuleTools


def build_workspace_toolset(*, root: Path) -> FunctionToolset[None]:
    """The tools that read the modules under `root/src`, with their instructions."""
    tools = ModuleTools(root=root)
    return FunctionToolset(
        tools=[tools.list_modules, tools.read_docstring],
        # Sent with every request, beside the agent's own instructions.
        instructions=f"Your workspace holds the Python project {root.resolve().name}.",
        # Set here: an agent's `tool_timeout` covers only its own `tools=`.
        timeout=10,
    )

Tip

Check: inspect the new toolset:

uv run python -c "from pathlib import Path; from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset as build; t = build(root=Path('work/tinyjobs')); print(list(t.tools), t.timeout)"

['list_modules', 'read_docstring'] 10

What it means

The toolset offers two tools and gives each call a ten-second limit. We have not run either tool yet.

docs.title: Step 2: Attach it to the chat
docs.text:
Goal: the chat is offered your two tools.

Open src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py. This adds Toolset to the agent's capabilities, built for the same folder as the others. Replace the file with:

"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Shell tools: run a few commands there.
- Toolset: the workspace's own tools.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import (
    AbstractCapability,
    LocalWorkspace,
    Toolset,
    WebSearch,
)
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem, Shell

from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset
from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")

# The commands the shell may start. A precaution, not a boundary: it checks
# only a command's first word, so `ls && cat .env` still runs.
SHELL_COMMANDS = ("pytest", "pwd", "ls", "cat")


def build_chat_agent(*, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
        # Shell tools: run the allowed commands in that workspace.
        Shell(allowed_commands=SHELL_COMMANDS),
        # Toolset: the workspace's own tools, built for this folder.
        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

This uses the same workspace root as the existing file and shell tools; it doesn't replace either capability.

Run workspace_reach.py again:

uv run demos/workspace_reach.py

Tip

Check: the first line is now tools the model is offered: 14. The other three are as before.

What it means

The model now sees fourteen tools, including the two you added. On the keyless test model (PYDANTIC_TUTOR_CHAT_MODEL=test) the chat still ends on its first message, as it has since the file tools: that model calls every tool it is offered, yours now included. demos/fresh_copy.py resets the copy.

docs.title: Step 3: Try two toolset views
docs.text:
Goal: see the same toolset offered under new names, then with one tool hidden.

We'll use a separate demonstration agent so we don't change our chat. A stand-in model will report the tool definitions and instructions it receives; it won't answer a question or call the tools. This lets us compare the two views without an API key.

prefixed(prefix="workspace") adds a prefix to both tool names; filtered(filter_func=only_listing) exposes only list_modules. The original toolset stays unchanged.

Create demos/toolset_views.py:

"""Show a second agent two views of the workspace toolset.

Needs no API key; run `demos/fresh_copy.py`
first.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext
from pydantic_ai.tools import ToolDefinition
from pydantic_ai.toolsets import AbstractToolset

from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset
from tutor_given.stand_ins import reports_what_it_is_sent

toolset = build_workspace_toolset(root=Settings().workspace_root)


def only_listing(ctx: RunContext[None], tool: ToolDefinition) -> bool:
    """Keep `list_modules`; hide every other tool."""
    return tool.name == "list_modules"


views: dict[str, AbstractToolset[None]] = {
    "prefixed": toolset.prefixed(prefix="workspace"),
    "filtered": toolset.filtered(filter_func=only_listing),
}
for title, view in views.items():
    print(title)
    reader = Agent[None, str](name="reader", toolsets=[view])
    reader.run_sync(user_prompt="hi", model=reports_what_it_is_sent())

Run it:

uv run demos/toolset_views.py

Tip

Check: ignoring any startup banner, you should see:

prefixed
tools: workspace_list_modules, workspace_read_docstring
instructions: 'Your workspace holds the Python project tinyjobs.'
filtered
tools: list_modules
instructions: 'Your workspace holds the Python project tinyjobs.'

What it means

Both agents received the toolset's instructions, but each saw different tools. Both views came from one toolset, which still has its two tools.

docs.title: Step 4: Ask about tinyjobs
docs.text:
Goal: see your continuing chat use the toolset to answer a question about the project it can inspect.

The previous checks confirmed that the tools were offered to the model. Now we'll give them a useful job. With a real model configured, run the same console chat as in the previous lesson, with web search disabled:

PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WEB_SEARCH=false uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Ask:

Where does tinyjobs record a job's status? Please inspect the project's modules.

Tip

Check: look for an answer grounded in the tinyjobs project, rather than a general guess about job queues. The model can use list_modules and read_docstring to discover relevant modules. It also has the earlier file tools, so its exact choice of tools and wording may vary.

Here's an example of a real conversation with the workspace toolset:

An actual agent session; your model's tool choices and wording may vary.

What it means

You've moved beyond checking a list of available tools: the chat now has project-specific information it can consult while answering. If you haven't configured a real model yet, the keyless checks in Steps 1–3 still confirm that the toolset is wired into the application.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text: You took two tools already supplied with the workspace, packaged them with instructions and a time limit, and made them available to the chat. You also saw how a second agent can see renamed or filtered tools without changing the original toolset. In Step 4, you can use that same chat to ask a project-specific question and see how the available tools help it answer.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson is about hooks: functions the agent calls at named points during a run. We'll use three hooks to build an activity log: it records each model request, each tool the agent is about to execute, and each tool call that finished, so we can read the loop from the log itself. We'll try everything in a separate demo; the next lesson connects the log to our regular chat.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Say where a hook runs in the agent's loop, and what it's given.
  • Write hooks that watch a run without changing it.

About 15 minutes. No API key is needed.

docs.title: Hooks run at named points in a run
docs.text:
One user question may require several exchanges with the model. The model can request a tool instead of giving a final answer; the agent executes that tool and sends its result back. This continues until the model answers.

The diagram marks three places where we'll observe that cycle:

flowchart TD
    A["The agent prepares a request"] -->|before_model_request| B["The model responds"]
    B --> C{"Did it ask for tools?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D["The agent runs each tool"]
    D -->|"before_tool_execute, after_tool_execute"| A
    C -->|"no"| E["The run ends"]

Pydantic AI runs the loop and calls our hooks at the points we choose.

You'll see names such as before_model_request and after_tool_execute. The names identify the hook; the arguments tell our function what happened there. Other hooks can wrap operations or handle errors, but we don't need those to build this log.

docs.title: Hooks can observe or change a run
docs.text:
Each hook receives ctx, a RunContext describing the current run. You met this object when we used dependencies. Here, ctx.run_step tells us which model-request step we're observing.

The remaining arguments depend on the hook. A tool hook receives the tool call and its validated arguments. A model-request hook receives a ModelRequestContext: the messages and tool definitions about to go to the model.

A hook's return value can change how the run continues. This before_tool_execute hook captures the model's request parameters and changes them literally changing how the tool will be called:

docs.title: example:
docs.text:
In this case the model asks for a file named a, but the hook below changes it to changed_by_hook.txt:

async def before_tool_execute(        
    ctx: RunContext[None],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {**args, "path": "changed_by_hook.txt"}

In the log we'll see that even though the model asked for a the before_tool_execute changes that to changed_by_hook.txt and the tool writes that file:

the model asked for: {'path': 'a', 'content': 'a'}
the model got back: Wrote 1 chars (1 lines) to changed_by_hook.txt. [hash:ca978112ca1b]

docs.title: Step 1: Write the activity log
docs.text:
Goal: write three hooks, and a function that hands them to an agent as one capability.

Each hook records one of the named points in the loop. Together they cover a whole cycle: the request the agent is about to send, the tools it's about to execute, and the tool calls that finished.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/activity_log.py. This is the whole log: the next lesson connects it to the chat without changing it.

It is the longest block of the lesson, but it does one thing: build_activity_hooks makes three hooks — before_model_request, before_tool_execute and after_tool_execute — and each hook writes one Entry, a line of the log.

"""Record what the agent does during a run, one JSON line per hook call.

Milestones:
1. HookName: names a hook the log can record.
2. Entry: one line of the log.
3. Hooks: one per name; each writes an entry and returns what it received.
4. Registration: only the chosen names get a hook.

The hooks return their input unchanged, so the log watches and changes nothing.
"""

from enum import StrEnum
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import ModelRequestContext, RunContext
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Hooks
from pydantic_ai.messages import ToolCallPart
from pydantic_ai.tools import ToolDefinition

# The only arguments copied into the log. Named one by one, so a file's
# contents passed to `write_file` never reach it.
LOGGED_ARGUMENTS = ("path", "command")


# 1. HookName
class HookName(StrEnum):
    """The hooks this log can record, named as in `Hooks(...)`."""

    BEFORE_MODEL_REQUEST = "before_model_request"
    BEFORE_TOOL_EXECUTE = "before_tool_execute"
    AFTER_TOOL_EXECUTE = "after_tool_execute"


# 2. Entry
class Entry(BaseModel):
    """One line of the log: names and counts, never contents.

    Fields left as `None` aren't written.
    """

    hook: HookName
    step: int
    tool: str | None = None
    target: str | None = None
    messages: int | None = None
    tools: int | None = None
    result_chars: int | None = None


def build_activity_hooks(
    *, path: Path, hooks: frozenset[HookName] = frozenset(HookName)
) -> Hooks[None]:
    """A capability that logs the chosen hooks to the file at `path`."""

    def write(*, entry: Entry) -> None:
        with path.open(mode="a") as log:
            log.write(entry.model_dump_json(exclude_none=True) + "\n")

    # 3. Hooks
    # `async`, with no `await` inside: when the model asks for several tools
    # at once, these hooks can't write over each other.
    async def before_model_request(
        ctx: RunContext[None], request_context: ModelRequestContext
    ) -> ModelRequestContext:
        write(
            entry=Entry(
                hook=HookName.BEFORE_MODEL_REQUEST,
                step=ctx.run_step,
                messages=len(request_context.messages),
                tools=len(request_context.model_request_parameters.function_tools),
            )
        )
        return request_context

    async def before_tool_execute(
        ctx: RunContext[None],
        *,
        call: ToolCallPart,
        tool_def: ToolDefinition,
        args: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        targets = [str(args[name]) for name in LOGGED_ARGUMENTS if name in args]
        write(
            entry=Entry(
                hook=HookName.BEFORE_TOOL_EXECUTE,
                step=ctx.run_step,
                tool=call.tool_name,
                target=targets[0] if targets else None,
            )
        )
        return args

    async def after_tool_execute(
        ctx: RunContext[None],
        *,
        call: ToolCallPart,
        tool_def: ToolDefinition,
        args: dict[str, Any],
        result: object,
    ) -> object:
        write(
            entry=Entry(
                hook=HookName.AFTER_TOOL_EXECUTE,
                step=ctx.run_step,
                tool=call.tool_name,
                result_chars=len(str(result)),
            )
        )
        return result

    # 4. Registration
    return Hooks[None](
        before_model_request=(
            before_model_request if HookName.BEFORE_MODEL_REQUEST in hooks else None
        ),
        before_tool_execute=(
            before_tool_execute if HookName.BEFORE_TOOL_EXECUTE in hooks else None
        ),
        after_tool_execute=(
            after_tool_execute if HookName.AFTER_TOOL_EXECUTE in hooks else None
        ),
    )

What's in it:

  • HookName names the three hooks the log can record, one per point in the loop. A StrEnum limits them to these names, so a typo fails at once instead of quietly recording nothing.
  • Entry is a Pydantic model, because each line leaves the program for a file. It holds names and counts, never contents.
  • LOGGED_ARGUMENTS names the only arguments we copy. Listing them keeps a file's contents, passed to write_file, out of the log.
  • before_model_request receives a ModelRequestContext, and counts the messages and tool definitions about to go to the model.
  • before_tool_execute receives the tool call and its validated arguments. It records what the agent attempted, before we can tell whether the call finished.
  • after_tool_execute also receives the tool's result, and records that the call finished, with the result's length.
  • Each hook ends by returning what it was given: request_context, args, result. That's what makes them watchers.

build_activity_hooks returns Hooks(...). Each keyword names a hook, which tells the framework when to call the function given to it; a keyword given None gets no hook. The hooks parameter chooses which hooks are registered. Here we keep its default, all three; in the next lesson a setting chooses.

Hooks is a supplied capability: a component we attach to an agent to provide behavior. We've already used capabilities such as FileSystem and Shell.

Run a syntax check before connecting the hooks to the agent and validate that there are no errors:

uv run python -m py_compile src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/activity_log.py

Tip

Check: the command finishes without an error.

What it means

The file is valid Python. We haven't checked the hooks' behavior yet; the next step runs them with an agent.

docs.title: Step 2: Run the agent and read the log
docs.text:
Goal: attach the log for one run and read the loop from its records.

We've built our hooks. Now let's write a small program to see them in action.

We'll use TestModel to ask the agent to call two tools. This gives us a predictable run without needing an API key. We'll also attach our new activity log just for this test, leaving the chat application unchanged.

TestModel uses a for string arguments, so one of its tool calls will create a small file named a in our disposable workspace.

Create demos/watch_run.py: 

"""Run the chat's agent on a stand-in model, and print its activity log.

Needs no API key; run `demos/fresh_copy.py` first. It starts the log again,
so the file holds this run only.
"""

from pydantic_ai.models.test import TestModel

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.activity_log import build_activity_hooks
from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# Beside the workspace copy and not in it, so the file tools can't reach it.
# `work/` is already ignored by git.
LOG_PATH = project_root() / "work" / "activity.jsonl"
LOG_PATH.unlink(missing_ok=True)

chat = build_chat_agent(web_search=False, workspace_root=Settings().workspace_root)
chat.run_sync(
    user_prompt="What does this project do?",
    model=TestModel(call_tools=["list_modules", "write_file"]),
    # Added for this run only: the chat itself doesn't change.
    capabilities=[build_activity_hooks(path=LOG_PATH)],
)
print(LOG_PATH.read_text())

fresh_copy.py clears anything earlier runs left in the workspace copy:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/watch_run.py

Tip

Check: ignoring any startup banner, you should see:

{"hook":"before_model_request","step":1,"messages":1,"tools":14}
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"list_modules"}
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"write_file","target":"a"}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"list_modules","result_chars":137}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"write_file","result_chars":49}
{"hook":"before_model_request","step":2,"messages":3,"tools":14}

What it means

We can read the run from our own log. The agent prepared a model request, executed the requested tools, and prepared a second model request with their results:

  • Both tool calls say step: 1. They came from the same model response; a run step is not the same as one tool call.
  • write_file's line records its target path, a, but not the file's contents.
  • Each before_tool_execute has a matching after_tool_execute, so both tools finished.
  • The second request carries three messages: your question, the model's response asking for the tools, and the request carrying the tools' returns.
  • All fourteen tool definitions go with every request.
  • The run ends after step 2, because the model answered instead of asking for more tools.

The last line is another before_model_request, not an after_tool_execute: the agent is ready to ask the model again. TestModel then gives its final answer, so there is no third request. Each hook passed its received value back unchanged. The agent behaved as it would without our log.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• A run is a loop with named hooks. You can place a function on one, and find the others by their pattern.
  • A hook gets ctx, then what its hook passes, and the run carries on with what it returns. Yours return what they were given, so they only watch.

docs.text:
We can now observe the agent's loop without changing its behavior. In the next lesson, we'll connect this same activity log to the continuing chat, configure which hooks it records, and inspect a real conversation.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Put the activity log in the chat
Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson adds the activity log we created in the previous lesson to our chat. We'll connect the hooks from the previous lesson to the application and choose which events to record.

Last time, the log ran only in a demo with a stand-in model. Now we will integrate these hooks into our chat, and every conversation you have with the chat leaves a record, and you'll read what a real model did, including something it was refused.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Say why a hook is the right place for a rule only your application knows.
  • Choose which hooks an agent gets from Settings.
  • Read an activity log, and tell a call that finished from one that didn't.

About 15 minutes. Steps 1-6 need no API key. Step 7 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: Your application decides what to log
docs.text:
Our chat can read files and run commands. We want to record what it attempted and what finished. These hooks write that record to a local file.

The activity log helps us understand a run. It isn't a security audit: settings can disable it, and other programs can change the file.

docs.title: Settings control which hooks run
docs.text: Hooks(...) accepts one function for each event. We can omit events we don't want to record. We'll make that choice through Settings.

docs.title: The log records attempted calls
docs.text: before_tool_execute records an attempt before a tool runs. after_tool_execute records a completed call. If a call doesn't finish, the log may contain only the first event.

Four small changes in src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py. First, add Hooks to the pydantic_ai.capabilities import:

from pydantic_ai.capabilities import (

Add activity_log to the signature. The parameter is optional, so earlier scripts still work without a log:

def build_chat_agent(

In the same function, add this after the if web_search: block. The log goes last, so it records what the other capabilities have left:

    if activity_log is not None:

docs.title: Step 5: Check your work
docs.text:
Show the finished files `src/pydantic_tutor/settings.py`: 
"""Every value the app is configured with, typed and checked at startup.

Values only: strings and flags read from the environment. The objects built
from them are in `composition.py`.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.activity_log import HookName
from pydantic_tutor.model import CHAT_MODEL
from tutor_given.paths import project_root


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Read from variables named `PYDANTIC_TUTOR_<FIELD>`; frozen once created."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_prefix="PYDANTIC_TUTOR_",
        frozen=True,
        # Read here, into these fields only: a key in `.env` never enters
        # the process environment. A shell variable wins over `.env`.
        env_file=project_root() / ".env",
        # `OPENAI_API_KEY=` with nothing after it counts as unset.
        env_ignore_empty=True,
        # `.env` may hold variables for other tools; skip them.
        extra="ignore",
    )

    # A `<provider>:<model>` string, the name of the model: not the model.
    chat_model: str = CHAT_MODEL
    # Whether the chat may search the web. Each search is billed.
    web_search: bool = True
    # The folder the chat works in. `demos/fresh_copy.py` makes the default.
    workspace_root: Path = project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
    # The activity log's file. Beside the workspace and not in it, so the file
    # tools can't reach it. `work/` is already ignored by git.
    activity_log_path: Path = project_root() / "work" / "activity.jsonl"
    # Which hooks the activity log records. An empty list turns it off.
    activity_log: frozenset[HookName] = frozenset(HookName)
    # One key per provider the composition root can build. SecretStr:
    # printing the settings shows `**********`, never the key.
    openai_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="OPENAI_API_KEY"
    )
    anthropic_api_key: SecretStr | None = Field(
        default=None, validation_alias="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
    )
`src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py`: 
"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Shell tools: run a few commands there.
- Toolset: the workspace's own tools.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
- Activity log: a record of the run, if one is given.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import (
    AbstractCapability,
    Hooks,
    LocalWorkspace,
    Toolset,
    WebSearch,
)
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem, Shell

from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset
from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")

# The commands the shell may start. A precaution, not a boundary: it checks
# only a command's first word, so `ls && cat .env` still runs.
SHELL_COMMANDS = ("pytest", "pwd", "ls", "cat")


def build_chat_agent(
    *, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path, activity_log: Hooks[None] | None = None
) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
        # Shell tools: run the allowed commands in that workspace.
        Shell(allowed_commands=SHELL_COMMANDS),
        # Toolset: the workspace's own tools, built for this folder.
        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    if activity_log is not None:
        # Activity log: last, so it records what the other capabilities have
        # left.
        capabilities.append(activity_log)
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)
`src/pydantic_tutor/composition.py`: 
"""The composition root: the one place the app's objects are built.

`build_app` turns `Settings` (values) into the agent and the model (objects).
The model is built here, at startup, so an unknown provider or a missing API key
stops the app before the chat opens, not when the first message is sent.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UserError
from pydantic_ai.models import Model, infer_model

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.activity_log import build_activity_hooks
from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.providers import ProviderFactory, build_provider
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class App:
    """What the chat needs to run, built once from the settings."""

    agent: Agent[None, str]
    model: Model


def build_app(*, settings: Settings) -> App:
    """Build the agent and the model from `settings`.

    Raises `pydantic_ai.exceptions.UserError` if the model name's provider is
    unknown or its API key is not set.
    """
    if not settings.workspace_root.is_dir():
        raise UserError(
            f"PYDANTIC_TUTOR_WORKSPACE_ROOT is {str(settings.workspace_root)!r}, "
            "which is not a folder. Make the default with "
            "`uv run demos/fresh_copy.py`, or set the variable to another folder."
        )
    return App(
        agent=build_chat_agent(
            web_search=settings.web_search,
            workspace_root=settings.workspace_root,
            activity_log=build_activity_hooks(
                path=settings.activity_log_path, hooks=settings.activity_log
            ),
        ),
        model=build_model(settings=settings),
    )


def build_model(
    *, settings: Settings, provider_factory: ProviderFactory | None = None
) -> Model:
    """Build the model `settings.chat_model` names, its provider holding its key.

    `infer_model` picks the model class from the string, and asks
    `provider_factory` for the provider, by the part before the colon. The
    default is `build_provider`; pass another function to replace it.
    """
    return infer_model(
        model=settings.chat_model,
        # `infer_model` calls this with one argument, the provider's name.
        provider_factory=provider_factory
        or (lambda name: build_provider(name=name, settings=settings)),
    )

docs.title: Step 7: Read a real chat's activity log
docs.text:
This step uses your API key, and the model decides what it does, so your lines will differ from anyone else's. Start the chat:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Ask it something that takes a few tools, then ask for something the chat's shell doesn't allow:

Which module in this project handles retries? Read it and summarize it.

Please run the command rm -rf build, then tell me what happened.

End the chat with an empty line, then open work/activity.jsonl in your editor.

Tip

Check: you should see a before_model_request line for each trip to the model, and tool lines between them. step starts again at 1 for your second question, because each question is a new run. messages keeps growing across questions, because each run is sent the chat so far.

If the model tried the command, you'll find a line like this, with no after_tool_execute for that call:

{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"run_command","target":"rm -rf build"}

The model may decline without trying. Then there's no such line, and the log is still telling the truth.

What it means

A before_tool_execute with no matching after_tool_execute means the call didn't finish. The shell refused this one, because rm isn't an allowed command. The refusal went back to the model, and no after_tool_execute fired.

The log can't tell you why a call didn't finish. A crash inside a tool could leave the same gap. It does tell you that the agent tried, and that's something only a hook sitting in the run could record.

There's one more thing a hook being part of the run means. If the log can't be written, the error stops the run before the tool starts. For a log you'd rather lose than stop a chat for, you'd catch that error in write.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Hooks hold what only your application knows. The chat now keeps a record of what it did on your machine.
  • A setting can decide which hooks an agent gets. Settings chooses how much the log records, or turns it off.
  • The log shows what was tried. You can tell a call that finished from one that didn't.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Our log only watches. Next we'll write hooks that change a run, and see why the order of the capabilities list starts to matter.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson uses hooks to change a run. Our earlier hooks observed events and returned their inputs unchanged. Now we'll use hooks to refuse some tool calls and change some tool returns.

In Chapter 3, we allowed selected shell commands, but the check looked only at the first word. A command could therefore chain another operation onto an allowed command. We'll demonstrate that gap in a disposable workspace, then write one hook to refuse chained commands and another to remove our practice tokens from tool returns. Finally, we'll adjust the activity log so it records refused calls too.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Change what the model is sent by returning something else from a hook.
  • Refuse a tool call from a hook, and say what the model sees.
  • Choose a hook's place in the list by what it needs to see.

About 20 minutes. Steps 1 to 3 need no API key. Step 4 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: Hooks can change or refuse tool calls
docs.text:
The run carries on with whatever a hook returns. So a before_tool_execute hook can return different arguments, and an after_tool_execute hook can return a different result. The model then sees the changed version and nothing else.

A hook can also refuse. If before_tool_execute raises ModelRetry, the tool doesn't run, and the model gets your message and can try something else. ModelRetry is the same exception you raised from a tool earlier in the series. Any other exception stops the whole run.

These two hooks hold rules only this application knows: which shell commands we consider safe, and what our tokens look like. The library ships general versions you'd reach for first. ToolOutputLimits shortens oversized results, and ToolGuardrail runs checks you supply on a tool's arguments and results.

docs.title: Hook order changes what gets recorded
docs.text:
For each tool call, before_ hooks run in list order. The tool runs next. Then after_ hooks run in reverse order.

So a hook sees what the hooks before it have done. A before_ hook first in the list sees every attempt, including ones a later hook will refuse. An after_ hook first in the list runs last, so it sees the result in its final form.

  • demos/guard_check.py, new: runs the chat's agent on a given model that reads a token and asks for a chained command
