docs.title: Step 1: Demonstrate the unsafe command
docs.text:
Goal: watch two ways a token reaches the model today.

We'll reproduce the gap in a disposable workspace before adding the guards. The script adds a deploy.toml holding a fake token to your workspace copy. That's a file nobody thought to add to SECRET_PATTERNS. The given model reads it, then asks to run pytest --version && cat .env.

Everything secret here is fake, including the .env that fresh_copy.py puts in the workspace copy. Your real .env isn't involved.

Create demos/guard_check.py:

"""Run the chat's agent on a model that reads a token and chains a command.

Needs no API key. It resets the log, and adds a `deploy.toml` with a fake token
to the workspace copy; run `demos/fresh_copy.py` first.
"""

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.activity_log import HookName, build_activity_hooks
from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.stand_ins import reads_a_token_then_chains_a_command

settings = Settings()
(settings.workspace_root / "deploy.toml").write_text(
    'runner_token = "tj-FAKE-0000-not-a-real-secret"\n'
)
log_path = settings.activity_log_path
log_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)

chat = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=False,
    workspace_root=settings.workspace_root,
    activity_log=build_activity_hooks(
        path=log_path,
        hooks=frozenset({HookName.BEFORE_TOOL_EXECUTE, HookName.AFTER_TOOL_EXECUTE}),
    ),
)
chat.run_sync(
    user_prompt="Check the deployment settings.",
    model=reads_a_token_then_chains_a_command(),
)
print("the log:")
print(log_path.read_text(), end="")

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/guard_check.py

Tip

Check: ignoring any startup banner, you should see:

model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "tj-FAKE-0000-not-a-real-secret"
model got, from run_command:
[stdout]
pytest 9.1.1
# FAKE VALUES. A fixture: the agent must not be able to read this file.
TINYJOBS_RUNNER_TOKEN=tj-FAKE-0000-not-a-real-secret
TINYJOBS_RUNNER_URL=https://runner.example.invalid
the log:
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","target":"deploy.toml"}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","result_chars":99}
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":2,"tool":"run_command","target":"pytest --version && cat .env"}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":2,"tool":"run_command","result_chars":198}

What it means

Both fake secrets reached the model. read_file returned the token, because deploy.toml isn't on the deny list. run_command returned the fake .env, because Shell checks only the first word, pytest, and the rest of the line ran too. The file tools refuse .env, but the shell doesn't use them.

docs.title: Step 2: Add guards for commands and tokens
docs.text:
Goal: the model no longer gets either secret.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/guards.py:

  • refuse_chained_commands raises ModelRetry when a command holds more than one command.
  • remove_tokens returns the result with anything shaped like our tokens replaced. Results that aren't text pass through.
"""Two rules only this application knows, as hooks on the chat's tool calls.

A safety net for mistakes, not a security boundary: `pytest` still runs any code
it is given, and `TOKEN` matches one known format, not every secret.
"""

import re
from typing import Any

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Hooks
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import ModelRetry
from pydantic_ai.messages import ToolCallPart
from pydantic_ai.tools import ToolDefinition

# What joins one shell command to another, or runs one inside another.
CHAINING = ("&&", "||", ";", "|", "`", "$(", "\n")
# The shape of this project's tokens.
TOKEN = re.compile(r"tj-[A-Za-z0-9-]+")


async def refuse_chained_commands(
    ctx: RunContext[None],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Refuse a shell command that holds more than one command."""
    command = str(args.get("command", ""))
    if any(mark in command for mark in CHAINING):
        raise ModelRetry("Run one command at a time, with no chaining.")
    return args


async def remove_tokens(
    ctx: RunContext[None],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],
    result: object,
) -> object:
    """Return the tool's result with this project's tokens removed."""
    if isinstance(result, str):
        return TOKEN.sub("[token removed]", result)
    return result


guards: Hooks[None] = Hooks(
    before_tool_execute=refuse_chained_commands,
    after_tool_execute=remove_tokens,
)

In src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, import it after the other pydantic_tutor.capabilities import:

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.guards import guards

Then add it to the end of the capabilities list in build_chat_agent, after the Toolset(...) entry:

        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
        # Our rules for tool calls: see the module's limits.
        guards,
    ]

And name it in the docstring's piece list, after "Activity log":

- Activity log: a record of the run, if one is given.
- Guards: our rules for tool calls.

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/guard_check.py

Tip

Check: you should see:

model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "[token removed]"
model got, from run_command:
Run one command at a time, with no chaining.
the log:
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","target":"deploy.toml"}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","result_chars":99}

What it means

The token is gone from the first result, and the second command never ran. The model got your refusal message instead, and could try again with one command. Both hooks changed the run without touching FileSystem, Shell or the tools themselves.

Now look at the log. It doesn't mention run_command, and it says read_file returned 99 characters, though the model got fewer. Our log has stopped telling the truth about this run, which is the next step's subject.

docs.title: Step 3: Move the activity log to see every attempt
docs.text:
Goal: a log that records refused attempts, and the result the model got.

The log is last in the list, so its before_ hook runs after the guard's. A refused call never reaches it. Its after_ hook runs first on the way out, before remove_tokens has done anything, so it counts the original result.

We want the opposite on both counts, and one move does it. In build_chat_agent, find the lines that add the log, and replace them:

    if activity_log is not None:
        # First: its `before_` hooks see every attempt, and its `after_` hooks
        # run last, so they see the result the model gets.
        capabilities.insert(0, activity_log)

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/guard_check.py

Tip

Check: what the model got is unchanged, and the log now reads:

{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","target":"deploy.toml"}
{"hook":"after_tool_execute","step":1,"tool":"read_file","result_chars":84}
{"hook":"before_tool_execute","step":2,"tool":"run_command","target":"pytest --version && cat .env"}

What it means

The refused command is now in the log, as a before_tool_execute with no after_tool_execute. The size is now 84, the result with the token removed. Nothing about the hooks changed, only their place.

The same hook at either end of the list sees different things, and nothing warns you. Whenever two hooks share the same point, it's worth asking which should see the other's work.

Optional: compare your finished chat/agent.py 
"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Shell tools: run a few commands there.
- Toolset: the workspace's own tools.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
- Activity log: a record of the run, if one is given.
- Guards: our rules for tool calls.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import (
    AbstractCapability,
    Hooks,
    LocalWorkspace,
    Toolset,
    WebSearch,
)
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem, Shell

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.guards import guards
from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset
from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")

# The commands the shell may start. A precaution, not a boundary: it checks
# only a command's first word, so `ls && cat .env` still runs.
SHELL_COMMANDS = ("pytest", "pwd", "ls", "cat")


def build_chat_agent(
    *, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path, activity_log: Hooks[None] | None = None
) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
        # Shell tools: run the allowed commands in that workspace.
        Shell(allowed_commands=SHELL_COMMANDS),
        # Toolset: the workspace's own tools, built for this folder.
        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
        # Our rules for tool calls: see the module's limits.
        guards,
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    if activity_log is not None:
        # First: its `before_` hooks see every attempt, and its `after_` hooks
        # run last, so they see the result the model gets.
        capabilities.insert(0, activity_log)
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

What it means

The model asks, and your program decides. A real model reads your refusal message and chooses what to do next, which is why the message says what to do instead.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
remove_tokens has a flaw: the model sees [token removed] and nobody has told it what that means. Fixing that takes something a hook can't do alone, an instruction to the model. Next we'll see what a capability really is, and turn this hook into one.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson is about custom capabilities: classes we write to give an agent new behavior. You've been adding them to a list since Chapter 2, and Hooks was one too. Now we'll build one of our own.

Last time we left a flaw. remove_tokens puts [token removed] into a tool's result, and nothing has told the model what that means. Fixing it takes a hook and an instruction that travel together, and that's what a capability you write yourself is for. We'll look at what's already in the chat's list, then turn the hook into a class.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Say what a capability is, and name what the chat's capabilities bring.
  • Write a capability with a setting, an instruction and a hook.
  • Choose between Hooks(...) and a class of your own.

About 15 minutes. Steps 1 and 2 need no API key. Step 3 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: Capabilities add behavior to an agent
docs.text:
The library's base class, AbstractCapability, has a method for each thing a capability can bring. Each one does nothing by default, and a capability overrides the ones it needs:

A capability can bring By overriding Instructions get_instructions() Tools get_toolset() A workspace get_workspace() Hooks before_tool_execute(), after_tool_execute() and the rest

Shell, FileSystem, WebSearch and Hooks are all subclasses of it. To the agent, they're the same kind of thing, so the capabilities list can hold them side by side. Capabilities can also supply model settings; we'll return to that later.

docs.title: A class keeps related behavior together
docs.text:
Use Hooks(...) when a function can stand on its own. We'll keep refuse_chained_commands that way.

remove_tokens also needs to explain the replacement text to the model. We'll put the hook and that instruction in one class. The class will hold the token pattern as a setting.

  • src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/guards.py, changed: remove_tokens moves out
  • src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, changed: the chat takes RedactTokens

Given: demos/show_capabilities.py, which lists what each of the chat's capabilities brings. You don't need to read it.

The steps:

  1. See what's in the chat's list.
  2. Turn the hook into a capability.
  3. Try it in a real chat.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:

docs.text:
Goal: see that the things you've been adding are all one kind of thing.

uv run demos/show_capabilities.py

Tip

LocalWorkspace: a workspace
FileSystem: tools, hooks
Shell: tools, hooks
Toolset: tools
Hooks: hooks

What it means

Each line is one entry in the chat's list, and each brings something different. LocalWorkspace brings only a workspace. Toolset brings only tools. FileSystem and Shell bring tools and hooks of their own. Hooks is the guards you wrote last time, and brings hooks only.

None of them brings instructions yet. That's what we'll add.

docs.title: Step 2: Build the redaction capability
docs.text:
Goal: one object that removes tokens and tells the model it does.

We'll create RedactTokens to keep the redaction hook and its explanation together. The pattern becomes a setting on the class.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/redact_tokens.py. Three Python features matter here:

  • @dataclass(kw_only=True) makes each field a keyword argument: RedactTokens(pattern=...).
  • __post_init__ runs at the end of the constructor, so a bad pattern stops the app at startup, not in the middle of a run.
  • [DepsT] means "for whatever deps type the agent has". This capability reads none, so any agent can take it.
  • after_tool_execute is the same hook as before, now a method. It has to be async. A plain def fails the run with a TypeError at the first tool call, and a method with any other name is never called, with no error at all.
"""Remove tokens from tool results, and tell the model that it happens.

A safety net for mistakes, not a security boundary: it matches one known
format, not every secret.
"""

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability
from pydantic_ai.messages import ToolCallPart
from pydantic_ai.tools import ToolDefinition

REPLACEMENT = "[token removed]"


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class RedactTokens[DepsT](AbstractCapability[DepsT]):
    """Replace anything matching `pattern` in tool results, and say so."""

    # A regular expression for the tokens to remove.
    pattern: str
    compiled: re.Pattern[str] = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        """Compile the pattern now, so a bad one fails when the app starts."""
        self.compiled = re.compile(self.pattern)

    def get_instructions(self) -> str:
        """Tell the model what the replacement text means."""
        return (
            f"{REPLACEMENT} in a tool result marks a secret removed on purpose. "
            "The file isn't broken. Don't try to recover the secret."
        )

    async def after_tool_execute(
        self,
        ctx: RunContext[DepsT],
        *,
        call: ToolCallPart,
        tool_def: ToolDefinition,
        args: dict[str, Any],
        result: object,
    ) -> object:
        """Return the tool's result with the tokens removed."""
        if isinstance(result, str):
            return self.compiled.sub(REPLACEMENT, result)
        return result

Now guards.py only needs the refusal. In src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/guards.py, delete the remove_tokens function, the TOKEN constant and its comment, and the import re line. Then replace the last lines of the file, which make guards:

guards: Hooks[None] = Hooks(before_tool_execute=refuse_chained_commands)

And replace the module's docstring, which no longer describes it:

"""A rule only this application knows, as a hook on the chat's shell commands.

A safety net for mistakes, not a security boundary: `pytest` still runs any code
it is given.
"""

In src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, add this import after the guards import:

Add the token format after SHELL_COMMANDS:

And add the capability after guards in the list:

And name it in the docstring's piece list, after "Guards":

- Guards: our rules for tool calls.
- Token redaction: secrets removed before the model sees them.

show_chat_request.py prints the tools, then these instructions:

What it means

The tokens are removed just as before, and the model is now told what the replacement means. Both came from one line in the list. RedactTokens is the first entry that brings instructions and hooks together, and a second agent could take the whole thing with that one line.

guards stayed a Hooks, because it's one function with nothing to say to the model. That's the choice from Concepts: reach for a class when pieces have to travel together.

Optional: compare your finished files `src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/guards.py`: 
"""A rule only this application knows, as a hook on the chat's shell commands.

A safety net for mistakes, not a security boundary: `pytest` still runs any code
it is given.
"""

from typing import Any

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Hooks
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import ModelRetry
from pydantic_ai.messages import ToolCallPart
from pydantic_ai.tools import ToolDefinition

# What joins one shell command to another, or runs one inside another.
CHAINING = ("&&", "||", ";", "|", "`", "$(", "\n")


async def refuse_chained_commands(
    ctx: RunContext[None],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Refuse a shell command that holds more than one command."""
    command = str(args.get("command", ""))
    if any(mark in command for mark in CHAINING):
        raise ModelRetry("Run one command at a time, with no chaining.")
    return args


guards: Hooks[None] = Hooks(before_tool_execute=refuse_chained_commands)
`src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py`: 
"""The agent the chat talks to.

No model here, as for every agent in this project: the chat passes one on
each run.

Built from these pieces:
- Workspace: the folder the tools work in.
- File tools: read and write files there.
- Shell tools: run a few commands there.
- Toolset: the workspace's own tools.
- Web search: switched on by a setting.
- Activity log: a record of the run, if one is given.
- Guards: our rules for tool calls.
- Token redaction: secrets removed before the model sees them.
"""

from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import (
    AbstractCapability,
    Hooks,
    LocalWorkspace,
    Toolset,
    WebSearch,
)
from pydantic_ai_harness import FileSystem, Shell

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.guards import guards
from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.redact_tokens import RedactTokens
from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset
from tutor_given.paths import project_root

# File names the file tools may not touch. A precaution, not a complete
# data-security policy.
SECRET_PATTERNS = ("**/.env", "**/.env.*", "*.pem", "*.key", "**/secrets*")

# The commands the shell may start. A precaution, not a boundary: it checks
# only a command's first word, so `ls && cat .env` still runs.
SHELL_COMMANDS = ("pytest", "pwd", "ls", "cat")

# The shape of this project's tokens.
TOKEN_PATTERN = r"tj-[A-Za-z0-9-]+"


def build_chat_agent(
    *, web_search: bool, workspace_root: Path, activity_log: Hooks[None] | None = None
) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent."""
    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # Workspace: a place for tools to work in. It adds no tool: they use
        # `ctx.workspace`.
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=workspace_root),
        # File tools: read and write files in that workspace, minus the secret
        # patterns.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=SECRET_PATTERNS),
        # Shell tools: run the allowed commands in that workspace.
        Shell(allowed_commands=SHELL_COMMANDS),
        # Toolset: the workspace's own tools, built for this folder.
        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
        # Our rules for tool calls: see the module's limits.
        guards,
        RedactTokens(pattern=TOKEN_PATTERN),
    ]
    if web_search:
        # Web search: the model may search when it needs to. Each search is
        # billed by the provider, on top of the tokens.
        capabilities.append(WebSearch())
    if activity_log is not None:
        # First: its `before_` hooks see every attempt, and its `after_` hooks
        # run last, so they see the result the model gets.
        capabilities.insert(0, activity_log)
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )


# Earlier demos import this name; the console chat builds its agent in build_app.
chat_agent = build_chat_agent(
    web_search=True, workspace_root=project_root() / "work" / "tinyjobs"
)

docs.title: Step 3: Test redaction in the chat
docs.text:
Goal: see whether a real model understands the replacement.

This step uses your API key, and the model decides what it says. guard_check.py adds deploy.toml to the workspace copy, so run it first and don't reset the copy afterwards:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/guard_check.py
uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Read deploy.toml and tell me what's in it.

Tip

Check: the answer doesn't contain tj-FAKE. The model should describe the value as removed, rather than call the file broken. It's the model's wording, so yours will differ.

What it means

The hook guarantees what the model is sent, and that part isn't up to the model. The instruction only asks, and a real model's response to it can vary. That's the difference between code and a prompt, and a capability can carry both.

docs.text:

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
RedactTokens brings an instruction and a hook. Next we'll write a capability with no hooks at all, one that moves the chat's prompt out of Python and into a file.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Move the chat prompt into a file
Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson moves the chat's main instructions into a Markdown file. Last time, you wrote a capability with a hook and an instruction. Now we'll write one that supplies instructions without a hook. We'll compare what the model receives before and after the change, then look at instruction order.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Put the chat's behavioral instructions in a file and keep the application working.
  • Explain how instructions supplied from different places reach the model.

About 15 minutes. Steps 1 and 2 need no API key. Step 3 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: Capabilities can supply instructions
docs.text:
A capability can supply instructions without a hook. It implements get_instructions(), which returns text or a function that produces text. The agent keeps returned text for later requests. If it receives a function, it calls that function for each request.

Our PromptFile capability will read its instructions from a file. PromptFile is our name, not the library's. Keeping the prompt in its own file lets us edit the instructions without changing Python. PromptFile reads the file when we construct the capability. The agent reuses that text for each request, and edits take effect when we restart the application. We could instead return a function that reads the file on every request. We won't need that behavior in this lesson.

docs.title: Static instructions come first
docs.text:
Pydantic AI treats instructions as static text or dynamic functions. Static text stays the same across requests. Dynamic instructions are computed for each request. What a piece is given as decides its kind, not where it comes from. Pydantic AI records whether each piece is dynamic.

An agent takes instructions in four places: its constructor, its capabilities, the run (run_sync(..., instructions=...)) and its toolsets. A function added with @agent.instructions counts as the constructor's. The model is sent every static piece first, then every dynamic one, and within each kind the places go in this order:

Order Static: text Dynamic: functions 1 the constructor's instructions= the constructor's instructions=, and @agent.instructions functions 2 each capability's get_instructions(), in list order each capability's get_instructions(), in list order 3 the run's instructions= the run's instructions= 4 each toolset's instructions= each toolset's instructions=

All static instructions come before dynamic ones. Within each kind, their source determines the order. The pieces are joined with a blank line between them and sent as one block. Static goes first for prompt caching: a provider that caches prompts can reuse a request's unchanged beginning, so text that changes goes after it.

docs.text:

  • demos/instruction_order.py (new): a second agent with instructions in all four places, printed in the order the model is sent them

docs.title: Step 1: Move the prompt into a file
docs.text:
Goal: put the chat's prompt in a file, give the agent a capability that reads it, and see that the model is sent the same instruction text.

We'll keep the chat's current wording so moving it won't change its behavior. Create src/pydantic_tutor/prompts/chat.md with this line:

You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.

Next, create src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/prompt_file.py. This capability reads the Markdown file when the agent is built and supplies its text as instructions:

"""A capability that gives an agent its instructions from a text file.

An agent's prompt is text, not code: in a file of its own, it can be read,
reviewed and changed without touching Python. `PromptFile` reads the file once, when it is made, and supplies the
text as the agent's instructions. It reads no deps, so any agent can take it.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AbstractCapability


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class PromptFile[DepsT](AbstractCapability[DepsT]):
    """Supply the text of a file as the agent's instructions."""

    # The file the prompt is read from, as UTF-8 text.
    path: Path
    # The file's text, without the blank lines and spaces around it.
    text: str = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        """Read the prompt now, so a missing or empty file fails at once."""
        self.text = self.path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
        if not self.text:
            raise ValueError(f"the prompt file {self.path} is empty")

    def get_instructions(self) -> str:
        """Return the prompt, as text."""
        # Text, not a function: the agent sends text it was given before
        # any it computes for a request, and does not ask for it again.
        # An edit to the file is read when the program next starts.
        return self.text

In src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, import PromptFile after the guards import, and add the prompt file's path after TOKEN_PATTERN:

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.prompt_file import PromptFile

# The chat's prompt, in the package's `prompts` folder, so it is found whichever
# folder the program runs from.
PROMPT_PATH = Path(__file__).parents[1] / "prompts" / "chat.md"

Then, in build_chat_agent, put PromptFile(path=PROMPT_PATH) first in the capabilities, and delete the instructions= line from the Agent(...) call:

    capabilities: list[AbstractCapability[None]] = [
        # The chat's instructions, read from PROMPT_PATH when the agent is
        # built. Text, so it is sent ahead of any computed for a request.
        PromptFile(path=PROMPT_PATH),

    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )

Run the script from Before you start again:

uv run demos/show_chat_request.py

Tip

Check: the instructions: line is exactly what it was:

instructions: "You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.\n\n[token removed] in a tool result marks a secret removed on purpose. The file isn't broken. Don't try to recover the secret.\n\nYour workspace holds the Python project tinyjobs."

What it means

The instructions the model receives haven't changed. The prompt's words are in no .py file now, yet the model is sent the same pieces. PromptFile returns a str, so its text is static, like the constructor's was, and still goes ahead of the others.

Now change the prompt without touching Python. Edit chat.md to read You are a helpful assistant. Answer in one short sentence. and run the script again:

  instructions: "You are a helpful assistant. Answer in one short sentence.\n\n[token removed] in a tool result marks a secret removed on purpose. The file isn't broken. Don't try to recover the secret.\n\nYour workspace holds the Python project tinyjobs."

Put the file back as it was. __post_init__ is what a dataclass calls at the end of its constructor, so the file is read when PromptFile(...) is made, which is when the agent is built. A missing file raises FileNotFoundError then; an empty one raises ValueError: the prompt file .../chat.md is empty. Either way the program fails at startup, not in a run that goes out without its prompt. text is field(init=False): the constructor takes only path, and __post_init__ sets text.

PROMPT_PATH starts from Path(__file__), the file chat/agent.py itself, and parents[1] is the package folder above it. Because PromptFile reads once, an edit made while the chat is running is not seen until you start it again: the choice from Concepts.

docs.title: Step 2: Observe instruction order
docs.text:
Goal: see in which order the model is sent instructions given in all four places.

This step builds a second agent, reader, with instructions in all four places, and runs it on a stand-in model that prints each piece it is sent. We'll deliberately list the instructions out of order so the output shows how Pydantic AI arranges them.

Create demos/instruction_order.py:

"""In which order instructions from several places reach the model.

A second agent is given instructions in every place an agent takes them: its
constructor, a capability, a toolset and the run, some as text and some as a
function. A stand-in model prints each part of the instructions it is sent, in
order. Needs no API key.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage, ModelResponse, TextPart
from pydantic_ai.models.function import AgentInfo, FunctionModel

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.prompt_file import PromptFile
from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import PROMPT_PATH
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from pydantic_tutor.tools.workspace_toolset import build_workspace_toolset


def from_the_constructor(ctx: RunContext[None]) -> str:
    """Instructions given to the constructor as a function."""
    return "From the constructor, a function."


def show_instructions(messages: list[ModelMessage], info: AgentInfo) -> ModelResponse:
    """Stand in for a model: print each part of its instructions, then answer."""
    for part in info.model_request_parameters.instruction_parts or []:
        kind = "dynamic" if part.dynamic else "static"
        print(f"{kind:>7}: {part.content}")
    return ModelResponse(parts=[TextPart(content="Done.")])


# The function is listed before the text, so that the order you write would
# be wrong.
reader: Agent[None, str] = Agent(
    name="reader",
    instructions=[from_the_constructor, "From the constructor, text."],
    toolsets=[build_workspace_toolset(root=Settings().workspace_root)],
    capabilities=[PromptFile(path=PROMPT_PATH)],
)
reader.run_sync(
    user_prompt="Hi.",
    model=FunctionModel(function=show_instructions),
    instructions="From the run, text.",
)

uv run demos/instruction_order.py

Tip

Check: ignoring any startup banner, you should see exactly:

static: From the constructor, text.
static: You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly.
static: From the run, text.
static: Your workspace holds the Python project tinyjobs.
dynamic: From the constructor, a function.

What it means

Four static pieces come first, in the order of places: the constructor's text, PromptFile's prompt, the run's text, the workspace toolset's sentence. Then the one dynamic piece, the constructor's function.

The constructor listed its function first, and the text still went first: kind decides before place. That is also why Step 1 changed nothing, since the prompt is text.

Two placements are worth a second look. The run's text was passed to run_sync, last, yet it lands before the function: it is a str, so it is static. And the toolset's sentence is static too: the workspace toolset was given a string (instructions=f"Your workspace holds ..."), and a string is static wherever it comes from. The Agents page, as read on 2026-10-20, lists "toolset instructions" among the dynamic ones; at 2.56.0 only a function is.

docs.title: Step 3: Change the prompt in a real chat
docs.text:
Goal: see a prompt edit change a real model's behaviour.

This step uses your API key. Ask a question, then edit the file, then ask it again:

uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

What does tinyjobs do?

End the chat with an empty line. Edit src/pydantic_tutor/prompts/chat.md to read You are a helpful assistant. Answer in one short sentence., start the chat again, and ask the same question.

Tip

Check: the second answer should be noticeably shorter. It's the model's wording, so yours will differ. Put the file back when you're done.

What it means

You changed the chat's behaviour without touching Python. PromptFile reads the file when the agent is built, which is why the edit needed a restart.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:

  • Static text goes before dynamic, each in the order of places. You can work out the order the model gets instructions in, from the table in Concepts.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
PromptFile brings instructions and nothing else. Next, the chat gets a capability that brings tools and instructions together: a notebook it keeps between sessions.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson is about memory: notes the chat keeps between sessions. Suppose you explain a project convention today and open a new chat tomorrow. A new session doesn't automatically receive yesterday's conversation history. We'll give the chat a notebook to save project decisions and conventions. Then we'll see how it can retrieve those notes without sending every note with every request.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Store a useful project note, start a fresh session, and retrieve it.
  • Explain the trade-off between letting the model request notes and injecting notes into every model request.

About 20 minutes. Steps 1 to 4 need no API key: the model is a stand-in that follows a script. Step 5 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: Saved notes survive a chat session
docs.text: The Memory capability stores notes as Markdown files that outlast a run. MEMORY.md is the main file, and the model can create others. It uses write_memory to save notes, read_memory to retrieve them, search_memory to find matching files, and delete_memory to remove files other than MEMORY.md. Memory also brings guidance, text in the instructions that says when to use them. The model reads these files through tools. The notes are not a second conversation history. A store keeps the files; FileStore keeps them in the run's workspace, in a folder you name.

docs.title: Injection adds notes to requests
docs.text:
By default, Memory uses memory injection. Before each request, it adds the contents of MEMORY.md and the names of other note files alongside the latest question. The block isn't kept in the history: Memory takes the old one off the earlier question and puts a new one beside the latest, so it moves.

Injection on Injection off Sent with each request The guidance, and the notebook, up to 2,000 tokens together The guidance only The start of each request Changes each turn, from the previous question on The same as the request before The notebook reaches the model Beside your question, every time In a tool result, when it asks

The second row costs the most. A provider that caches prompts reuses the unchanged start of a request; with injection on, each request changes from the previous question onward, even when the notebook hasn't. The library's Memory page recommends inject_memory=False for prompts that should stay the same. Turning injection off keeps the memory tools and guidance available.

docs.title: The model can request saved notes
docs.text:
With injection off, the model no longer receives the file names automatically. It needs a way to discover them before calling read_memory. We'll add a list_memory tool and update the guidance to explain how to use it.

A capability gives the model tools, as PromptFile gave it instructions, by overriding a method: get_toolset(), which returns a toolset. ListableMemory (ours, not the library's) is a subclass of Memory whose get_toolset() adds one tool. A subclass, so one capability keeps all its tools together: prefix_tools renames the lot.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: You write capabilities/listable_memory.py, give it to the chat in chat/agent.py, and add two scripts, notebook.py and memory_injection.py. Given, and not written by you: the replacement guidance and the shape list_memory returns (tutor_given/memory_text.py), and the scripts' stand-in models (tutor_given/stand_ins.py).

docs.title: Step 1: Add a notebook to the chat
docs.text:
Goal: write ListableMemory, give it to the chat with injection off, and see what the model is now sent.

We'll use the harness's Memory capability to save notes, but we'll leave injection off. That means the model needs a way to discover note names before reading them. Our subclass adds a list_memory tool.

Create src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/listable_memory.py. LISTING_GUIDANCE is the guidance text, which names list_memory, and MemoryListing is what the tool returns: its file names, and truncated, true when there were more than max_list_files, so a cut list isn't taken for the whole.

"""The library's `Memory`, plus a tool that lists the notebook's files.

With injection off nothing names the files to the model, and none of `Memory`'s
tools lists them: `ListableMemory` adds `list_memory`, and guidance that names it.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic_ai import RunContext
from pydantic_ai.toolsets import AgentToolset, FunctionToolset
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory

from tutor_given.memory_text import LISTING_GUIDANCE, MemoryListing


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class ListableMemory[DepsT](Memory[DepsT]):
    """`Memory`, with a `list_memory` tool beside its own four."""

    guidance: str | None = LISTING_GUIDANCE
    max_list_files: int = 100  # the most names one call returns

    def get_toolset(self) -> AgentToolset[DepsT] | None:
        """Return `Memory`'s own toolset, with `list_memory` added once."""
        memory_tools = super().get_toolset()
        # `Memory` returns its one FunctionToolset: tells mypy, fails if not.
        if not isinstance(memory_tools, FunctionToolset):
            raise TypeError("Memory.get_toolset() did not return a FunctionToolset")
        # The same object every time, never a new one: `Memory`'s tools find
        # the run's copy of the capability by it. The agent asks on every
        # memory tool call, hence "once".
        if "list_memory" not in memory_tools.tools:
            memory_tools.add_function(func=self.list_memory, name="list_memory")
        return memory_tools

    async def list_memory(self, ctx: RunContext[DepsT]) -> MemoryListing:
        """List the files in your memory notebook, MEMORY.md included.

        Call it before `read_memory` when you do not know a file's name.
        """
        # The run's store and this notebook's folder: the other tools' own.
        store, scope = self.resolve_scope(ctx=ctx)
        prefix = f"{scope}/"
        # One over the limit, so exactly that many files is not "cut".
        paths = await store.list_paths(prefix=prefix, limit=self.max_list_files + 1)
        # Only names `read_memory` takes: Markdown, not in a folder below.
        names = sorted(
            name
            for name in (path.removeprefix(prefix) for path in paths)
            if "/" not in name and name.endswith(".md")
        )
        return MemoryListing(
            files=names[: self.max_list_files],
            truncated=len(paths) > self.max_list_files,
        )

In src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py, import FileStore from pydantic_ai_harness.memory and ListableMemory from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.listable_memory, add the notebook's folder after SECRET_PATTERNS, and add the capability after Toolset(...):

# The notebook's folder, in the workspace.
NOTEBOOK = ".agent-memory"
...
        Toolset(toolset=build_workspace_toolset(root=workspace_root)),
        # Injection off: the model lists and reads the notebook with tools.
        ListableMemory(store=FileStore(directory=NOTEBOOK), inject_memory=False),

uv run demos/show_chat_request.py

Tip

Check: the tools: line now ends ..., read_docstring, write_memory, read_memory, delete_memory, search_memory, list_memory, and its instructions: line holds the prompt, then the guidance (You have a persistent memory: ...), then what RedactTokens says, then the workspace sentence.

What it means

The guidance is a str, so it is static, in the capabilities' list order. get_toolset() returns Memory's own toolset with list_memory added, never a new one: Memory's tools find the run's copy of the capability through it, and the agent asks for it on every memory tool call, hence the if.

docs.title: Step 2: Retrieve a note in a new session
docs.text:
Goal: run two sessions with no history between them, and see a note written in the first found in the second.

We'll prove that the notes survive without carrying conversation history forward. Create demos/notebook.py to run two separate sessions against the same notebook:

"""Two sessions with the chat's agent: one stores a note, the next finds it.

The notebook lives in the workspace, so run `demos/fresh_copy.py` first.
"""

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.stand_ins import remembers_then_recalls

chat = build_chat_agent(web_search=False, workspace_root=Settings().workspace_root)
model = remembers_then_recalls()
for prompt in ["Remember that we log to stderr.", "What did we decide about logging?"]:
    # No message_history: a new session, as far as the model can tell.
    print(f"session: {prompt}")
    result = chat.run_sync(user_prompt=prompt, model=model)
    print("  output", result.output)

The given stand-in writes a note when a prompt starts with "Remember", and otherwise looks one up:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/notebook.py

Tip

Check: you should see the output below (the version is a hash of the note, so it matches too), and cat work/tinyjobs/.agent-memory/main/logging.md prints the note.

session: Remember that we log to stderr.
request ['user-prompt']
call   write_memory {"content": "- Logging goes to stderr, so stdout stays pipeable.\n", "file": "logging.md"}
request ['tool-return']
result {"file":"logging.md","version":"9eb4a459b5f2bb5a0a1554df7230342c45d02c6c53231a4115be9b8d8a22a291","replayed":false,"status":"created"}
output Noted.
session: What did we decide about logging?
request ['user-prompt']
call   list_memory {}
request ['tool-return']
result {"files":["logging.md"],"truncated":false}
call   read_memory {"file": "logging.md"}
request ['tool-return']
result - Logging goes to stderr, so stdout stays pipeable.

output We decided: - Logging goes to stderr, so stdout stays pipeable.

What it means

The second session's first request is ['user-prompt']: the question and nothing else. With no history and no memory part, the note can reach the model only through a tool call, and it does: list_memory for the name, then read_memory. The note is .agent-memory/main/logging.md (main is Memory's agent_name; the model never sees it), and fresh_copy.py deletes it with the rest of the copy. A stand-in does what its script says: whether a real model writes a note, or looks, isn't shown.

docs.title: Step 3: Restrict file access to notes
docs.text:
Goal: deny the file tools the notebook's folder, and see two calls refused.

The notebook is in the workspace, so the chat's file tools reach it too. In a test run for this lesson, a write_file replaced the note outright, and the next write_memory appended to the file tool's text. The memory tools append and keep a record; a file tool does neither. So the notebook gets one owner. In chat/agent.py, put its folder in the file tools' deny list, next to the secrets:

        # The notebook is denied too, for reads and writes alike.
        FileSystem(denied_patterns=(*SECRET_PATTERNS, f"**/{NOTEBOOK}/**")),

and say so in NOTEBOOK's comment: "The file tools may not touch it: the memory tools are its only way in." Add two calls to CALLS in demos/file_tools.py, before the last: ("read_file", ".agent-memory/main/logging.md", {}) and ("write_file", ".agent-memory/main/logging.md", {"content": "mine\n"}).

uv run demos/file_tools.py

Tip

Check: the earlier calls print as before, then:

read_file .agent-memory/main/logging.md:
Path '.agent-memory/main/logging.md' is denied by pattern '**/.agent-memory/**'.
write_file .agent-memory/main/logging.md:
Path '.agent-memory/main/logging.md' is denied by pattern '**/.agent-memory/**'.

and cat of the note still prints it.

What it means

denied_patterns stops reads and writes alike; FileStore doesn't go through the file tools, so the memory tools are unaffected. It is a guard against mistakes, not a boundary: pytest runs any code it is given. In a real project the notebook belongs in .gitignore as .agent-memory/; here all of work/ is already there.

docs.title: Step 4: Compare memory injection
docs.text:
Goal: run a second agent on the same notebook with injection on, and see what the chat doesn't send.

Create demos/memory_injection.py:

"""What memory injection would send: the notebook beside every question.

A second agent reads the notebook `demos/notebook.py` left in the workspace, with
injection on.
"""

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import LocalWorkspace
from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelMessage
from pydantic_ai_harness import Memory
from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import FileStore

from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import NOTEBOOK
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.stand_ins import prints_every_message

# The chat's notebook; only `inject_memory` differs.
injecting: Agent[None, str] = Agent(
    capabilities=[
        LocalWorkspace(working_dir=Settings().workspace_root),
        Memory(store=FileStore(directory=NOTEBOOK), inject_memory=True),
    ],
)
model = prints_every_message()
history: list[ModelMessage] = []
for prompt in ["What does tinyjobs do?", "And how is it tested?"]:
    print(f"turn: {prompt}")
    result = injecting.run_sync(
        user_prompt=prompt, model=model, message_history=history
    )
    history = result.all_messages()

Run it on the same workspace, so logging.md is there:

uv run demos/memory_injection.py

Tip

Check: each line is one message of a request:

turn: What does tinyjobs do?
request: ['What does tinyjobs do?', '<memory> ### Other memory files - logging.md </memory>']
turn: And how is it tested?
request: ['What does tinyjobs do?']
response: ['ok']
request: ['And how is it tested?', '<memory> ### Other memory files - logging.md </memory>']

What it means

Every request carries the block, beside the newest question and only there: on turn two the first question has lost it. It lists "Other memory files": that is how this agent learns logging.md, and why it needs no list_memory. The moving is the cost: this request's start differs from the previous one's, though the notebook didn't change, so a provider's cache has less to reuse. The block is also cut to a budget, 2,000 tokens at four characters a token, shared with the guidance.

docs.title: Step 5: Try memory in real chats
docs.text:
Goal: see whether a real model saves a note and finds it again.

This step uses your API key, and the model decides what it does.

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Please remember that this project logs to stderr, so stdout stays pipeable.

End the chat with an empty line, then start it again and ask:

What did we decide about logging?

Tip

Check: the second chat starts with no history. If the model saved and looked up the note, work/activity.jsonl has a write_memory call from the first chat, and list_memory or read_memory from the second. A model may also choose not to use the notebook, and the log shows that too.

What it means

The note survived because it's in a file, not in the conversation. With injection off, using it is the model's choice, which is the trade-off from Concepts. Your activity log shows you which choice it made.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• Memory is a notebook the model reads and writes with tools. Kept in the workspace, it outlasts a run.
  • Injection sends the notebook beside every question. With it off, the model asks, and needs a tool to list the files.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The chat now has a prompt file, a capability of its own and a notebook. The next lesson brings build_chat_agent together in one place.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
This lesson is about agent settings and capability order. We'll separate the settings that define our agent from the capabilities that add behavior. Our chat now has tools, guards, an activity log, a prompt file, and a notebook. We'll separate constructor settings from capability behavior. Then we'll make the ordering requirements explicit.

By the end, you'll be able to:

  • Explain why some settings belong on Agent(...) and others in capabilities.
  • Make important ordering constraints explicit so adding another capability doesn't silently change behavior.

About 15 minutes. Steps 1 to 3 need no API key. Step 4 uses your OpenAI key.

docs.title: The constructor sets agent defaults
docs.text:
Capabilities can supply instructions, tools, a model, model settings, a workspace, and hooks. The Agent(...) constructor sets the agent's name, output type, and loop policy. Some of those choices can be overridden for a run.

We'll keep the agent's identity and defaults on the constructor, and put its tools and behavior in capabilities:

On the constructor In a capability Name, types, loop policy name, description, deps_type, output_type, retries, end_strategy, tool_timeout, max_concurrency No way to set them Instructions instructions get_instructions() Tools tools, toolsets get_toolset() Model settings model_settings get_model_settings() Model model get_model() A workspace, hooks at each stage No way to set them get_workspace(), before_model_request() and the rest

Some settings can appear in either place. In this project, capabilities supply what the model receives and what acts during a run. That lets us move related behavior between agents as one object. We'll keep ordinary request defaults, such as a timeout, on the constructor. The library's Capabilities page also shows model settings there. If both sides set the same setting, they merge key by key: a capability's value beats the constructor's, and a run's beats both.

docs.title: Capabilities can declare their order
docs.text:
Capability order matters. PromptFile supplies the chat's initial instructions, and the activity log needs to see every tool attempt. Rearranging the list could change either behavior.

A capability can say where it belongs instead, with get_ordering(). It returns a CapabilityOrdering, whose position is "outermost", first of all, or "innermost", last before the model. When the agent is made, it sorts its capabilities so that every declared place holds, and keeps your list's order for the rest; two that declare the same position share it, and list order decides between them. A Hooks object takes the same thing as ordering=. (CapabilityOrdering can also say that one capability wraps another: see "Ordering" on the Custom capabilities page.) The harness does this itself: its input guardrail declares innermost, so it checks the prompt as every other capability has left it.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: You split build_chat_agent into chat_capabilities(), the list of everything the chat does, and build_chat_agent(), whose constructor holds only what the agent is. Then demos/stack_order.py builds the agent with its list forwards and reversed, to show what the order changes, and PromptFile and the activity log declare their places.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Carry on in your pydantic-tutor project from the last lesson.

Tip

Check: run uv run demos/fresh_copy.py, then uv run demos/guard_check.py. Its log's last line is the refused pytest --version && cat .env.

Warning

Joining here, or has your project gone wrong? If your project works, skip this. To refresh a broken project, delete its folder first: you lose your work and anything else in it, including your .env and its API keys.

git clone --branch 04-07-memory/end --single-branch https://github.com/chrislomeli/pydanticai-tutorial-student.git pydantic-tutor
cd pydantic-tutor
uv sync

Then run the check above.

docs.title: Step 1: Separate settings from capabilities
docs.text:
Goal: turn build_chat_agent into two functions: one returns the chat's capabilities, one builds the agent from them.

We'll separate building the capability list from constructing the agent. The list stays the same, so this refactor should not change what the model receives.

In src/pydantic_tutor/chat/agent.py:

  • Add from collections.abc import Sequence and from pydantic_ai.settings import ModelSettings, and import AgentCapability from pydantic_ai.capabilities in place of AbstractCapability.
  • Rename build_chat_agent to chat_capabilities. It returns list[AgentCapability[None]], as does its capabilities variable, and its docstring is """Everything the chat does, as a list of capabilities, each one new.""". Its list stays as it is.
  • At the end of that function, replace return Agent(...) with return capabilities, and write build_chat_agent after it:
        capabilities.insert(0, activity_log)
    return capabilities


def build_chat_agent(
    *,
    web_search: bool,
    workspace_root: Path,
    activity_log: Hooks[None] | None = None,
    capabilities: Sequence[AgentCapability[None]] | None = None,
) -> Agent[None, str]:
    """Build the chat's agent: what it is here, what it does in `capabilities`.

    The constructor sets what no capability can. `capabilities` defaults to
    `chat_capabilities(...)`; pass another list to rearrange or extend the
    stack, and the other arguments are not used.
    """
    if capabilities is None:
        capabilities = chat_capabilities(
            web_search=web_search,
            workspace_root=workspace_root,
            activity_log=activity_log,
        )
    return Agent[None, str](
        name="chat",
        # The type the type checker holds every run to.
        output_type=str,
        # Each attempt at a request that takes longer fails; most hosted
        # models honour it, the given stand-in models do not.
        model_settings=ModelSettings(timeout=120),
        capabilities=capabilities,
    )

The chat_agent = build_chat_agent(...) line below doesn't change. Nothing the model is sent should change either:

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/guard_check.py
uv run python -c "from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import chat_agent as a; print(a.name, a.output_type, a.model_settings)"

Tip

Check: guard_check.py prints what it printed in Before you start. The second command prints:

chat <class 'str'> {'timeout': 120}

What it means

Nothing the model is sent changed: the capabilities are the same, in the same order. The constructor holds the agent's name and output type (output_type=str was the default; written out, it says what the agent is) and a request default, the one middle row this project's rule keeps there. The timeout is new, and is the library's: a model that honours it fails an attempt that takes longer than 120 seconds. The stand-in models here don't, so nothing in this lesson shows it working.

chat_capabilities() makes new objects on each call, so two agents built from it share no capability that holds state of its own, such as the notebook's. build_app and chat_agent call build_chat_agent as before, so neither changed.

docs.title: Step 2: Reverse the list
docs.text:
Goal: build the agent with its capabilities forwards and reversed, and see what the order changes.

Now we'll compare the normal list with its reverse. This shows which behaviors depend on a capability's position. It reuses the given model from the guards lesson, which also prints how each piece of its instructions starts.

Create demos/stack_order.py:

"""The chat's agent with its capabilities listed forwards, then reversed.

Needs no API key. It adds a `deploy.toml` with a fake token to the workspace copy;
run `demos/fresh_copy.py` first.
"""

from pydantic_ai.capabilities import AgentCapability

from pydantic_tutor.capabilities.activity_log import HookName, build_activity_hooks
from pydantic_tutor.chat.agent import build_chat_agent, chat_capabilities
from pydantic_tutor.settings import Settings
from tutor_given.stand_ins import reads_a_token_then_chains_a_command

settings = Settings()
ROOT = settings.workspace_root
LOG = settings.activity_log_path
(ROOT / "deploy.toml").write_text('runner_token = "tj-FAKE-0000-not-a-real-secret"\n')


def stack() -> list[AgentCapability[None]]:
    """The chat's capabilities, each one new."""
    return chat_capabilities(
        web_search=False,
        workspace_root=ROOT,
        activity_log=build_activity_hooks(
            path=LOG, hooks=frozenset({HookName.BEFORE_TOOL_EXECUTE})
        ),
    )


for label, capabilities in [("forwards", stack()), ("reversed", stack()[::-1])]:
    print(label)
    LOG.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    chat = build_chat_agent(
        web_search=False, workspace_root=ROOT, capabilities=capabilities
    )
    chat.run_sync(
        user_prompt="Check the deployment settings.",
        model=reads_a_token_then_chains_a_command(show_instructions=True),
    )
    print("  logged:", len(LOG.read_text().splitlines()), "tool calls")

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/stack_order.py

Tip

Check: ignoring any startup banner, you should see:

forwards
instructions: You are a helpful ...
instructions: You have a persistent ...
instructions: [token removed] in a ...
instructions: Your workspace holds the ...
model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "[token removed]"
model got, from run_command:
Run one command at a time, with no chaining.
logged: 2 tool calls
reversed
instructions: [token removed] in a ...
instructions: You have a persistent ...
instructions: You are a helpful ...
instructions: Your workspace holds the ...
model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "[token removed]"
model got, from run_command:
Run one command at a time, with no chaining.
logged: 1 tool calls

What it means

Two things differ, and they're the two facts the list's order was holding.

Reversed, the prompt isn't first: the notebook's guidance and RedactTokens's sentence reach the model ahead of it, because text is sent in list order. And the log records one tool call, not two, because it now sits after the guard, which refused the second before the log saw it. The workspace sentence stays last in both, because a toolset's instructions are sent after a capability's.

docs.title: Step 3: Set capability order
docs.text:
Goal: make PromptFile and the activity log declare their positions, so reversing the list no longer changes the behavior.

We'll give the prompt and activity log explicit positions so future edits don't depend on their list order.

In src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/prompt_file.py, import CapabilityOrdering beside AbstractCapability, and add a method to PromptFile, after get_instructions:

    def get_ordering(self) -> CapabilityOrdering:
        """Put this capability first, wherever it is listed."""
        # The prompt says what the agent is for, so it is the first text the
        # model is sent: of the instructions given as text, the agent sends
        # those of the outermost capability first.
        return CapabilityOrdering(position="outermost")

In src/pydantic_tutor/capabilities/activity_log.py, import CapabilityOrdering beside Hooks, and add one argument to the HooksNone that build_activity_hooks returns, after after_tool_execute:

        # Outermost, wherever it is listed: its `before_` hooks see every
        # attempt, and its `after_` hooks see the result the model gets.
        ordering=CapabilityOrdering(position="outermost"),

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/stack_order.py

Tip

Check: you should see:

forwards
instructions: You are a helpful ...
instructions: You have a persistent ...
instructions: [token removed] in a ...
instructions: Your workspace holds the ...
model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "[token removed]"
model got, from run_command:
Run one command at a time, with no chaining.
logged: 2 tool calls
reversed
instructions: You are a helpful ...
instructions: [token removed] in a ...
instructions: You have a persistent ...
instructions: Your workspace holds the ...
model got, from read_file:
[deploy.toml | 1 lines | hash:e3b623df92da]
1   runner_token = "[token removed]"
model got, from run_command:
Run one command at a time, with no chaining.
logged: 2 tool calls

What it means

The agent sorts its capabilities when it is made. PromptFile and the log declared outermost, so they go first whichever way the list runs: the prompt is the first text sent, and the log records both tool calls in both orders. Every other capability keeps its place from your list, which is why the guidance and RedactTokens's sentence still swap. Nothing relies on their order, so they don't declare one.

When something relies on a place, it belongs in a declaration, not a comment.

docs.title: Step 4: Inspect the finished chat
docs.text:
Goal: connect each thing the chat does to the part that brings it.

This step uses your API key, and the model decides what it does.

uv run demos/fresh_copy.py
uv run demos/show_capabilities.py
uv run python -m pydantic_tutor

Which module handles retries in this project? Save a note about it, then run the tests.

End the chat with an empty line, then open work/activity.jsonl.

Tip

Check: the log shows the tools the model chose, with a request between each round. Each tool came from a line that show_capabilities.py printed. Your calls will differ from anyone else's.

What it means

Everything the chat does beyond the model is in one list, and you can name what each entry brings. build_chat_agent itself says only what the agent is.

docs.title: What you can now do
docs.text:
• The constructor says what the agent is, and the list says what it does. You can put a choice on the right side.
  • A capability whose place matters declares it. The list can be rearranged and added to without breaking what relies on it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Chapter 4 is done: the agent is built from parts, and the list can grow. Next, the chat learns to ask you before it writes a file or runs a command.

Tested with pydantic-ai 2.56.0 and pydantic-ai-harness 0.56.0.
